cards.title: Angle between lines
points: tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|
Parallel: m₁ = m₂
Perpendicular: m₁m₂ = −1
Line ⊥ to ax + by + c = 0: bx − ay + k = 0

cards.title: Distances
points: Point (x₁, y₁) to ax + by + c = 0: |ax₁ + by₁ + c|/√(a² + b²)
Between parallel lines ax + by + c₁ = 0 and ax + by + c₂ = 0: |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²)

cards.title: Circle
points: Centre (h, k), radius r: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
General: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0
Centre (−g, −f); radius √(g² + f² − c)
Diameter ends A, B: (x − x₁)(x − x₂) + (y − y₁)(y − y₂) = 0

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: A line touches a circle exactly when its distance from the centre equals the radius. Use this instead of solving the two equations together — it turns a tangent question into one line of arithmetic.

cards.q: The slope of a line perpendicular to 3x − 4y + 5 = 0 is:
cards.explain: The given slope is −a/b = 3/4, so the perpendicular slope is −4/3.

cards.q: The distance between 3x + 4y − 5 = 0 and 3x + 4y + 10 = 0 is:
The centroid of the triangle with vertices (1, 2), (3, 4) and (5, 0) is:

notes.p:
Coordinate geometry turns figures into algebra. The **distance formula** comes from Pythagoras; the **section formula** finds the point dividing a segment in a given ratio.

**Example 1.** Find the point dividing the join of (2, 3) and (8, 9) internally in the ratio 1 : 2.
[(1 × 8 + 2 × 2)/3, (1 × 9 + 2 × 3)/3] = **(4, 5)**.

**Example 2.** Area of the triangle with vertices (1, 1), (4, 5), (7, 1).
½|1(5 − 1) + 4(1 − 1) + 7(1 − 5)| = ½|4 + 0 − 28| = **12** square units.

Choose the form that matches the data given.

**Example 3.** Find the line through (2, 3) and (4, 7).
Step 1: slope m = (7 − 3)/(4 − 2) = 2.
Step 2: y − 3 = 2(x − 2) ⇒ **y = 2x − 1**.
Step 3: Intercepts: x-intercept 1/2, y-intercept −1.

For ax + by + c = 0 the slope is −a/b, the x-intercept is −c/a and the y-intercept is −c/b. Lines parallel to the x-axis have the form y = k; lines parallel to the y-axis, x = k.

For slopes m₁ and m₂, **tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|**.

**Example 4.** Angle between y = x and y = √3x.
tan θ = |(√3 − 1)/(1 + √3)| = 2 − √3 = tan 15°, so θ = **15°**. (The lines make 45° and 60° with the x-axis.)

Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have m₁m₂ = −1. Three lines are concurrent when the determinant of their coefficients is zero.

The perpendicular distance from (x₁, y₁) to ax + by + c = 0 is |ax₁ + by₁ + c|/√(a² + b²).

**Example 5.** Distance of (2, 3) from 3x + 4y − 8 = 0 = |6 + 12 − 8|/5 = **2**.

The distance of the origin from the line is simply |c|/√(a² + b²). For two parallel lines, first make the x and y coefficients identical, then use |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²).

A **circle** is the set of points at a fixed distance r from a centre (h, k). In general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 the coefficients of x² and y² are equal and there is no xy term; the centre is (−g, −f) and r = √(g² + f² − c).

**Example 6.** For x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0, the centre is (2, −3) and r = 5.

A point P lies inside, on or outside the circle according as S(P) = x₁² + y₁² + 2gx₁ + 2fy₁ + c is negative, zero or positive. A line is a **tangent** when its distance from the centre equals r.
Revise before each mock.

Area = 0 ⇔ collinear

cards.title: What a conic is
cards.body: A **conic** is the path of a point whose distance from a fixed point (**focus**) is e times its distance from a fixed line (**directrix**). e is the **eccentricity**: e = 1 parabola, e < 1 ellipse, e > 1 hyperbola. A circle is the limiting case e = 0.

cards.title: Parabola y² = 4ax
points: Vertex (0, 0); focus (a, 0)
Directrix x = −a; axis y = 0
Latus rectum = 4a
x² = 4ay: focus (0, a), directrix y = −a

cards.title: Ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b)
points: b² = a²(1 − e²)
Foci (±ae, 0); directrices x = ±a/e
Major axis 2a, minor axis 2b
Latus rectum = 2b²/a
PS + PS′ = 2a

cards.title: Hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1
points: b² = a²(e² − 1)
Foci (±ae, 0); directrices x = ±a/e
Transverse axis 2a; latus rectum 2b²/a
|PS − PS′| = 2a
Rectangular hyperbola (a = b): e = √2

cards.title: Recognise the conic
cards.body: Only one variable squared → **parabola**. Both squared with the same sign and unequal coefficients → **ellipse**; equal coefficients → **circle**. Both squared with opposite signs → **hyperbola**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: If the larger denominator sits under y², the ellipse is vertical: swap the roles of x and y, and the foci move to (0, ±be). Check this before applying any formula.

cards.q: The focus of the parabola y² = 8x is:
cards.explain: 4a = 8 ⇒ a = 2, so the focus is (2, 0).

cards.q: The eccentricity of x²/16 − y²/9 = 1 is:
The eccentricity of a rectangular hyperbola is:
cards.explain: a = b, so e² = 1 + 1 = 2 and e = √2.

notes.p:
The circle, parabola, ellipse and hyperbola are called **conic sections** because each is cut from a double cone by a plane. In coordinate geometry they are defined by the **focus–directrix property**: PS = e × PM, where S is the focus, PM the distance to the directrix and e the eccentricity.

The **latus rectum** is the chord through a focus perpendicular to the major (or transverse) axis. The **axis** is the line of symmetry through the focus.

For **y² = 4ax** (a > 0) the parabola opens to the right, with focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a and latus rectum 4a. y² = −4ax opens left; x² = 4ay opens up; x² = −4ay opens down.

**Example 1.** For y² = 12x: 4a = 12 ⇒ a = 3. Focus (3, 0), directrix x = −3, latus rectum **12**.

**Example 2.** Find the parabola with focus (0, −2) and directrix y = 2.
The vertex is midway at (0, 0) and the parabola opens downward with a = 2, so **x² = −8y**.

For x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with a > b: b² = a²(1 − e²), foci (±ae, 0), latus rectum 2b²/a. The sum of distances from any point to the two foci is always **2a**.

**Example 3.** For x²/25 + y²/16 = 1: a = 5, b = 4, e = 3/5, foci (±3, 0), directrices x = ±25/3, latus rectum 32/5.

**Example 4.** 9x² + 4y² = 36. Divide by 36: x²/4 + y²/9 = 1. Here the larger denominator is under y², so the major axis is vertical with semi-major axis 3 and semi-minor axis 2. e = √(1 − 4/9) = **√5/3** and the foci are (0, ±√5).

For x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: b² = a²(e² − 1), foci (±ae, 0), latus rectum 2b²/a. The difference of focal distances is **2a**.

**Example 5.** For x²/16 − y²/9 = 1.
Step 1: a = 4, b = 3.
Step 2: e² = 1 + 9/16 = 25/16 ⇒ e = **5/4**.
Step 3: Foci (±5, 0); directrices x = ±16/5; latus rectum = 2 × 9/4 = 9/2.

When a = b the curve is a **rectangular hyperbola** (e = √2). xy = c² is also a rectangular hyperbola, rotated by 45°.
Keep the three standard forms side by side to avoid mixing up signs.
points: Circle: e = 0; x² + y² = r²
Parabola: e = 1; y² = 4ax; latus rectum 4a
Ellipse: e < 1; b² = a²(1 − e²); latus rectum 2b²/a
Hyperbola: e > 1; b² = a²(e² − 1); latus rectum 2b²/a
Ellipse: PS + PS′ = 2a; hyperbola: |PS − PS′| = 2a

notes.p: Revise before each mock.

cards.title: Points in space
points: Distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²]
Division m:n: [(mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), …] for each coordinate
Centroid of a triangle: average of the three vertices

cards.title: Direction cosines and ratios
cards.body: If a line makes angles α, β, γ with the axes, l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ are its **direction cosines**, and **l² + m² + n² = 1**. Any numbers a, b, c proportional to them are **direction ratios**; l = a/√(a² + b² + c²) and so on.

cards.title: Angle between two lines
points: cos θ = |a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂| / [√(a₁² + b₁² + c₁²) √(a₂² + b₂² + c₂²)]
Perpendicular: a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0
Parallel: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂
DRs of the line through two points: (x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁)

cards.title: Plane
points: General: ax + by + cz + d = 0; normal DRs (a, b, c)
Through (x₁, y₁, z₁) with normal (a, b, c): a(x − x₁) + b(y − y₁) + c(z − z₁) = 0
Intercept form: x/a + y/b + z/c = 1
Point–plane distance: |ax₁ + by₁ + cz₁ + d|/√(a² + b² + c²)
Angle between planes = angle between normals

cards.title: Line and sphere
points: Line: (x − x₁)/a = (y − y₁)/b = (z − z₁)/c
Sphere: (x − p)² + (y − q)² + (z − r)² = R²
General sphere: x² + y² + z² + 2ux + 2vy + 2wz + d = 0
Centre (−u, −v, −w); radius √(u² + v² + w² − d)

cards.title: Direction cosines
cards.body: A line has direction ratios 2, −1, 2. √(4 + 1 + 4) = 3, so the direction cosines are **(2/3, −1/3, 2/3)**. Check: 4/9 + 1/9 + 4/9 = 1.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: The x-axis has direction cosines (1, 0, 0), the y-axis (0, 1, 0) and the z-axis (0, 0, 1). The xy-plane is z = 0. Plugging these in quickly answers many "angle with an axis" questions.

cards.q: The distance of the origin from the plane 2x − y + 2z = 9 is:
A line makes 45° with the x-axis and 60° with the y-axis. The acute angle it makes with the z-axis is:
cards.explain: cos²45° + cos²60° + cos²γ = 1 ⇒ 1/2 + 1/4 + cos²γ = 1 ⇒ cos γ = 1/2, so γ = 60°.

cards.q: The radius of the sphere x² + y² + z² − 2x + 4y − 6z − 11 = 0 is:

notes.p:
Three mutually perpendicular axes give every point coordinates (x, y, z). The formulas are the 2D ones with a z-term added.

**Example 1.** Distance between (1, 2, 3) and (4, 6, 15).
√(3² + 4² + 12²) = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √169 = **13**.

The point on the x-axis is (x, 0, 0); a point in the yz-plane has x = 0. The distance of (x, y, z) from the x-axis is √(y² + z²).

The **direction cosines** l, m, n of a line satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1. **Direction ratios** are any multiples of them. To convert DRs (a, b, c) into DCs, divide each by √(a² + b² + c²).

**Example 2.** Find the DCs of the line through A(1, 2, 3) and B(3, 5, 9).
Step 1: DRs = (3 − 1, 5 − 2, 9 − 3) = (2, 3, 6).
Step 2: √(4 + 9 + 36) = 7.
Step 3: DCs = **(2/7, 3/7, 6/7)**.
Its equation is (x − 1)/2 = (y − 2)/3 = (z − 3)/6.

The angle between two lines uses the dot product of their DRs. The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals. The angle φ between a line (DRs a) and a plane (normal n) satisfies sin φ = |a · n|/(|a||n|).

**Example 3.** Angle between the planes 2x − y + z = 6 and x + y + 2z = 7.
Step 1: Normals (2, −1, 1) and (1, 1, 2); dot product = 2 − 1 + 2 = 3.
Step 2: Each normal has length √6, so cos θ = 3/6 = 1/2.
Step 3: θ = **60°**.

A plane is fixed by a point and a normal direction.

**Example 4.** Find the plane through (1, 2, 3) with normal DRs (2, −1, 4).
2(x − 1) − (y − 2) + 4(z − 3) = 0 ⇒ **2x − y + 4z − 12 = 0**.
Check with the point: 2 − 2 + 12 − 12 = 0 ✓.

In intercept form x/a + y/b + z/c = 1 the plane cuts the axes at a, b and c. The plane 2x + 3y + 6z = 12 becomes x/6 + y/4 + z/2 = 1. Parallel planes differ only in d, and the distance between ax + by + cz + d₁ = 0 and ax + by + cz + d₂ = 0 is |d₁ − d₂|/√(a² + b² + c²).

A **sphere** is the set of points at a fixed distance R from a centre. For x² + y² + z² + 2ux + 2vy + 2wz + d = 0 the centre is (−u, −v, −w) and R = √(u² + v² + w² − d).

**Example 5.** x² + y² + z² − 2x + 4y − 6z − 11 = 0 has centre (1, −2, 3) and radius √(1 + 4 + 9 + 11) = **5**.

The sphere with A and B as ends of a diameter is (x − x₁)(x − x₂) + (y − y₁)(y − y₂) + (z − z₁)(z − z₂) = 0.
Revise before each mock.

cards.title: Domain and range
cards.body: The **domain** is the set of inputs for which f is defined; the **range** is the set of outputs. Exclude values that make a denominator zero, an even root negative, or a log argument ≤ 0. f(x) = √(x − 2) has domain x ≥ 2; 1/(x − 3) has domain ℝ − {3}.

cards.title: Kinds of functions
points: One-one: f(a) = f(b) ⇒ a = b
Onto: range = codomain
Inverse exists only for a bijection (one-one + onto)
Composite: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)); usually f∘g ≠ g∘f
Even: f(−x) = f(x); odd: f(−x) = −f(x)

cards.title: Standard limits (x → 0)
points: sin x/x → 1; tan x/x → 1
(1 − cos x)/x² → 1/2
(xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → naⁿ⁻¹ as x → a

cards.title: When does a limit exist?
cards.body: lim x→a f(x) exists only if the **left-hand limit equals the right-hand limit**. For 0/0 forms, factorise, rationalise, or reduce to a standard limit. For x → ∞ with polynomials, divide by the highest power of x.

cards.title: Continuity
cards.body: f is **continuous at a** if lim x→a f(x) = f(a), i.e. LHL = RHL = f(a). Polynomials, sin, cos and eˣ are continuous everywhere; sums, products and quotients (denominator ≠ 0) of continuous functions are continuous. Every differentiable function is continuous, but not conversely.

cards.title: Making a function continuous
cards.body: f(x) = (sin 2x)/x for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = k. Continuity at 0 needs k = lim x→0 (sin 2x)/x = 2 × lim (sin 2x)/(2x) = **2**.

cards.q: The domain of f(x) = 1/√(4 − x²) is:
cards.explain: Need 4 − x² > 0 (strictly, since it is in the denominator), so −2 < x < 2.

cards.q: lim x→0 (1 − cos 2x)/x² equals:
cards.explain: 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin²x, so the limit is 2 × (sin x/x)² → 2.

cards.q: If f(x) = x² and g(x) = x + 1, then (f∘g)(2) equals:

notes.p:
A **function** f: A → B assigns exactly one element of B to each element of A. A is the domain, B the codomain, and the set of actual outputs is the range.

To find a domain, list the restrictions: denominators ≠ 0, expressions under even roots ≥ 0, log arguments > 0, and for sin⁻¹ or cos⁻¹ the input must lie in [−1, 1].

**Example 1.** f(x) = √(x − 1) + 1/(x − 3). Need x ≥ 1 and x ≠ 3, so the domain is **[1, 3) ∪ (3, ∞)**.

The range of x² + 1 is [1, ∞) because x² ≥ 0.

A function is **one-one** when different inputs give different outputs (a horizontal line meets the graph at most once) and **onto** when every element of the codomain is used. Only a **bijection** has an inverse.

**Example 2.** Find the inverse of f(x) = (2x + 3)/5.
Step 1: y = (2x + 3)/5 ⇒ 5y = 2x + 3.
Step 2: x = (5y − 3)/2, so **f⁻¹(x) = (5x − 3)/2**.

Other common functions: |x| (modulus), [x] (greatest integer ≤ x) and the signum function. x², cos x and |x| are **even**; x³ and sin x are **odd**.

A **limit** describes what f(x) approaches as x approaches a, not the value at a.

**Example 3.** lim x→0 [√(1 + x) − 1]/x. Rationalise: multiply top and bottom by √(1 + x) + 1 to get 1/[√(1 + x) + 1] → **1/2**.

**Example 4.** lim x→∞ (3x² + 2)/(5x² − x). Divide by x²: (3 + 2/x²)/(5 − 1/x) → **3/5**.

If the degree of the numerator is less than that of the denominator, the limit at ∞ is 0; if greater, it does not exist (finite).
Reshape the expression so that a standard form appears.
points: lim sin 5x/sin 3x = (5x/3x) × 1 = 5/3
lim (e³ˣ − 1)/x = 3 × lim (e³ˣ − 1)/(3x) = 3
lim tan x/x = 1 (x in radians)

notes.p:
f is continuous at a when **LHL = RHL = f(a)**. A jump, a hole or an infinite break makes it discontinuous.

**Example 5.** f(x) = x + 1 for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 3 − kx for x > 1. Find k for continuity at 1.
Step 1: LHL = f(1) = 2.
Step 2: RHL = 3 − k.
Step 3: 3 − k = 2 ⇒ **k = 1**.

|x| is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at 0 (a corner). [x] is discontinuous at every integer.
Revise before each mock.

Inverse exists only for a bijection
sin x/x → 1, (1 − cos x)/x² → 1/2, (eˣ − 1)/x → 1
(xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → naⁿ⁻¹
Limit exists ⇔ LHL = RHL
Continuous ⇔ LHL = RHL = f(a)
Differentiable ⇒ continuous, not conversely

cards.title: Derivatives to memorise
points: d(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹; d(eˣ) = eˣ; d(aˣ) = aˣ ln a; d(ln x) = 1/x
d(sin x) = cos x; d(cos x) = −sin x; d(tan x) = sec²x
d(sec x) = sec x tan x; d(cot x) = −cosec²x
d(sin⁻¹x) = 1/√(1 − x²); d(tan⁻¹x) = 1/(1 + x²)

cards.title: Rules of differentiation
points: Product: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
Quotient: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²
Chain: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) g′(x)
Parametric: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)
f w.r.t. g: (df/dx)/(dg/dx)

cards.title: What a derivative means
cards.body: Geometrically, f′(a) is the **slope of the tangent** at x = a; the normal has slope −1/f′(a). Physically, if s(t) is position, ds/dt is **velocity** and d²s/dt² is **acceleration**. Any dy/dx is a rate of change of y with x.

cards.title: Increasing and decreasing
cards.body: On an interval, f′(x) > 0 ⇒ f is **increasing**; f′(x) < 0 ⇒ f is **decreasing**. Points where f′(x) = 0 are critical points where the function may turn.

cards.title: Maxima and minima
cards.body: At a critical point c (f′(c) = 0): if **f″(c) < 0** there is a local **maximum**; if **f″(c) > 0** a local **minimum**. On a closed interval, compare these values with f at the end-points to get the absolute maximum or minimum.

cards.title: Logarithmic differentiation
cards.body: y = xˣ. Take logs: ln y = x ln x. Differentiate: (1/y) dy/dx = ln x + 1. So **dy/dx = xˣ(1 + ln x)**. Use logs whenever the variable appears in both base and exponent.

cards.q: The derivative of tan⁻¹x at x = 1 is:
cards.explain: d/dx tan⁻¹x = 1/(1 + x²) = 1/2 at x = 1.

cards.q: f(x) = x² − 4x + 5 is decreasing for:
cards.explain: f′(x) = 2x − 4 < 0 when x < 2.

cards.q: The slope of the tangent to y = x³ at x = 2 is:
cards.explain: dy/dx = 3x² = 12 at x = 2.

notes.p:
The **derivative** f′(a) = lim h→0 [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h measures the instantaneous rate of change. On a graph it is the slope of the tangent line at the point; in motion it is velocity. A function is **differentiable** at a point only if the left and right derivatives are equal — |x| fails this at 0.

The **second derivative** f″(x) is the rate of change of the slope. It tells whether the curve bends upward (f″ > 0) or downward (f″ < 0).

**Example 1 (quotient).** y = (x² + 1)/(x − 1).
dy/dx = [2x(x − 1) − (x² + 1)(1)]/(x − 1)² = **(x² − 2x − 1)/(x − 1)²**.

**Example 2 (chain).** y = sin(x³). dy/dx = cos(x³) × 3x² = **3x² cos(x³)**.

**Example 3 (parametric).** x = at², y = 2at. dx/dt = 2at, dy/dt = 2a, so dy/dx = **1/t**.

**Example 4 (one function w.r.t. another).** Differentiate sin x with respect to cos x: (cos x)/(−sin x) = **−cot x**.

In **implicit** differentiation, differentiate both sides and treat y as a function of x. For x² + y² = 25: 2x + 2y dy/dx = 0 ⇒ **dy/dx = −x/y**.

Use **logarithmic differentiation** for products of many factors or for variable powers such as xˣ, giving xˣ(1 + ln x).

**Second derivative:** for y = e²ˣ, y′ = 2e²ˣ and y″ = 4e²ˣ, so y″ − 4y = 0. NDA often asks which equation a given function satisfies — differentiate twice and compare.

**Example 5.** Tangent and normal to y = x² at (1, 1).
Step 1: slope = 2x = 2.
Step 2: tangent: y − 1 = 2(x − 1) ⇒ **y = 2x − 1**.
Step 3: normal slope −1/2: y − 1 = −½(x − 1) ⇒ **x + 2y = 3**.

**Example 6.** The radius of a circle grows at 2 cm/s. How fast does the area grow when r = 5 cm?
dA/dt = 2πr × dr/dt = 2π × 5 × 2 = **20π cm²/s**.

Steps: find f′, solve f′ = 0, then test the sign of f″ (or the sign change of f′).

**Example 7.** Two positive numbers add to 20. Maximise their product.
Step 1: P = x(20 − x) = 20x − x².
Step 2: P′ = 20 − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = 10.
Step 3: P″ = −2 < 0, so a maximum: **P = 100**.

The same idea proves that among rectangles of fixed perimeter the **square** has the largest area, and a quadratic ax² + bx + c has its turning point at x = −b/2a.
Revise before each mock.
points: Product, quotient and chain rules
Parametric: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)
Variable power: take logs first
Tangent slope f′(a); normal slope −1/f′(a)
f′ > 0 increasing; f′ < 0 decreasing
f′ = 0 and f″ < 0 ⇒ max; f″ > 0 ⇒ min
Rates: chain rule with d/dt

cards.title: Standard integrals
points: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1); ∫dx/x = ln|x| + C
∫eˣ dx = eˣ; ∫sin x dx = −cos x; ∫cos x dx = sin x
∫sec²x dx = tan x; ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹x
∫dx/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹x
∫sinh x dx = cosh x; ∫cosh x dx = sinh x

cards.title: Properties of definite integrals
points: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)
∫ₐᵇ f = −∫ᵦₐ f; ∫ₐᵇ f = ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫꜀ᵇ f
∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx
∫₋ₐᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f if f is even; 0 if f is odd

cards.title: Results worth remembering
points: ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx = π/4
∫₀^(π/2) sinⁿx dx = ∫₀^(π/2) cosⁿx dx
∫₀^π sin x dx = 2
∫₀¹ xⁿ dx = 1/(n + 1)

cards.title: Area as an integral
cards.body: The area between y = f(x), the x-axis and x = a, x = b is **∫ₐᵇ |f(x)| dx**. Parts below the axis give negative integrals, so split at the crossing points and add absolute values. Between two curves, area = ∫(upper − lower) dx.

cards.title: Standard areas
points: Circle x² + y² = r²: πr²
Ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1: πab
Between y² = 4ax and x² = 4ay: 16a²/3
Between y = x and y = x²: 1/6

cards.title: Area between y = x and y = x²
cards.body: They meet at x = 0 and x = 1, and x ≥ x² on [0, 1]. Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = **1/6**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Before integrating, check whether the limits are symmetric (−a to a) and whether the integrand is odd. An odd integrand gives 0 instantly — NDA sets this trap several times a paper.

cards.q: ∫₀^(π/2) cos x dx equals:
∫ from −π/2 to π/2 of sin³x dx equals:
cards.explain: sin³x is an odd function and the limits are symmetric, so the integral is 0.

cards.q: The area bounded by y = x², the x-axis and the line x = 3 is:
cards.explain: ∫₀³ x² dx = 27/3 = 9.

notes.p:
The **fundamental theorem of calculus** says that if F′ = f then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). The constant C cancels.

**Example 1.** ∫₁² (3x² + 2x) dx = [x³ + x²]₁² = (8 + 4) − (1 + 1) = **10**.

With substitution, change the limits too.
**Example 2.** ∫₀¹ 2x e^(x²) dx. Put t = x², dt = 2x dx; x = 0 → t = 0, x = 1 → t = 1. The integral becomes ∫₀¹ eᵗ dt = **e − 1**.
Beyond the basic table, three forms with a constant a appear often.
points: ∫dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C
∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C
∫dx/(x² − a²) = (1/2a) ln|(x − a)/(x + a)| + C
sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2, cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2; d(sinh x) = cosh x, d(cosh x) = sinh x
Integration by parts: ∫u v dx = u∫v dx − ∫[u′ ∫v dx] dx (choose u by ILATE)

notes.p:
**Example 3.** I = ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx.
Step 1: Replace x by π/2 − x: I = ∫₀^(π/2) cos x/(cos x + sin x) dx.
Step 2: Add the two forms: 2I = ∫₀^(π/2) 1 dx = π/2.
Step 3: **I = π/4**.

**Example 4.** ∫₀² |x − 1| dx. Split at x = 1: ∫₀¹ (1 − x) dx + ∫₁² (x − 1) dx = 1/2 + 1/2 = **1**.

For symmetric limits, even functions double and odd functions vanish: ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx = 0 and ∫₋₁¹ x² dx = 2/3.

Area is always positive, but an integral can be negative.

**Example 5.** Area bounded by y = sin x and the x-axis from 0 to 2π.
Step 1: ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2 (above the axis).
Step 2: ∫_π^(2π) sin x dx = −2 (below the axis).
Step 3: Area = 2 + |−2| = **4**, whereas the plain integral from 0 to 2π is 0.

For a region bounded by x = g(y) and the y-axis, integrate with respect to y instead.

Find the intersection points, decide which curve is on top, and integrate (upper − lower).

**Example 6.** Area between y² = 4x and x² = 4y.
Step 1: They meet where (x²/4)² = 4x ⇒ x⁴ = 64x ⇒ x = 0 or x = 4.
Step 2: On [0, 4], the upper curve is y = 2√x and the lower is y = x²/4.
Step 3: Area = ∫₀⁴ (2√x − x²/4) dx = [(4/3)x^(3/2) − x³/12]₀⁴ = 32/3 − 16/3 = **16/3**, matching 16a²/3 with a = 1.

The ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 encloses **πab**.
Revise before each mock.
points: ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a); change limits when substituting
∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx
Odd function, symmetric limits ⇒ 0
Split |f| or curves at crossing points
Area between curves = ∫(upper − lower)
Ellipse πab; y² = 4ax and x² = 4ay enclose 16a²/3
∫₀^π sin x dx = 2

cards.title: Order and degree
cards.body: **Order** = the highest derivative present. **Degree** = the power of that highest derivative once the equation is free of radicals and fractions in the derivatives. If a derivative sits inside sin, eˣ or log, the degree is **not defined**.

cards.title: Forming a differential equation
cards.body: A family of curves with n arbitrary constants gives a DE of **order n**. Differentiate n times and eliminate the constants. Example: y = mx (one constant) ⇒ dy/dx = y/x.

cards.title: General vs particular solution
cards.body: The **general solution** contains as many arbitrary constants as the order. A **particular solution** fixes the constants using given conditions such as y(0) = 1.

cards.title: Variable separable
points: Form: dy/dx = g(x) h(y)
Rewrite: dy/h(y) = g(x) dx
Integrate both sides and add one constant

cards.title: Homogeneous equations
points: Form: dy/dx = F(y/x)
Put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx
The equation becomes variable separable in v and x

cards.title: Linear first-order equations
points: Form: dy/dx + P(x) y = Q(x)
Integrating factor IF = e^(∫P dx)
Solution: y × IF = ∫Q × IF dx + C

cards.title: Growth and decay
cards.body: If a quantity changes at a rate proportional to itself, **dN/dt = kN**, so **N = N₀e^(kt)**. k > 0 means growth (population, compound interest); k < 0 means decay (radioactivity). Half-life T = ln 2/|k|.

cards.q: The order and degree of (d²y/dx²)² + (dy/dx)³ = x are:
cards.explain: The highest derivative is d²y/dx² (order 2), and it is raised to the power 2 (degree 2).

cards.q: The integrating factor of dy/dx + y/x = x² (x > 0) is:
cards.explain: P = 1/x, so IF = e^(∫dx/x) = e^(ln x) = x.

cards.q: The general solution of a third-order differential equation contains how many arbitrary constants?
cards.explain: The number of arbitrary constants equals the order, which is 3.

notes.p:
A **differential equation** (DE) links a function with its derivatives. Its **order** is the highest derivative that appears; its **degree** is the power of that derivative after the equation is made polynomial in all derivatives.

**Example 1.** d²y/dx² = √[1 + (dy/dx)²]. Square both sides: (d²y/dx²)² = 1 + (dy/dx)². **Order 2, degree 2.**

**Example 2.** d²y/dx² + sin(dy/dx) = 0. Order 2; the degree is **not defined**, because dy/dx appears inside sine.

Count the arbitrary constants, differentiate that many times and eliminate them.

**Example 3.** Form the DE of y = A cos x + B sin x.
Step 1: Two constants, so expect order 2.
Step 2: y′ = −A sin x + B cos x; y″ = −A cos x − B sin x = −y.
Step 3: **y″ + y = 0**.

For all circles through the origin with centres on the x-axis, x² + y² = 2ax has one constant, so the DE is of order 1.

Collect all y-terms with dy and all x-terms with dx, then integrate.

**Example 4.** Solve dy/dx = xy with y(0) = 2.
Step 1: dy/y = x dx.
Step 2: ln|y| = x²/2 + C ⇒ y = Ke^(x²/2).
Step 3: y(0) = 2 ⇒ K = 2. Particular solution: **y = 2e^(x²/2)**.

When every term has the same total degree in x and y, write dy/dx = F(y/x) and substitute y = vx.

**Example 5.** Solve dy/dx = (x + y)/x.
Step 1: dy/dx = 1 + y/x. Put y = vx: v + x dv/dx = 1 + v.
Step 2: x dv/dx = 1 ⇒ dv = dx/x ⇒ v = ln|x| + C.
Step 3: **y = x ln|x| + Cx**.

For dy/dx + Py = Q, multiply by IF = e^(∫P dx) so that the left side becomes d(y × IF)/dx.

**Example 6.** Solve dy/dx + y = eˣ.
Step 1: IF = eˣ.
Step 2: d(yeˣ)/dx = e²ˣ ⇒ yeˣ = e²ˣ/2 + C.
Step 3: **y = eˣ/2 + Ce⁻ˣ**.

**Example 7 (growth).** Bacteria double in 3 hours under dN/dt = kN. Then e^(3k) = 2, so after 9 hours N = N₀(e^(3k))³ = **8N₀**. Radioactive decay follows the same law with k < 0; after each half-life the amount halves.

**Example 8 (half-life).** A radioactive sample has a half-life of 10 years. After 30 years, three half-lives have passed, so (1/2)³ = **1/8** of the original amount remains.
Revise before each mock.
points: Order = highest derivative; degree = its power (polynomial form)
Derivative inside sin/log/exp ⇒ degree not defined
Constants in family = order of its DE
Separable: dy/h(y) = g(x) dx
Homogeneous: y = vx
Linear: IF = e^(∫P dx); y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C
dN/dt = kN ⇒ N = N₀e^(kt)

cards.title: Organising data
cards.body: **Raw data** becomes a **frequency distribution** when grouped into classes. Class mark = (lower + upper limit)/2. **Cumulative frequency** adds frequencies up to a class ("less than" type) or from a class onwards ("more than" type). Data may be discrete (counts) or continuous (measurements).

cards.title: Graphs of data
points: Histogram: adjacent bars for continuous classes; area ∝ frequency
Frequency polygon: join the mid-points of histogram tops
Ogive: cumulative frequency curve; the two ogives cross at the median
Pie chart: sector angle = (value/total) × 360°
Bar chart: separate bars for categories

cards.title: Grouped averages
points: Mean x̄ = Σfx/Σf
Median = l + [(N/2 − cf)/f] × h
Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h
Empirical: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean

cards.title: Dispersion
points: Variance σ² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n = Σx²/n − x̄²
SD σ = √variance
CV = (σ/x̄) × 100; lower CV = more consistent
Adding a constant: SD unchanged
Multiplying by k: SD × |k|, variance × k²

cards.title: Correlation and regression
points: r = cov(x, y)/(σₓσᵧ); −1 ≤ r ≤ 1
Regression of y on x: y − ȳ = bᵧₓ(x − x̄), bᵧₓ = r σᵧ/σₓ
r² = bᵧₓ × bₓᵧ; r has the sign of the coefficients
Both regression lines pass through (x̄, ȳ)

cards.title: Pie-chart angle
cards.body: A family spends ₹4,500 on food out of a total of ₹18,000. Sector angle = (4500/18000) × 360° = **90°**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For "which is more consistent", compare coefficients of variation, not standard deviations. For regression questions, solving the two line equations together gives the means directly.

cards.q: The standard deviation of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is:
cards.explain: Mean = 6; squared deviations 16, 4, 0, 4, 16 sum to 40; variance = 40/5 = 8; SD = √8 = 2√2.

cards.q: If bᵧₓ = 0.8 and bₓᵧ = 0.2, the correlation coefficient r is:
cards.explain: r² = 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.16, and both coefficients are positive, so r = 0.4.

cards.q: If every observation is multiplied by 3, the variance becomes:
cards.explain: Variance scales by k² = 9.

notes.p:
**Statistics** begins with collecting and classifying data. **Primary data** is collected first-hand; **secondary data** comes from existing records. Grouping data into **class intervals** (such as 0–10, 10–20, …) gives a **frequency distribution**. In the exclusive method, the upper limit belongs to the next class.

The **class mark** is the mid-point of a class, used as its representative value. **Cumulative frequency** of a class is the total frequency up to its upper limit; the last cumulative frequency equals N.
Each graph suits a different purpose.
points: Histogram — for continuous data; bars touch; with unequal class widths, plot frequency density
Frequency polygon — join mid-points of the bar tops, closing at both ends on the axis
Ogive — plot cumulative frequency against upper limits (less than) or lower limits (more than); their intersection gives the median
Pie chart — each sector angle = (item/total) × 360°
Bar diagram — for discrete categories, with gaps between bars

notes.p:
**Variance** is the mean of squared deviations from the mean; the **standard deviation** is its square root and has the same unit as the data.

**Example 2.** For 2, 4, 6, 8, 10: mean 6; Σ(x − x̄)² = 40; variance = 8; SD = 2√2 ≈ 2.83.

**Example 3 (comparison).** Batsman A: mean 50, SD 5 ⇒ CV = 10%. Batsman B: mean 40, SD 6 ⇒ CV = 15%. **A is more consistent** because his CV is lower.

Shifting all data by a constant does not change the SD; scaling by k multiplies the SD by |k|.

The **correlation coefficient** r measures the strength of a linear relationship: r = +1 perfect positive, r = −1 perfect negative, r = 0 no linear relation. **Regression** gives the best-fit line to predict one variable from the other.

**Example 4.** The regression lines are 3x + 2y = 26 and 6x + y = 31. Find x̄ and ȳ.
Step 1: From the second, y = 31 − 6x.
Step 2: 3x + 2(31 − 6x) = 26 ⇒ −9x = −36 ⇒ x = 4.
Step 3: y = 31 − 24 = 7. So **x̄ = 4, ȳ = 7**.

Also, r² = bᵧₓ × bₓᵧ, so both coefficients must have the same sign and their product cannot exceed 1.
Revise before each mock.
points: Class mark = (lower + upper)/2
Ogives meet at the median; pie angle = share × 360°
Median = l + [(N/2 − cf)/f] × h
Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean
σ² = Σx²/n − x̄²; CV = σ/x̄ × 100
Scaling by k: SD × |k|, variance × k²
r² = bᵧₓ bₓᵧ; regression lines meet at (x̄, ȳ)

cards.title: Language of probability
points: Sample space S: all possible outcomes
Mutually exclusive: cannot happen together (A ∩ B = φ)
Exhaustive: together cover S
Complement A′: "not A"
Impossible event P = 0; certain event P = 1

cards.title: Basic rules
points: Classical: P(A) = favourable/total (equally likely)
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
Mutually exclusive: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)

cards.title: Conditional probability
points: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), P(B) ≠ 0
P(A ∩ B) = P(B) P(A | B)
Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B)

cards.title: Bayes' theorem
cards.body: If E₁, E₂, … are exhaustive, mutually exclusive causes and A is observed:
points: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ) P(A | Eᵢ) (total probability)
P(Eᵢ | A) = P(Eᵢ) P(A | Eᵢ) / P(A)

cards.title: Random variables
cards.body: A **random variable** X assigns a number to each outcome, e.g. the number of heads in three tosses. Its probability distribution lists P(X = x) for each value; the probabilities add to 1. Mean E(X) = Σx P(x).

cards.title: Binomial distribution
points: n independent trials, each success with probability p (q = 1 − p)
P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ
Mean = np; variance = npq; variance < mean

cards.q: A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. P(A ∪ B) equals:
A binomial distribution has mean 4 and variance 3. The value of n is:
cards.explain: q = variance/mean = 3/4, so p = 1/4 and n = mean/p = 16.

cards.q: Two dice are thrown. The probability that the sum is 7 is:

notes.p:
A **random experiment** has well-defined outcomes but an unpredictable result. The set of outcomes is the **sample space**; an **event** is a subset of it. Tossing two coins gives S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.

An **elementary event** has one outcome; a **compound event** has several. Events are **mutually exclusive** if they cannot occur together and **exhaustive** if at least one must occur.

The **classical** definition P(A) = n(A)/n(S) needs equally likely outcomes. The **statistical** (empirical) definition uses the relative frequency of A over many trials.

**Example 1.** A card is drawn from a pack of 52. P(king or heart)?
P(K) = 4/52, P(H) = 13/52, P(K ∩ H) = 1/52.
P = (4 + 13 − 1)/52 = 16/52 = **4/13**.

**Example 2.** A die is thrown three times. P(at least one six)?
Use the complement: P(no six) = (5/6)³ = 125/216.
P(at least one six) = 1 − 125/216 = **91/216**.

"At least one" questions are almost always faster through the complement.

P(A | B) is the probability of A once B is known to have happened: it shrinks the sample space to B.

**Example 3.** A family has two children and at least one is a boy. P(both boys)?
The reduced sample space is {BB, BG, GB}, so P = **1/3** (not 1/2).

Events are **independent** when P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities can never be independent, because P(A ∩ B) = 0.

Bayes' theorem reverses a conditional probability: from P(effect | cause) it finds P(cause | effect).

**Example 4.** Bag I has 4 red and 6 black balls; Bag II has 7 red and 3 black. A bag is chosen at random and a red ball is drawn. Find P(Bag I | red).
Step 1: P(I) = P(II) = 1/2; P(R | I) = 0.4; P(R | II) = 0.7.
Step 2: P(R) = 0.5 × 0.4 + 0.5 × 0.7 = 0.55.
Step 3: P(I | R) = 0.2/0.55 = **4/11**.

notes.h: Random variables and the binomial distribution
notes.p:
A **binomial** experiment has a fixed number n of independent trials, two outcomes each, and the same success probability p. Then P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ, mean = np and variance = npq.

**Example 5.** A die is thrown 5 times. P(exactly two sixes)?
⁵C₂ (1/6)² (5/6)³ = 10 × 125/7776 = **625/3888** ≈ 0.16. The mean number of sixes is np = 5/6.

**Example 6.** Mean 4 and variance 3 ⇒ q = 3/4, p = 1/4, n = 16. If a question gives variance > mean, no binomial distribution fits.
Revise before each mock.
points: P(A′) = 1 − P(A); "at least one" via the complement
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B)
Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B)
Bayes: P(Eᵢ | A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A | Eᵢ)/ΣP(Eⱼ)P(A | Eⱼ)
Binomial: ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ; mean np; variance npq
Two dice: 36 outcomes; sum 7 is the most likely

chapters.title: Vectors: section formula, projection, work & moment

cards.title: Position vectors
points: AB⃗ = b − a (head minus tail)
Point dividing AB in m:n internally: (mb + na)/(m + n)
Mid-point: (a + b)/2; centroid: (a + b + c)/3
A, B, C collinear ⇔ AB⃗ = λ AC⃗

cards.title: Angle and projection
points: cos θ = a·b/(|a||b|)
Scalar projection of a on b = a·b/|b|
a ⊥ b ⇔ a·b = 0; a ∥ b ⇔ a × b = 0
i·i = 1, i·j = 0; i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j

cards.title: Work done by a force
cards.body: When a constant force F moves a particle through a displacement d, the **work done W = F·d**, a scalar. If several forces act, add them first. Work is zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement.

cards.title: Moment of a force
cards.body: The **moment (torque)** of force F about a point O is **M = r × F**, where r is the position vector from O to any point on the line of action. Its magnitude |r||F| sin θ equals force × perpendicular distance.

cards.title: Areas and volume
points: Parallelogram with sides a, b: |a × b|
Triangle ABC: ½|AB⃗ × AC⃗|
Parallelogram from diagonals d₁, d₂: ½|d₁ × d₂|
Parallelepiped volume: |[a b c]| = |a·(b × c)|

cards.title: Work done
cards.body: F = 2i + 3j + k moves a particle from (1, 1, 1) to (3, 2, 4). d = 2i + j + 3k, so W = 2×2 + 3×1 + 1×3 = **10 units**.

cards.q: The scalar projection of a = 2i + 3j + 2k on b = i + 2j + k is:
cards.explain: a·b = 2 + 6 + 2 = 10 and |b| = √6, so the projection is 10/√6.

cards.q: A force 3i + 4j moves a body through 2i − j. The work done is:
cards.explain: W = F·d = 6 − 4 = 2 units.

cards.q: If AB⃗ = 3i and AC⃗ = 4j, the area of triangle ABC is:
cards.explain: AB⃗ × AC⃗ = 12k, so area = ½ × 12 = 6.

notes.h: Position vectors and the section formula
notes.p:
Fix an origin O; the **position vector** of point A is a = OA⃗. Then AB⃗ = b − a. The point dividing AB internally in m : n has position vector **(mb + na)/(m + n)**.

**Example 1.** A(1, 2, 3), B(4, 5, 6). Find the point dividing AB in 1 : 2.
(1 × b + 2 × a)/3 = [(4 + 2)/3, (5 + 4)/3, (6 + 6)/3] = **(2, 3, 4)**.

**Example 2.** Are A(1, 2, 3), B(2, 3, 4), C(3, 4, 5) collinear? AB⃗ = (1, 1, 1) and AC⃗ = (2, 2, 2) = 2AB⃗, so **yes**.

The dot product gives both the angle between vectors and the projection of one on another.

**Example 3.** Angle between i + j and j + k.
Dot product = 1; each has magnitude √2; cos θ = 1/2, so θ = **60°**.

The **scalar projection** of a on b is a·b/|b| — the length of a's shadow along b. The **vector projection** is (a·b/|b|²) b. Projection of 2i + 3j + 2k on i + 2j + k is 10/√6.

Work is the dot product of force and displacement. Only the component of force along the motion does work.

**Example 4.** Forces F₁ = 2i + j and F₂ = i − j + 3k act together on a particle that moves from A(0, 0, 0) to B(1, 2, 1).
Step 1: Resultant F = 3i + 0j + 3k.
Step 2: d = i + 2j + k.
Step 3: W = 3 + 0 + 3 = **6 units**.

For a body moving in a circle under a centripetal force, F ⊥ d at each instant, so no work is done.

The **moment of F about O** is M = r × F, a vector perpendicular to both r and F. Its magnitude is F × (perpendicular distance of O from the line of action).

About a point P with position vector p, use (r − p) × F. For F = i + 2j − k at r = 2i + j + k, the moment about the origin is −3i + 3j + 3k, of magnitude √27 = 3√3.

A **couple** (two equal, opposite, parallel forces) has the same moment about every point.

**Example 5.** Area of triangle with A(1, 1, 1), B(1, 2, 3), C(2, 3, 1).
Step 1: AB⃗ = (0, 1, 2), AC⃗ = (1, 2, 0).
Step 2: AB⃗ × AC⃗ = i(0 − 4) − j(0 − 2) + k(0 − 1) = (−4, 2, −1).
Step 3: Magnitude √(16 + 4 + 1) = √21, so area = **√21/2**.

The volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c is |a·(b × c)|. For i, j, k it is 1; when it is 0 the three vectors are **coplanar**.
Revise before each mock.
points: AB⃗ = b − a; section point (mb + na)/(m + n)
Collinear ⇔ AB⃗ = λAC⃗
Projection of a on b = a·b/|b|
Work W = F·d (add forces first)
Moment M = r × F; |M| = F × perpendicular distance
Triangle area ½|AB⃗ × AC⃗|

chapters.title: Matrices: types, algebra & systems of equations

cards.title: Types of matrices
points: Row (1 × n), column (m × 1), square (n × n)
Diagonal: all off-diagonal entries 0
Scalar: diagonal with equal entries; identity I: all diagonal entries 1
Zero matrix O; upper/lower triangular

cards.title: Special square matrices
points: Symmetric: Aᵀ = A; skew-symmetric: Aᵀ = −A (diagonal entries 0)
Orthogonal: AAᵀ = I
Idempotent: A² = A; involutory: A² = I
Nilpotent: Aᵏ = O for some k
Singular: |A| = 0

cards.title: Rules of matrix algebra
points: A (m × n) × B (n × p) = AB (m × p)
In general AB ≠ BA
(AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ; (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹
A(adj A) = |A| I; A⁻¹ = adj A/|A|

cards.title: Symmetric + skew-symmetric
cards.body: Every square matrix A can be written uniquely as **½(A + Aᵀ) + ½(A − Aᵀ)**: the first part is symmetric and the second is skew-symmetric.

cards.title: Matrix method for AX = B
points: If |A| ≠ 0: unique solution X = A⁻¹B
If |A| = 0 and (adj A)B ≠ O: no solution
If |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = O: infinitely many or none — check the equations
Homogeneous AX = O has a non-trivial solution ⇔ |A| = 0

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Check the order before multiplying: inner numbers must match and outer numbers give the answer. Many options in NDA are "not defined" — that is the correct choice when the inner orders differ.

cards.q: If A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 4, the order of AB is:
The diagonal elements of a skew-symmetric matrix are:
cards.explain: aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ ⇒ aᵢᵢ = 0.

cards.q: For AX = B, if |A| = 0 and (adj A)B ≠ O, the system has:
cards.explain: This is the test for an inconsistent system: no solution.

notes.p: A **matrix** is a rectangular array of numbers; an m × n matrix has m rows and n columns and mn entries.
points: Square matrix: m = n; its principal diagonal runs top-left to bottom-right
Diagonal, scalar and identity matrices are special square matrices
Upper triangular: all entries below the diagonal are 0
Trace = sum of diagonal entries
Two matrices are equal only if they have the same order and equal corresponding entries

notes.p:
Matrices of the same order add entry by entry. The product AB exists only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B; the (i, j) entry is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.

**Example 1.** A = [1 2; 3 4], B = [2 0; 1 3].
AB = [1·2 + 2·1, 1·0 + 2·3; 3·2 + 4·1, 3·0 + 4·3] = **[4 6; 10 12]**.
BA = [2 4; 10 14]. So AB ≠ BA: matrix multiplication is **not commutative**, although it is associative.

**Example 2.** Write A = [1 3; 5 2] as symmetric + skew-symmetric.
Step 1: Aᵀ = [1 5; 3 2].
Step 2: P = ½(A + Aᵀ) = [1 4; 4 2] (symmetric).
Step 3: Q = ½(A − Aᵀ) = [0 −1; 1 0] (skew-symmetric).
Check: P + Q = A ✓.

The rotation matrix [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ] is **orthogonal**: its transpose is its inverse and its determinant is 1. The identity matrix is both idempotent and involutory.

notes.h: Solving equations by the matrix method
notes.p:
Write the system as AX = B, where A holds the coefficients. If |A| ≠ 0, X = A⁻¹B.

**Example 3.** x + y = 5 and x − y = 1.
Step 1: |A| = (1)(−1) − (1)(1) = −2 ≠ 0, so the solution is unique.
Step 2: A⁻¹ = (1/−2)[−1 −1; −1 1] = [½ ½; ½ −½].
Step 3: X = A⁻¹[5; 1] = [3; 2], so **x = 3, y = 2**.

For 3 × 3 systems, either find A⁻¹ through the adjoint or use **Cramer's rule** x = Δ₁/Δ, y = Δ₂/Δ, z = Δ₃/Δ.

A system is **consistent** if it has at least one solution.

**Example 4.** For which k do x + 2y = 3 and 2x + ky = 6 have infinitely many solutions?
Step 1: |A| = k − 4 = 0 ⇒ k = 4.
Step 2: With k = 4 the second equation is twice the first, so there are **infinitely many** solutions.
By contrast, x + 2y = 3 and 2x + 4y = 7 have |A| = 0 but contradict each other: **no solution**.

A homogeneous system AX = O always has the trivial solution X = O; it has other solutions only when |A| = 0.
Revise before each mock.
points: (m × n)(n × p) = m × p; AB ≠ BA in general
(AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ; (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹
Skew-symmetric ⇒ zero diagonal
A = ½(A + Aᵀ) + ½(A − Aᵀ)
Orthogonal: AAᵀ = I; idempotent: A² = A
|A| ≠ 0 ⇒ unique solution X = A⁻¹B
Homogeneous non-trivial ⇔ |A| = 0

cards.title: What NDA English tests
cards.body: Part A of the GAT paper has 50 English questions worth 200 marks — a third of the GAT total. Typical areas: spotting errors, sentence improvement, synonyms, antonyms, ordering of words/sentences, cloze test and comprehension.

cards.title: Subject-verb agreement
cards.body: The verb agrees with the real subject, not with the noun closest to it.
points: 'Each', 'every', 'either', 'neither' take a singular verb
'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb
Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb
With 'neither…nor' / 'either…or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject

cards.title: Tenses and time markers
cards.body: Words like 'since', 'for', 'yesterday', 'already' fix the tense. Use the past simple with a definite past time ('I met him **yesterday**'), not the present perfect. 'Since' marks a point in time (since 2020); 'for' marks a duration (for two years).

cards.title: Articles and prepositions
cards.body: Use 'an' before a vowel **sound** (an hour, an MBA) and 'a' before a consonant sound (a university, a one-rupee coin). Common preposition traps: 'married **to**', 'senior **to**', 'prefer X **to** Y', 'discuss the matter' (no 'about').

cards.title: Spotting the error
cards.body: 'Each of the cadets (A) / have completed (B) / the drill (C) / No error (D).' The subject is 'Each', which is singular, so 'have' should be 'has'. Answer: **(B)**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Read the full sentence once for meaning, then check: subject-verb, tense, article, preposition, pronoun — in that order. If nothing is wrong after this 5-point check, mark 'No error' with confidence.

cards.q: Choose the correct option: 'One of my friends ___ a pilot.'
cards.explain: 'One of + plural noun' takes a singular verb: 'One of my friends is a pilot.'

cards.q: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He is more senior than me.
cards.explain: Latin comparatives like senior, junior, superior, prefer take 'to', not 'than'.

cards.q: Fill in the blank: 'She has been living here ___ 2019.'
cards.explain: 'Since' is used with a point in time; 'for' is used with a duration.

notes.p:
In **error spotting**, a sentence is split into parts (a), (b), (c) and an option (d) "No error". You must find the part with the grammatical mistake. In **sentence improvement**, a part is underlined and you choose the better replacement or "No improvement".

The trick is to have a checklist. Read the whole sentence once for meaning, then test it rule by rule: subject–verb agreement, tense, pronoun, article, preposition, modifier, comparison and parallel structure. Most UPSC errors fall into these eight boxes.
A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. The trap is the words placed in between.
points: 'The quality of the mangoes **was** good' — the subject is 'quality', not 'mangoes'
'Each', 'every', 'either', 'neither', 'everyone' take singular verbs: 'Each of the boys **has** a book'
'Along with', 'as well as', 'together with' do not change the subject: 'The captain, along with his players, **was** present'
With 'either…or' / 'neither…nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'Neither the teacher nor the students **were** late'
'The number of' is singular; 'A number of' is plural

notes.p:
**Tenses.** Use the past perfect for the earlier of two past actions: "The train **had left** before we reached." Don't use "will" in the 'if' or 'when' clause of a future condition: "If it **rains**, we will stay home" (not "if it will rain"). "Since" is used with a point of time and needs the perfect tense: "I **have lived** here since 2020."

**Pronouns.** After "than" or "as", complete the clause mentally: "He is taller than **I** (am)." After prepositions use the object form: "between you and **me**." "One" is followed by "one's": "One should do **one's** duty."

**Articles.** "A" or "an" depends on the **sound**, not the letter: **an** hour, **an** MBA, **a** university, **a** one-rupee coin. Use "the" with superlatives, unique objects (the sun), rivers, oceans and mountain ranges (the Ganga, the Himalayas), but not with single mountain peaks (Mount Everest).

**Prepositions** are tested through fixed pairs. Learn them as phrases: "**senior to**", "**junior to**", "**prefer** tea **to** coffee", "**married to**", "**comply with**", "**invest in**", "**discuss** the matter" (no 'about'), "**accompanied by**".

**Comparisons.** Don't use double comparatives ("more better"). With "superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior", use "to", not "than". Compare like with like: "The climate of Shimla is better than **that of** Delhi."

**Modifiers.** A describing phrase must sit next to what it describes. "Walking in the park, a snake bit him" wrongly suggests the snake was walking; correct it to "While he was walking in the park, a snake bit him."

**Parallelism.** Items in a list must have the same form: "She likes **reading, writing and painting**," not "reading, writing and to paint."

**Example 1.** "Neither of the two candidates (a) / are suitable (b) / for the post. (c) / No error (d)"
Answer: (b). "Neither of" takes a singular verb: "is suitable".

**Example 2.** "He has been working here (a) / since five years (b) / and wants a transfer. (c) / No error (d)"
Answer: (b). For a period of time use "for": "for five years".

**Example 3.** Improve: "Hardly had he reached the station **than the train left**."
Answer: "when the train left". "Hardly/scarcely" pairs with "when"; "no sooner" pairs with "than".

Spend no more than 45 seconds on each question. If two parts look doubtful, check the verb first — subject–verb agreement is the single most common error. Don't choose "No error" just because you are unsure; but don't avoid it either — it is sometimes the correct answer. Remember that NDA has negative marking (one-third of the marks for that question), so skip genuine guesses.

Build accuracy by reading one well-edited English newspaper daily and noting sentences that use tricky structures. Wren & Martin's exercises remain excellent practice.
Revise these rules before every English mock.
points: Find the real subject; ignore phrases in between
Each/every/either/neither → singular verb
Since + point of time; for + period of time
No sooner…than; hardly/scarcely…when
a/an depends on sound: an hour, a university
Senior/junior/prefer/superior + to
Keep lists parallel; place modifiers next to what they describe

cards.title: Building vocabulary smartly
cards.body: Synonym/antonym questions are direct marks. Learn words in clusters (e.g. generous: benevolent, magnanimous, liberal) and their opposites together. Roots help: 'bene' = good, 'mal' = bad, 'chron' = time, 'phil' = love.

cards.title: Cloze test strategy
cards.body: Read the whole passage first to catch its tone and tense. Then fill each blank by checking grammar (part of speech, tense, preposition) and meaning together. The answer must fit both the sentence and the passage.

cards.title: Reading comprehension
cards.body: Read the questions first, then the passage. Answers must come **from the passage**, not your general knowledge. Watch for extreme words like 'always', 'never', 'only' in options — they are usually wrong.
points: Main idea questions: look at the first and last lines
Inference questions: choose what the author implies, not what you assume

cards.title: Ordering of sentences (PQRS)
cards.body: Find the opening sentence (introduces the subject, has no pronoun pointing back). Then link pairs using pronouns, connectors (however, therefore) and time order. Eliminating options with a fixed pair is faster than building the whole order.

cards.title: Using roots
cards.body: 'Benevolent': bene (good) + volent (wishing) = kind and generous. Its antonym is **malevolent** (mal = bad), meaning wishing harm. One root can unlock several words: benefactor, benefit, malice, malfunction.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Read one English editorial a day and note 5 new words with a sentence each. Revise the list weekly. Over 6 months this gives you a few hundred active words — enough for most NDA vocabulary questions.

cards.q: Choose the synonym of 'Candid':
cards.explain: Candid means open and honest — 'frank'.

cards.q: Choose the antonym of 'Benevolent':
cards.explain: Benevolent (well-wishing) is the opposite of malevolent (wishing harm).

cards.q: In a comprehension question, the best answer is the one that:
cards.explain: Comprehension answers must be backed by the text, not by outside knowledge or opinion.

notes.p:
NDA English tests vocabulary through **synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutions, idioms, cloze tests and reading comprehension**. Memorising long word lists without context rarely works. Instead, learn words in families using **roots**, and always write one sentence of your own with every new word.

A notebook with 10 new words a day, revised every Sunday, gives you more than 1,000 words before the exam.
points: bene = good: benefit, benevolent, benefactor
mal = bad: malice, malnutrition, malpractice
chron = time: chronic, chronology, synchronise
phil = love: philanthropy, philosophy; mis = hate: misanthrope
omni = all: omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent
graph/scrib = write: biography, inscribe, manuscript

notes.h: Synonyms, antonyms and the elimination method
notes.p:
In synonym and antonym questions, first decide whether the given word is **positive or negative** in tone. This alone often removes two options. Then look for the option with the closest meaning in the **same part of speech**.

**Example 1.** Synonym of "candid": (a) secretive (b) frank (c) clever (d) rude.
Step 1: "Candid" means honest and open — a positive, truthful word.
Step 2: Secretive is the opposite; clever and rude don't fit. Answer: **(b) frank**.

**Example 2.** Antonym of "frugal": (a) thrifty (b) careful (c) extravagant (d) poor.
Step 1: Frugal = careful with money.
Step 2: Thrifty is a synonym; the opposite is **(c) extravagant**.

Trap: options often include a synonym in an antonym question — read the instruction twice.
Idioms have meanings different from their literal words, so they must be learned as units. Some frequently tested ones:
points: To burn the midnight oil — to study or work late into the night
A bolt from the blue — a complete surprise
To bell the cat — to take on a risky task for the group
To be at one's wits' end — completely puzzled, not knowing what to do
To turn over a new leaf — to change one's behaviour for the better
To pay through the nose — to pay too much
To hit the nail on the head — to be exactly right

notes.p:
A **cloze test** is a passage with blanks. Read the entire passage once before filling anything — the theme and tense become clear. Then fill blanks using three checks: (1) grammar — does the word fit the tense, number and part of speech? (2) collocation — do the words naturally go together ("heavy rain", "make a decision")? (3) meaning — does it match the passage's tone?

**Example:** "Despite his injury, the soldier ___ to complete the march." Options: refused / continued / managed / stopped. "Despite" signals contrast, so the soldier did something positive; "managed to complete" is the natural collocation. Answer: **managed**.
NDA passages are usually short and factual. A reliable approach:
points: Read the questions first to know what to look for
Read the passage once, noting the main idea of each paragraph in a word or two
Answer from the passage only — not from your own general knowledge
Beware options with extreme words like 'always', 'never', 'all' — they are often wrong
For 'main idea' or 'best title' questions, pick the option that covers the whole passage, not one detail

notes.p: Five minutes with this list before the paper helps.
points: Learn words by roots and use each in a sentence
Check the tone (positive/negative) first in synonym/antonym questions
Read the instruction: synonym or antonym?
Idioms must be learned as fixed units
Cloze: grammar → collocation → meaning
RC: answer only from the passage; avoid extreme options
Revise your word notebook every week

cards.title: How the question works
cards.body: A sentence is split into three parts (a), (b), (c), with (d) "No error". At most one part is wrong. The error is usually grammatical — agreement, tense, pronoun, preposition, comparison or a redundant word — not spelling or punctuation.

cards.title: Noun and pronoun traps
points: Uncountable nouns have no plural: information, advice, furniture, luggage, scenery, equipment
"Between you and **me**" — pronouns after prepositions take the object case
"One should keep **one's** word"
"Each/every/either/neither" take singular verbs and pronouns

cards.title: Verb and tense traps
points: "No sooner … **than**"; "Hardly/Scarcely … **when**"
"If I **were** you" for imagined situations
"It is high time we **left**" (past form)
"Lest" is followed by "should" or the base verb, never "not"
Do not use "since" with a period: "for two years", "since 2020"

cards.title: Adjective and adverb traps
points: "Senior/junior/superior/inferior/prefer" take **to**, not "than"
No double comparatives: "more better" ✗
"Elder" for family members; "older" for general age
"He is the **tallest** of all" (superlative needs "of all", not "than all")

cards.title: Prepositions and redundancy
points: No preposition after discuss, resemble, attack, order: "discuss the plan"
Redundant pairs: return back, repeat again, revert back, final conclusion
"Both … and", "not only … but also", "though … yet" are fixed pairs
"Cope **with**", "comply **with**", "abide **by**"

cards.title: Spot it
cards.body: "Each of the students (a)/ have been given (b)/ a new textbook. (c)/ No error (d)". The subject is "each" (singular), so (b) should read **"has been given"**. Answer: (b).

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use a fixed checklist: subject–verb, tense, pronoun, preposition, comparison, redundancy. Choose "No error" only after the full checklist finds nothing — but do choose it; it is the correct answer in a fair share of questions.

cards.q: Find the error: "The committee discussed (a)/ the proposal at length (b)/ and returned it back to the author. (c)/ No error (d)"
cards.explain: "Returned back" is redundant; "returned it to the author" is correct.

cards.q: Find the error: "No sooner had he reached the station (a)/ when the train (b)/ started moving. (c)/ No error (d)"
cards.explain: "No sooner" pairs with "than": "than the train started moving".

cards.q: Find the error: "The scenery of Kashmir (a)/ is very beautiful (b)/ in spring. (c)/ No error (d)"
cards.explain: "Scenery" is uncountable and singular, so "is" is correct. There is no error.

notes.p:
Error-spotting is the single largest block of English questions in many NDA papers. Each sentence is divided into parts and you must pick the part containing the mistake, or "No error". There is never more than one error.

Read the **whole sentence** first. Many errors are only visible from another part — a plural verb in (b) may be wrong because of a singular subject in (a). Then run the checklist below in the same order every time so that it becomes automatic.
These rules cover a large share of noun and pronoun errors.
points: Uncountable nouns (advice, information, furniture, luggage, scenery, machinery, news) take singular verbs and no "a/an": "a piece of advice"
Some nouns are always plural: scissors, trousers, spectacles, cattle, police
Pronoun case: "between you and me", "He is taller than I (am)"
"Who" is a subject, "whom" an object: "the man whom we met"
"Each of", "one of", "every one of" take singular verbs: "One of my friends **is** a pilot"

notes.p: Tense errors are the most common trap after agreement.
points: Past perfect for the earlier of two past actions: "The train **had left** before I reached"
"No sooner had … than"; "Hardly had … when"
Unreal present: "If I **were** rich"; "I wish I **knew**"
"It is time / high time" + past tense
Present perfect continuous with "for/since": "I **have been living** here since 2019"
Do not use the continuous form with stative verbs: "I **know**", not "I am knowing"

notes.p: Comparison words and degree rules are tested every year.
points: Latin comparatives take "to": senior to, junior to, superior to, inferior to, prior to, prefer to
No double comparison: "more better", "most cleverest" ✗
Compare like with like: "The climate of Shimla is better than **that of** Delhi"
"Few" (hardly any) vs "a few" (some); "little" vs "a little" for uncountables
Adverbs modify verbs: "She sings **beautifully**", but linking verbs take adjectives: "The rose smells **sweet**"

notes.p:
**Example 1.** "Neither the captain (a)/ nor his players (b)/ was present at the meeting. (c)/ No error (d)".
Step 1: With "neither … nor", the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "players" (plural).
Step 2: "was" should be "were". **Answer: (c).**

**Example 2.** "He is senior (a)/ than me (b)/ by two years. (c)/ No error (d)".
"Senior" takes "to": "senior to me". **Answer: (b).**

**Example 3.** "Let us discuss about (a)/ the plan before (b)/ we leave. (c)/ No error (d)".
"Discuss" takes no preposition. **Answer: (a).**

Aim to spend about 30–40 seconds on each sentence. If two parts both look doubtful, return to the subject and the main verb — agreement errors are the most frequent. Avoid choosing a part just because it "sounds informal"; the test is grammar, not style. Mark questions you are unsure of and revisit them only after finishing the section, since negative marking applies.
Revise these rules before each mock.
points: Uncountables: advice, information, luggage, scenery — no plural
Between you and **me**; one … one's
No sooner … than; hardly … when
Senior/superior/prefer … **to**
No double comparatives; compare like with like
Remove redundancy: return back, repeat again
Neither … nor: verb follows the nearer subject

cards.title: How the question works
cards.body: A part of the sentence is in **bold** or underlined. You choose the option that improves it, or "No improvement" if it is already correct. Unlike error-spotting, you must also recognise the **right replacement**, so knowing correct idioms matters.

cards.title: Sequence of tenses
cards.body: A past reporting verb usually pushes the reported verb into the past: "He said that he **would** come" (not "will"). Universal truths stay in the present: "The teacher said that the Earth **revolves** round the Sun".

cards.title: Fixed verb patterns
points: look forward to / be used to / object to + **-ing**
would rather / had better + **base verb**
make / let / help + object + **base verb**
used to + base verb (past habit)

cards.title: Conditionals
points: Zero: If + present, present (facts)
First: If + present, will + base verb
Second: If + past, would + base verb
Third: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle

cards.title: Parallelism and modifiers
cards.body: Items joined by "and", "or", "not only … but also" must share one form: "She likes reading, writing and **swimming**". A modifier must sit next to what it describes: "Walking down the road, **I saw** a tree fall", not "a tree fell".

cards.title: Improve it
cards.body: "If he **had worked** harder, he **will pass** the exam." The if-clause is third conditional, so the main clause needs "would have passed". Improved: "If he had worked harder, he **would have passed** the exam."

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Reject any option that changes the meaning or adds new grammar errors. Between two correct options, prefer the shorter one. Pick "No improvement" only when you can say exactly why the original is right.

cards.q: Improve: "I look forward **to meet you** next week."
cards.explain: "Look forward to" is followed by the -ing form: "to meeting you".

cards.q: Improve: "You **had better to consult** a doctor."
cards.explain: "Had better" takes the base verb without "to".

cards.q: Improve: "If it **will rain** tomorrow, the match will be cancelled."
cards.explain: First conditional: If + present simple ("rains"), will + base verb.

notes.p:
Sentence improvement tests whether you can recognise standard written English and choose the correct replacement for a highlighted phrase. The options often include the right idea in a wrong form, so read each one fully.

A dependable method:
Step 1: Read the full sentence and locate the grammar rule involved.
Step 2: Predict the correct phrase before looking at the options.
Step 3: Choose the option that matches your prediction without changing the meaning.
Step 4: If the original is already correct, choose "No improvement".

After a past reporting verb, shift present to past (will → would, can → could, is → was). Exceptions are universal truths and habitual facts.

**Example 1.** "She told me that she **is going** to Delhi." → "She told me that she **was going** to Delhi."

**Example 2.** "By the time we reached, the film **started**." The film started earlier than we reached, so use the past perfect: "**had started**".
Many questions test patterns that must be learned rather than reasoned out.
points: be used to / look forward to / object to / with a view to + -ing: "with a view to **improving**"
would rather / had better + base verb: "I would rather **stay**"
make / let + object + base verb: "He made me **wait**"
"Prevent someone **from** doing"; "insist **on** doing"
"Hardly had … when"; "No sooner had … than"
"Unless" already means "if not" — do not add "not"

notes.p:
Match the two clauses of a conditional sentence.

**Example 3.** "If I **was** a bird, I would fly." For an imaginary present situation, the formal form is "If I **were** a bird".

**Example 4.** "If he had left early, he **would catch** the train." The if-clause is past perfect (third conditional), so the result must be "**would have caught**".

**Example 5.** "If you **will heat** ice, it melts." General facts take the zero conditional: "If you **heat** ice, it melts."

Parallel structure: "He was asked to clean the room, wash the car and **to buy** groceries" → "**buy** groceries".

Dangling modifiers: "Having finished the work, the TV was switched on" suggests the TV finished the work. Improve to "Having finished the work, **he switched on** the TV".

Redundancy: "The reason is **because** …" → "The reason is **that** …"; "each and every" and "free gift" are wordy. The shortest grammatical option is usually best.
Revise before each mock.
points: Past reporting verb ⇒ past in the reported clause (except universal truths)
Look forward to / used to (be) + -ing
Had better / would rather + base verb
Third conditional: had + pp … would have + pp
If I were (imaginary present)
Keep lists parallel; place modifiers next to their noun
"The reason is that", not "because"

chapters.title: English: synonyms, antonyms, idioms & one-word substitution

cards.title: A method for word questions
cards.body: Decide the word's **part of speech** and its **tone** (positive or negative) first. The answer must match both. If the word appears in a sentence, use the context — words like "fair" or "bank" change meaning with use.

cards.title: Roots that unlock words
points: bene (good): benevolent, benefactor; mal (bad): malice, malign
chron (time): chronic, chronology; loqu (speak): loquacious, eloquent
phil (love): philanthropy; mis/miso (hate): misanthrope
omni (all): omniscient; -cide (kill): homicide, regicide

cards.title: Prefix traps
cards.body: un-, in-, im-, dis- usually make opposites, but not always. **Inflammable** means the same as flammable (easily set on fire). **Invaluable** means extremely valuable, not worthless. **Infamous** means famous for a bad reason.

cards.title: High-frequency synonyms
points: Abate — lessen; Candid — frank
Diligent — hard-working; Ephemeral — short-lived
Frugal — thrifty; Gregarious — sociable
Obstinate — stubborn; Lethargic — sluggish
Placid — calm; Zeal — enthusiasm

cards.title: Idioms often asked
points: A bolt from the blue — a sudden shock
To bell the cat — to take a risk for others
Burn the midnight oil — work late into the night
At sixes and sevens — in confusion
To smell a rat — to suspect something wrong

cards.title: One-word substitutions
points: One who knows many languages — polyglot
One who hates mankind — misanthrope
Government by one person with total power — autocracy
Published after the author's death — posthumous
Incapable of making mistakes — infallible

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For antonyms, first find a synonym in your head, then flip it. Distractors often include a synonym of the given word — read the instruction (synonym or antonym) twice before marking.

cards.q: Choose the word closest in meaning to EPHEMERAL:
cards.explain: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time, i.e. transient.

cards.q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to FRUGAL:
cards.explain: Frugal means sparing with money; its opposite is extravagant.

cards.q: "To smell a rat" means:
options: to suspect that something is wrong
cards.explain: The idiom means to sense that something is wrong or dishonest.

notes.p:
Vocabulary appears in several forms in the GAT English section: synonyms, antonyms, idioms and phrases, one-word substitution, and words used in context in cloze and comprehension passages. The words are usually common in newspapers and serious magazines rather than obscure.

A reliable method:
Step 1: Note the part of speech (noun, verb, adjective).
Step 2: Decide the tone — positive, negative or neutral.
Step 3: Use roots and prefixes to guess the meaning.
Step 4: Eliminate options of the wrong part of speech or tone, then choose.
Learning about 30 roots gives you a way into hundreds of words.
points: ante (before): antecedent; post (after): posthumous
anthrop (man): anthropology; theo (god): theology, atheist
bio (life): biography; graph (write): calligraphy
dict (say): verdict, contradict; ver (truth): verify, veracity
pan (all): panacea, panorama; poly (many): polygamy, polyglot
a-/an- (without): anarchy, apathy, amoral

notes.p: Learn words as pairs with their opposites; it doubles the value of each entry.
points: Abundant — plentiful ↔ scarce
Affluent — wealthy ↔ impoverished
Benevolent — kind ↔ malevolent
Cordial — friendly ↔ hostile
Lucid — clear ↔ obscure
Meticulous — careful ↔ careless
Prudent — wise ↔ rash
Transparent — clear ↔ opaque

notes.p: Idioms cannot be understood word by word; learn them as whole units.
points: To beat about the bush — to avoid the main point
A white elephant — a costly, useless possession
To be in hot water — to be in trouble
To turn over a new leaf — to change for the better
To keep one's fingers crossed — to hope for a good result
A wild goose chase — a hopeless search
To call a spade a spade — to speak plainly
To pay lip service — to support in words only

notes.p: These appear in most papers. Group them by theme to remember them.
points: Fear: of heights — acrophobia; of water — hydrophobia; of closed spaces — claustrophobia
Government: by the people — democracy; by a few — oligarchy; by the wealthy — plutocracy
People: one who walks in sleep — somnambulist; one unable to pay debts — insolvent
Study: of birds — ornithology; of insects — entomology; of handwriting — graphology
Murder: of a king — regicide; of a brother — fratricide

notes.p:
**Example.** "The minister's **candid** reply surprised the reporters." Choose the synonym: (a) evasive (b) frank (c) lengthy (d) angry.
Step 1: "Candid" is an adjective describing a reply.
Step 2: Its root sense is "white, pure" — honest and open.
Step 3: "Evasive" is the opposite; "lengthy" and "angry" do not fit the meaning.
Answer: **(b) frank**. For the antonym, "evasive" would be the best choice.
Revise before each mock.
points: Match part of speech and tone first
Inflammable = flammable; invaluable = priceless
Ephemeral — short-lived; frugal ↔ extravagant
A bolt from the blue — sudden shock; to smell a rat — suspect
Polyglot, misanthrope, posthumous, infallible
Read "synonym" vs "antonym" instruction twice

cards.title: Two types of ordering
cards.body: **Parts of a sentence**: a sentence is split into labelled parts (P, Q, R, S) to be arranged into a correct sentence. **Sentences of a passage**: four to six sentences must be arranged into a coherent paragraph, sometimes with the first and last fixed.

cards.title: Finding the opener
cards.body: An opening sentence introduces the topic with a full noun, not a pronoun. It does not begin with linkers such as "however", "therefore", "this", "such" or "he", which point back to something already said.

cards.title: Clues that link sentences
points: Pronouns (he, it, they, this) refer to an earlier noun
Article shift: "a scientist" is introduced before "the scientist"
Time markers: first, then, later, finally
Cause before effect; general statement before example
Contrast words (but, however) follow the idea they contrast

cards.title: Mandatory pairs
cards.body: Look for two parts that must sit together — a noun and its relative clause ("the man" + "who …"), a question and its answer, or a pronoun and its noun. Fixing one pair often eliminates two or three options at once.

cards.title: Ordering parts of a sentence
cards.body: Build the skeleton subject → verb → object → place → time. Prepositions need an object after them; "who/which" clauses follow the noun they describe; adverbs of time usually go at the end.

cards.title: Arrange the parts
cards.body: The old man / P: on Indian history / Q: who lives next door / R: gave me a book / S: yesterday. Subject "The old man" + Q (who …) + R (gave me a book) + P (on Indian history) + S (yesterday). Order: **QRPS**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use the options. Find the opener and one mandatory pair, then check which options contain both. You rarely need to build the whole order yourself.

cards.q: Arrange: "P: the Prime Minister / Q: inaugurated / R: in New Delhi / S: the new bridge"
cards.explain: "The Prime Minister inaugurated the new bridge in New Delhi" — subject, verb, object, place: PQSR.

cards.q: Which sentence is most likely the opening sentence of a paragraph?
options: However, this did not stop them.
He then returned to his village.
Many students fear mathematics, but this fear can be overcome.
It was the last of these steps.
cards.explain: It introduces the topic with full nouns. The others begin with linkers or pronouns that refer back.

cards.q: A sentence beginning with "Therefore" is usually placed:
options: at the start of the paragraph
after the sentence giving the reason
before the sentence giving the reason
cards.explain: "Therefore" introduces a result, so it follows the reason.

notes.p:
Ordering questions test **cohesion** — how ideas and words connect. The syllabus describes this as "comprehension and cohesion in extended text". You must use grammar (for parts of a sentence) and logic (for sentences of a passage) to rebuild the original.

The skill also helps in comprehension: noticing pronouns, linkers and time words makes long passages easier to follow.

Start with the grammatical skeleton.
Step 1: Find the subject (often given as the fixed opening words).
Step 2: Find the main verb that agrees with it.
Step 3: Attach the object or complement.
Step 4: Add phrases of place and time, usually at the end.

**Example 1.** "Despite / P: the team / Q: the heavy rain / R: continued / S: its march". "Despite" needs a noun after it: Q. Then subject P, verb R and object S. Order: **QPRS** — "Despite the heavy rain, the team continued its march."
Follow a fixed routine.
points: Find the opener: a general statement with full nouns and no backward-pointing words
Find mandatory pairs: noun → pronoun, "a" → "the", question → answer, cause → "therefore"
Look for time order: dates, "first", "later", "finally"
Find the closer: a conclusion, summary or result
Check the options that contain your opener and pairs

notes.p:
**Example 2.** Arrange:
P: This habit helps them stay alert during long watches.
Q: Soldiers on sentry duty are trained to scan their sector in a fixed pattern.
R: As a result, very little movement escapes their notice.
S: They move their eyes slowly from near to far and from left to right.

Step 1: Q introduces the subject with a full noun — the opener.
Step 2: S uses "they" and describes the pattern — it follows Q.
Step 3: P's "this habit" refers to the pattern in S.
Step 4: R gives the result, so it closes.
Order: **QSPR**.

notes.h: Questions with fixed first and last sentences
notes.p: Some versions give S1 and S6 and ask you to order P, Q, R, S between them. Treat S1 as the opener and S6 as the conclusion, then work inward: find the sentence that continues S1 directly (it often repeats a key noun from S1 or uses a pronoun for it) and the one that leads into S6 (it often sets up the result or final point S6 states). Once both ends of the middle are fixed, only one or two options remain. Always read S1, your middle order and S6 together as one paragraph before marking the answer.
These mistakes cost the most marks.
points: Choosing an opener that starts with "this", "such" or a pronoun
Ignoring article clues ("a" introduces, "the" refers back)
Breaking a noun from its "who/which" clause
Placing a conclusion ("thus", "hence") before its reason
Spending too long — if two options remain, test only the point where they differ

notes.p: Revise before each mock.
points: Skeleton: subject → verb → object → place → time
Opener: full noun, no linker or pronoun
Pronoun/"the" refer back; "a" introduces
Therefore/hence/as a result follow the reason
Fix one mandatory pair, then use the options
Read the final order once to check it flows

cards.title: What is asked
cards.body: Passages of 250–400 words are followed by questions on the **main idea**, a **specific detail**, an **inference**, the **meaning of a word in context** and the author's **tone**. The answers are always based on the passage, not on outside knowledge.

cards.title: A reading method
cards.body: Skim the passage once for the topic and the author's view. Then read each question and go back to the exact lines that answer it. Underline (mentally) topic sentences and words like but, however, therefore, which signal key turns.

cards.title: Question types
points: Main idea / title: covers the whole passage, not one paragraph
Detail: stated directly in the text
Inference: not stated, but must follow from the text
Vocabulary: meaning as used in that sentence
Tone: the author's attitude

cards.title: Wrong-answer patterns
points: Extreme words: always, never, all, only
True in real life but not stated in the passage
Partly correct: half right, half wrong
Too narrow (one detail) or too broad (beyond the passage)

cards.title: Tone words to know
points: Laudatory — praising; critical — finding fault
Ironic/sarcastic — saying the opposite of what is meant
Objective — factual and neutral
Optimistic / pessimistic; nostalgic — longing for the past

cards.title: A short inference
cards.body: "Although the village had a new school, most children still walked to the town school ten kilometres away." A safe inference: the new school was **not attracting** most children. It is not safe to infer that the new school was "badly built" — the passage does not say why.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For every option ask, "Where does the passage say or imply this?" If you cannot point to a line, eliminate it. This single test removes most distractors.

cards.q: Passage: "Discipline is not punishment; it is the habit of doing what must be done even when one does not feel like it." The author views discipline mainly as:
options: a habit of doing necessary work
cards.explain: The sentence defines discipline as a habit of doing what must be done.

cards.q: In inference questions, which option is most often wrong?
