options: One that closely follows from the passage
One that uses extreme words like "always" or "never"
One that restates the main idea
One that uses the passage's vocabulary
cards.explain: Extreme claims are rarely supported by a passage.

cards.q: "The policy, hailed as a masterstroke, managed to confuse everyone it was meant to help." The tone is:
cards.explain: Calling it a "masterstroke" while saying it confused everyone is ironic.

notes.p:
Comprehension checks whether you can follow an argument, pick out facts and read between the lines. NDA passages cover history, science, society, sport and personal qualities such as courage and discipline. The vocabulary is moderate; the challenge is precision under time pressure.

All answers must come from the passage. Even if you know more about the topic, use only what the author says or clearly implies.

Step 1: Skim the passage in about two minutes. Note the topic of each paragraph in two or three words.
Step 2: Identify the author's main point and attitude.
Step 3: Read the first question. Decide its type (main idea, detail, inference, vocabulary, tone).
Step 4: Go back to the relevant lines and predict the answer.
Step 5: Eliminate options using the wrong-answer patterns; choose the one you can support with a line.

Do not re-read the whole passage for each question — use your paragraph notes to jump to the right place.

**Passage.** "Mountains teach patience. A climber who rushes the first day often pays for it on the third, when thin air and tired legs combine. Experienced climbers therefore keep a slow, steady pace from the start. They know that reaching the summit is less about strength than about judgement."

**Q1. Main idea?** Successful climbing depends on patience and judgement more than strength.
**Q2. Detail: why do experienced climbers go slowly?** Because rushing early leads to exhaustion later.
**Q3. Inference: a strong but impatient climber is likely to …** struggle later in the climb. The passage does not say he will "never" reach the summit — that would be too extreme.

For a vocabulary question, replace the word with each option and read the sentence again; the right option keeps the meaning. For example, in "the climber paid **dearly** for his haste", "dearly" means "heavily", not "lovingly".

For tone, look at the adjectives and the author's comments. Praise suggests a laudatory tone; balanced facts suggest an objective tone; exaggerated praise of something that failed signals irony.

For **title** questions, choose the option that covers the whole passage in a few words. In the mountain passage above, "Patience on the Mountain" is better than "Thin Air", which covers only one detail, or "Adventure Sports in India", which goes beyond the passage.
Comprehension improves with daily reading rather than last-minute practice.
points: Read one editorial or feature article every day and write its main idea in one line
Note five new words a day with the sentence they appeared in
Practise timed passages: about 8–10 minutes for a passage with five questions
After each practice set, review why each wrong option was wrong

notes.p: Revise before each mock.
points: Answer only from the passage
Main idea covers the whole passage
Inference must follow; detail must be stated
Reject extreme, out-of-scope and half-true options
Test vocabulary by substitution
Tone: laudatory, critical, ironic, objective

chapters.title: English: cloze test & fill in the blanks

cards.title: What a cloze test is
cards.body: A passage has several blanks, each with four options. It tests grammar, vocabulary and the flow of ideas together. A word can be grammatically correct but still wrong because it does not fit the meaning of the passage.

cards.title: A method that works
points: Read the whole passage first to get its theme and tense
For each blank, decide the part of speech needed
Check grammar: tense, number, article, preposition
Check meaning and collocation
Re-read the completed passage

cards.title: Collocations
points: make a mistake / an effort / progress
take a step / a decision / part
pay attention / a visit / a compliment
heavy rain, strong tea, deep sleep
commit a crime; keep a promise; catch a cold

cards.title: Linking words
points: Contrast: but, however, although, despite
Cause: because, since, as, due to
Result: so, therefore, hence, consequently
Addition: moreover, besides, furthermore

cards.title: Articles and prepositions
cards.body: Use **an** before a vowel sound (an hour, an MBA) and **a** before a consonant sound (a university, a one-rupee coin). Use **the** for something unique or already mentioned. Time: **at** 5 p.m., **on** Monday, **in** June, **for** a period, **since** a point in time.

cards.title: A mini cloze
cards.body: "Despite the heavy rain, the match ___ on time." Options: start / started / starting / starts. The passage is in the past and needs a finite verb after "the match", so the answer is **started**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Do the easy blanks first; they reveal the tense and theme and make the harder ones obvious. If two options are both grammatical, choose the one that matches the tone of the passage.

cards.q: Fill in the blank: "He has been working here ___ 2019."
cards.explain: "Since" marks a point in time with the perfect continuous tense.

cards.q: Fill in the blank: "She is ___ honest woman."
cards.explain: "Honest" begins with a vowel sound (the h is silent), so "an".

cards.q: Fill in the blank: "He was ___ tired that he fell asleep at once."
cards.explain: "So … that" expresses a result: "so tired that".

notes.p: A cloze passage removes every few words and asks you to restore them. Each blank checks one of three things: **grammar** (tense, agreement, article, preposition), **vocabulary** (the word with the right meaning) or **cohesion** (linking words that fit the logic). Because the blanks are connected, getting one right often helps with the next.

Step 1: Read the full passage quickly, ignoring the blanks, to get the theme and tense.
Step 2: For each blank, predict a word before looking at the options.
Step 3: Eliminate options of the wrong part of speech.
Step 4: Check collocation — "pay attention", not "give attention".
Step 5: Read the sentence with your choice and the sentence after it to confirm the logic.

Never decide a blank from its own sentence alone when a linking word is involved; the previous sentence decides whether you need "but", "so" or "moreover".

**Passage.** "Physical fitness is (1) ___ for every cadet. Without it, even the most (2) ___ plan can fail in the field. (3) ___, fitness is built slowly, not in a week. Cadets who train daily (4) ___ far fewer injuries."
Options: (1) essential / essence / essentially; (2) brilliant / brilliance / brilliantly; (3) However / Because / Unless; (4) suffer / suffers / suffering.

(1) After "is" we need an adjective: **essential**.
(2) After "most" and before "plan": adjective **brilliant**.
(3) The sentence adds a caution to the previous idea: **However**.
(4) Plural subject "cadets": **suffer**.
These rules settle most grammar blanks.
points: So + adjective + that; such + a/an + adjective + noun + that
Too + adjective + to: "too weak to walk"
Since (point of time) vs for (period of time)
Each/every + singular noun and verb
Neither … nor / either … or: verb agrees with the nearer subject
Comparatives use "than"; superlatives use "the"

notes.p: Words that mean the same may not fit the same blank. "Strong tea" is natural; "powerful tea" is not. "Make a mistake" is correct; "do a mistake" is not. Learn words in phrases, and when practising, write the whole collocation in your notebook rather than a single word.
Many blanks test a preposition that is fixed by the word before it. Learn these as whole units.
points: Accuse **of**, charge **with**, deprive **of**, prevent **from**
Good **at**, fond **of**, aware **of**, capable **of**, responsible **for**
Agree **with** a person, **to** a proposal; angry **with** a person, **at** an act
Look after (care for), look into (investigate), put off (postpone), call off (cancel)
Give up (stop), carry out (perform), bring up (raise), turn down (reject)

notes.p: Revise before each mock.
points: Read the whole passage before filling blanks
Predict, then eliminate by part of speech
Check collocation and linking logic
a/an by sound; at/on/in for time
Since + point; for + period
So … that; too … to

cards.title: Active to passive
cards.body: The **object** of the active sentence becomes the **subject**; the verb becomes a form of **be + past participle**; the old subject moves into a "by" phrase (often dropped). "The cadet cleaned the rifle" → "The rifle **was cleaned** by the cadet".

cards.title: Passive forms by tense
points: Present simple: is/am/are + pp
Present continuous: is/am/are being + pp
Present perfect: has/have been + pp
Past simple: was/were + pp; past continuous: was/were being + pp
Past perfect: had been + pp; future: will be + pp; modals: can/must be + pp

cards.title: Special passive patterns
points: Imperative: "Shut the gate" → "Let the gate be shut"
Question: "Who wrote this?" → "By whom was this written?"
Intransitive verbs (sleep, arrive, die) have no passive
"People say that he is honest" → "He is said to be honest"

cards.title: Indirect speech: tense shift
cards.body: When the reporting verb is in the past, move the tense one step back: is → was, are writing → were writing, has done → had done, did → had done, will → would, can → could. If the reporting verb is present ("He says"), or the statement is a universal truth, the tense does not change.

cards.title: Indirect speech: other changes
points: now → then; today → that day; tonight → that night
tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day
here → there; this → that; ago → before
Pronouns change to match the speaker and listener

cards.title: Questions, commands, exclamations
cards.body: Questions: "asked" + if/whether (yes–no) or the wh-word, with statement word order. Commands and requests: told/ordered/requested + object + **to** + verb ("not to" for negatives). Exclamations: exclaimed with joy/sorrow that …

cards.title: Convert it
cards.body: He said, "I am writing a letter now." → He said that he **was writing** a letter **then**. The present continuous moves to the past continuous, and "now" becomes "then".

cards.q: Choose the passive form of: "They are building a bridge."
options: A bridge was being built by them.
A bridge is being built by them.
A bridge has been built by them.
A bridge is built by them.
cards.explain: Present continuous active → is/are being + past participle.

cards.q: Choose the indirect form of: She said to me, "Where do you live?"
options: She asked me where did I live.
She asked me where I lived.
She told me where I live.
She asked me that where I lived.
cards.explain: Use "asked", keep the wh-word, use statement order and shift the tense.

cards.q: Choose the indirect form of: He said, "I will come tomorrow."
options: He said that he will come tomorrow.
He said that he would come the next day.
He said that I would come the next day.
He says that he would come tomorrow.
cards.explain: will → would and tomorrow → the next day.

notes.h: Why voice and narration are tested
notes.p:
Transformation questions check whether you can keep the **meaning** while changing the **structure**. They also appear hidden inside error-spotting and sentence-improvement items, for instance a wrong tense after "said" or a missing "being" in a passive.

Work in a fixed order: identify the tense of the original, apply the rule for that tense, then check pronouns, time words and word order.

notes.h: Active and passive voice: worked examples
notes.p:
**Example 1.** "The committee will announce the results tomorrow."
Step 1: Tense — simple future.
Step 2: Passive — will be + past participle.
Answer: "The results **will be announced** by the committee tomorrow."

**Example 2.** "Has anyone seen my cap?"
Step 1: Present perfect question.
Answer: "**Has my cap been seen** by anyone?"

**Example 3.** "Do not insult the weak."
Answer: "**Let the weak not be insulted**." (Another accepted form: "The weak should not be insulted.")

The passive is preferred when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant ("The bridge was built in 1960"), and in formal or scientific writing ("The solution was heated"). Prefer the active when the doer matters, because it is clearer and shorter. Only **transitive** verbs, which take an object, can be made passive.

notes.h: Direct and indirect speech: worked examples
notes.p:
**Example 4.** The teacher said, "The Earth revolves round the Sun."
Answer: The teacher said that the Earth **revolves** round the Sun (universal truth — no change).

**Example 5.** The officer said to the cadets, "Stand in a line."
Answer: The officer **ordered** the cadets **to stand** in a line.

**Example 6.** He said, "I met her yesterday."
Answer: He said that he **had met** her **the previous day**.

**Example 7.** She said, "What a beautiful view it is!"
Answer: She **exclaimed** that it was a very beautiful view.

**Example 8 (modal passive).** "You must finish the work by evening." → "The work **must be finished** by evening." Modals keep their form and add **be + past participle**.

**Example 9 (yes–no question).** He said to me, "Are you ready?" → He **asked** me **if I was** ready. The auxiliary moves back after the subject, and "are" becomes "was".

**Example 10 (request).** She said to him, "Please help me." → She **requested** him **to help** her. "Please" disappears because "requested" already carries the politeness.

**Example 11 (negative command).** The coach said, "Don't waste time." → The coach told us **not to waste** time.
Avoid these frequent errors.
points: Keeping question order in indirect speech: "He asked where was I going" ✗ → "where I was going"
Using "said to" with a question: use "asked"
Forgetting "being" in continuous passives
Changing tense when the reporting verb is present
Using "that" before a wh-word in indirect questions

notes.p: Revise before each mock.
points: Passive = be + past participle; object becomes subject
Continuous passive needs "being"; perfect needs "been"
Imperative passive: Let + object + be + pp
Past reporting verb → shift tense back
now → then; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day
Questions: asked + if/whether/wh-word + statement order
Commands: told/ordered + to + verb

cards.title: Physics in GAT
cards.body: As per the UPSC syllabus, Physics carries the largest share of the GK section of GAT (about 100 of the 400 marks). Questions are conceptual and Class 9–10 NCERT level, with some 11–12 basics.

cards.title: Equations of motion (uniform acceleration)
points: v = u + at
s = ut + ½at²
v² = u² + 2as
Free fall: a = g ≈ 9.8 m/s²

cards.title: Newton's laws
cards.body: **First law**: a body stays at rest or uniform motion unless a net force acts (inertia). **Second**: F = ma (rate of change of momentum). **Third**: every action has an equal and opposite reaction — this is why rockets and guns recoil.
points: Momentum p = mv; conserved when no external force acts
Impulse = F × t = change in momentum

cards.title: Work, energy, power
points: Work W = F s cos θ (joule)
Kinetic energy = ½mv²; potential energy = mgh
Power = work/time (watt); 1 hp ≈ 746 W
Energy is conserved — it only changes form

cards.title: Gravitation and fluids
cards.body: g decreases with height and depth, and is greater at the poles than the equator. Escape velocity from Earth ≈ **11.2 km/s**. Archimedes' principle: a body in a fluid loses weight equal to the weight of fluid displaced; it floats if its density is less than the fluid's.

cards.title: Motion problem
cards.body: A car starts from rest with acceleration 2 m/s² for 5 s. v = u + at = 0 + 2×5 = **10 m/s**. Distance s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½×2×25 = **25 m**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Learn SI units and the scientist each is named after (newton, pascal, joule, watt, hertz). Units and 'which is a vector/scalar' questions appear almost every year.

cards.q: What is the SI unit of power?
cards.explain: Power is work per unit time; 1 watt = 1 joule per second.

cards.q: The escape velocity from Earth's surface is about:
cards.explain: Escape velocity from Earth ≈ 11.2 km/s; about 7.9 km/s is the orbital speed near the surface.

cards.q: A gun recoils when fired. This is explained by:
cards.explain: The bullet is pushed forward and the gun is pushed back equally — action and reaction (third law); equivalently, momentum is conserved.

notes.p:
Physics begins with measurement. The **SI system** has seven base units: **metre** (length), **kilogram** (mass), **second** (time), **ampere** (current), **kelvin** (temperature), **mole** (amount of substance) and **candela** (luminous intensity). All other units are derived: newton (force) = kg·m/s², joule (energy) = N·m, watt (power) = J/s, pascal (pressure) = N/m².

**Dimensions** express a quantity in terms of M, L and T. Force = [MLT⁻²], energy = [ML²T⁻²], power = [ML²T⁻³]. Quantities with the same dimensions (work and torque, for example) can be confused in exam options — check the definition.

Some non-SI units worth knowing: 1 light-year is a unit of **distance**, not time; 1 horsepower ≈ 746 W; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

**Distance** is a scalar (total path), **displacement** is a vector (shortest straight line from start to end). Speed is distance/time; **velocity** is displacement/time; **acceleration** is rate of change of velocity.

The three equations of motion (constant acceleration): **v = u + at**, **s = ut + ½at²**, **v² = u² + 2as**.

**Example 1.** A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s.
Step 1: v = 0 + 2 × 5 = **10 m/s**.
Step 2: s = 0 + ½ × 2 × 5² = **25 m**.

**Example 2.** A stone is dropped from 45 m (take g = 10 m/s²).
Step 1: s = ½gt² ⇒ 45 = 5t² ⇒ t² = 9 ⇒ t = **3 s**.
Step 2: v = gt = 10 × 3 = **30 m/s**.
In the absence of air resistance, a heavy and a light object dropped together land at the same time.

**First law (inertia):** a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an external force acts — why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes. **Second law:** F = ma, or force = rate of change of momentum. **Third law:** every action has an equal and opposite reaction — rocket propulsion, recoil of a gun, swimming.

**Momentum** p = mv. In the absence of external force, total momentum is **conserved**.

**Example 3.** A 4 kg gun fires a 20 g bullet at 400 m/s. Find the recoil velocity.
Step 1: Initial momentum = 0.
Step 2: 0.02 × 400 = 4 × V ⇒ 8 = 4V.
Step 3: V = **2 m/s** backward.

**Impulse** = force × time = change in momentum. That is why a cricketer pulls his hands back while catching — more time means less force.

**Work** W = F·s·cosθ; no work is done if force is perpendicular to motion (a coolie carrying a load horizontally does no work against gravity). **Kinetic energy** = ½mv²; **potential energy** = mgh. For a 2 kg ball at 10 m/s, KE = ½ × 2 × 100 = **100 J**. Doubling speed makes KE **four times**. **Power** = work/time.

**Gravitation:** F = Gm₁m₂/r². On the Earth's surface g ≈ 9.8 m/s². g **decreases** with height and with depth, and is zero at the centre of the Earth. g is slightly more at the poles than at the equator. The Moon's gravity is about 1/6 of the Earth's, so your **mass stays the same but your weight becomes about 1/6**. Escape velocity from Earth ≈ **11.2 km/s**. Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they are in continuous free fall.

The time period of a **simple pendulum**, T = 2π√(l/g), does not depend on the mass of the bob.
These are favourite distractors in NDA options.
points: Mass (kg) vs weight (N): weight changes with g, mass does not
Light-year measures distance, not time
Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity (acceleration towards the centre)
Pendulum period is independent of mass, and increases with length
Work can be zero even if a large force acts

notes.p: Read these aloud once — they cover most mechanics questions.
points: 7 SI base units: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd
v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as
F = ma; momentum p = mv is conserved
KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh; 1 hp ≈ 746 W
g decreases with height and depth; zero at the centre
Escape velocity from Earth ≈ 11.2 km/s
T = 2π√(l/g)

cards.title: Heat
cards.body: Heat flows by **conduction** (solids), **convection** (fluids) and **radiation** (no medium needed — that is how sunlight reaches us). Specific heat is heat needed to raise 1 kg by 1 K; water's high specific heat makes it a good coolant. Latent heat is absorbed or released during a change of state at constant temperature.

cards.title: Sound
cards.body: Sound is a mechanical, longitudinal wave and **cannot travel in vacuum**. It travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases (about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C). Humans hear about 20 Hz–20 kHz; above is ultrasound, below is infrasound. SONAR uses ultrasound.

cards.title: Light
cards.body: Light travels at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum. Key phenomena: reflection, refraction, **total internal reflection** (optical fibres, sparkle of diamond), dispersion (rainbow), scattering (blue sky, red sunset) and atmospheric refraction (twinkling of stars).

cards.title: Lenses and mirrors
points: Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
Power P = 1/f (f in metres), unit dioptre (D)
Convex lens: positive power; concave lens: negative power
Myopia corrected by concave lens; hypermetropia by convex lens

cards.title: Current electricity
points: Ohm's law: V = IR
Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …
Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …
Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R
1 kWh (one 'unit') = 3.6 × 10⁶ J

cards.title: Lens power
cards.body: A convex lens has focal length 50 cm = 0.5 m. Power P = 1/f = 1/0.5 = **+2 D**. If it were a concave lens of the same focal length, P = −2 D.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Make a one-page table of 'phenomenon → reason' (e.g. blue sky → scattering, mirage → total internal reflection, twinkling → atmospheric refraction). These are among the most repeated NDA physics questions.

cards.q: What is the power of a convex lens of focal length 50 cm?
cards.explain: P = 1/f (in metres) = 1/0.5 = +2 D; convex lenses have positive power.

cards.q: Two 4 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:
The twinkling of stars is due to:
cards.explain: Starlight bends unevenly through moving air layers of changing density, so the apparent position and brightness fluctuate.

notes.p:
**Heat** is energy in transfer (unit joule); **temperature** measures how hot a body is. Scales are linked by C/100 = (F − 32)/180 = (K − 273)/100. Body temperature 37°C = 37 × 9/5 + 32 = **98.6°F**. The Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read the same at **−40°**.

Heat travels by **conduction** (through solids), **convection** (by movement of fluids — sea breeze, land breeze) and **radiation** (no medium needed — sunlight reaching Earth). **Specific heat** is the heat needed to raise 1 kg by 1°C; water's is high, so it is used in car radiators and moderates coastal climates. **Latent heat** is absorbed during a change of state without a rise in temperature — steam at 100°C burns more than water at 100°C.

Water shows **anomalous expansion**: it is densest at **4°C**, so lakes freeze from the top and aquatic life survives below.

Sound is a **mechanical, longitudinal wave** and needs a medium — it cannot travel through vacuum. It travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases. In air it moves at roughly 340 m/s (it rises with temperature). Speed = frequency × wavelength (**v = fλ**).

Humans hear about **20 Hz to 20 kHz**. Below 20 Hz is **infrasound** (earthquakes, elephants); above 20 kHz is **ultrasound** (bats, dolphins, SONAR, medical scans). **Pitch** depends on frequency, **loudness** on amplitude (measured in decibels). An **echo** is heard clearly only if the reflecting surface is at least about 17 m away, because the ear holds a sound for about 0.1 s.

Light travels at about **3 × 10⁸ m/s** in vacuum. Mirror formula: **1/v + 1/u = 1/f**; lens formula: **1/v − 1/u = 1/f** (use the sign convention: distances measured from the pole/optical centre, against the light direction are negative). **Power** of a lens P = 1/f (f in metres), unit **dioptre**. A lens of f = 50 cm has P = 1/0.5 = **+2 D**.

**Example.** An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm.
Step 1: u = −30, f = −10.
Step 2: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/10 + 1/30 = −2/30.
Step 3: v = **−15 cm** (real, in front of the mirror). Magnification m = −v/u = −0.5, so the image is inverted and half the size.
points: Myopia (short-sight) → concave lens; hypermetropia (long-sight) → convex lens
Dispersion of white light by a prism or raindrops → rainbow
Scattering: blue sky, red sunrise/sunset (red scatters least)
Total internal reflection: sparkle of diamond, optical fibres, mirage
Rear-view mirrors are convex (wide field of view); shaving mirrors are concave

notes.p:
**Ohm's law:** V = IR. Resistance R = ρL/A — it increases with length and decreases with cross-section area. In **series** R = R₁ + R₂ + …; in **parallel** 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …. Household wiring is in parallel so each appliance gets the full voltage and can be switched independently.

**Example.** 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel: 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 1, so **R = 1 Ω**. In series they give **11 Ω**.

**Power** P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Electrical energy is billed in **kWh** ("units"): a 100 W bulb used for 10 hours uses 1 kWh. A **fuse** is a wire of low melting point in series; **earthing** protects against shocks. Magnetism links in: **Fleming's left-hand rule** (motor), **right-hand rule** (generator); Oersted showed a current produces a magnetic field.
Most NDA questions here are one-liners — these facts cover many of them.
points: Water is densest at 4°C
Sound needs a medium; fastest in solids
Audible range 20 Hz–20 kHz
P = 1/f (metres) in dioptres
Blue sky = scattering; diamond sparkle = total internal reflection
Series adds R; parallel adds 1/R

chapters.title: Physics: properties of matter, density & pressure

cards.title: States of matter
cards.body: **Solids** have fixed shape and volume; **liquids** have fixed volume but take the shape of the container; **gases** have neither. Plasma (ionised gas, as in the Sun) is often called the fourth state. Heating or cooling changes the state by changing the spacing and energy of particles.

cards.title: Mass vs weight
cards.body: **Mass** is the quantity of matter (kg) and stays the same everywhere. **Weight** is the gravitational force on it, W = mg (newtons), and changes with g. On the Moon a body weighs about one-sixth as much. A beam balance compares masses; a spring balance measures weight.

cards.title: Density and specific gravity
points: Density ρ = mass/volume (kg/m³)
Water: about 1000 kg/m³ (1 g/cm³), maximum at 4 °C
Relative density (specific gravity) = density of substance/density of water — no unit
RD > 1 sinks in water; RD < 1 floats

cards.title: Archimedes' principle
cards.body: A body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid experiences an upward **buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid displaced**. A body floats when its weight equals the buoyant force (law of flotation). Ice floats because it is less dense than water.

cards.title: Pressure
points: P = F/A; SI unit pascal (Pa) = N/m²
Liquid pressure P = hρg — depends on depth, not on container shape
Atmospheric pressure ≈ 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 76 cm of mercury
Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally — hydraulic press, lift and brakes

cards.title: Barometers
cards.body: A **mercury barometer** (Torricelli) balances air pressure against a mercury column of about 76 cm at sea level. An **aneroid barometer** uses a sealed metal box. A steady fall in reading suggests rain; a sudden fall signals a storm. An **altimeter** is an aneroid barometer marked in heights.

cards.title: Finding relative density
cards.body: A stone weighs 10 N in air and 6 N in water. Loss of weight = buoyant force = 4 N = weight of equal volume of water. RD = 10/4 = **2.5**, so its density is 2500 kg/m³.

cards.q: A body has relative density 2.5. Its density is:
cards.explain: Density = RD × 1000 kg/m³ = 2500 kg/m³.

cards.q: A ship sails from a river into the sea. It will:
cards.explain: Sea water is denser, so less volume needs to be displaced for the same buoyant force; the ship rises a little.

cards.q: A sudden fall in barometer reading usually indicates:
cards.explain: A sharp drop in air pressure is associated with approaching storms.

notes.p:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. In **solids**, particles are tightly packed and only vibrate; in **liquids**, they are close but can slide past each other; in **gases**, they are far apart and move freely, so gases are easily compressed.

Changes of state are caused by heating or cooling: melting, freezing, boiling, condensation and **sublimation** (solid directly to gas, as with camphor, naphthalene and dry ice).

**Mass** (kg) measures inertia and does not change from place to place. **Weight** = mg is a force in newtons. g is slightly greater at the poles than at the equator, so a body weighs slightly more at the poles. On the Moon g is about 1/6 of Earth's.

**Density** ρ = m/V. **Relative density** = ρ/ρ_water, a pure number.

**Example 1.** A block of mass 2 kg has volume 0.0008 m³.
ρ = 2/0.0008 = **2500 kg/m³**; RD = 2.5, so it sinks in water.

Every immersed body is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. This is why objects seem lighter in water.

**Example 2.** A stone weighs 10 N in air and 6 N in water.
Step 1: Upthrust = 10 − 6 = 4 N.
Step 2: RD = weight in air/loss of weight in water = 10/4 = **2.5**.

A floating body displaces its own weight of liquid. A ship made of steel floats because its hollow shape displaces a large volume of water. A **hydrometer** floats deeper in a less dense liquid, so its scale gives the liquid's density directly.

Pressure is force per unit area: P = F/A. A sharp knife cuts easily because its small edge area gives high pressure; wide tyres and camel's feet spread weight to reduce pressure.

In a liquid, **P = hρg**. **Example 3.** Pressure due to water at a depth of 10 m = 10 × 1000 × 9.8 = **98 000 Pa**, close to one atmosphere. Divers therefore feel roughly double the surface pressure at 10 m.

Dams are thicker at the bottom because pressure increases with depth. **Pascal's law** makes hydraulic lifts and brakes possible: a small force on a small piston produces a large force on a large piston.

The air above us exerts about 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa at sea level, equal to a mercury column about 76 cm high. Pressure decreases with altitude, which is why fountain pens may leak in aircraft and why it is harder to cook at high places (water boils below 100 °C).

Water is not used in barometers because the column would need to be over 10 m tall. Weather reading: a gradual fall suggests rain, a sudden fall a storm, and a steady rise fair weather.
Revise before each mock.
points: Mass constant; weight = mg (N)
ρ = m/V; water 1000 kg/m³, densest at 4 °C
RD = weight in air/loss of weight in water
Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced
P = hρg; 1 atm ≈ 76 cm Hg ≈ 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa
Pascal's law → hydraulic press and brakes
Sudden barometer fall → storm

chapters.title: Physics: heat, temperature & transfer of heat

cards.title: Heat vs temperature
cards.body: **Heat** is energy in transit due to a temperature difference (joule). **Temperature** measures how hot a body is (kelvin, or °C). Heat always flows from higher to lower temperature until both are equal (thermal equilibrium).

cards.title: Temperature scales
points: Normal body temperature ≈ 37 °C = 98.6 °F
Absolute zero: 0 K = −273.15 °C

cards.title: Thermometers
cards.body: Mercury thermometers cannot measure below about −39 °C because mercury freezes; **alcohol** thermometers are used for very low temperatures. A **clinical thermometer** has a narrow constriction so the reading stays after removal. **Pyrometers** measure very high temperatures, such as in furnaces.

cards.title: Expansion and water's anomaly
cards.body: Most substances expand on heating — hence gaps in railway tracks and sagging wires in summer. A **bimetallic strip** bends on heating and is used in thermostats. Water contracts from 0 °C to 4 °C and is densest at 4 °C, so lakes freeze from the top and fish survive below.

cards.title: Specific heat and latent heat
points: Q = mcΔT (c = specific heat capacity)
Water: c ≈ 4200 J/kg K — very high
Q = mL for change of state at constant temperature
Latent heat of fusion of ice ≈ 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg
Latent heat of vaporisation of water ≈ 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg

cards.title: Changing state
cards.body: **Evaporation** happens at any temperature from the surface and causes cooling (earthen pots, sweating). Higher pressure raises the boiling point (**pressure cooker**); at high altitude water boils below 100 °C. Pressure lowers the melting point of ice (**regelation**).

cards.title: Three modes of transfer
cards.body: **Conduction**: through solids, particle to particle. **Convection**: by movement of fluid — sea and land breezes. **Radiation**: needs no medium — sunlight reaches Earth. Dark, rough surfaces absorb and emit radiation well; shiny white surfaces reflect it.

cards.q: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read the same?
cards.explain: Put C = F in F = 9C/5 + 32: C = −40.

cards.q: A burn from steam at 100 °C is more severe than from water at 100 °C because:
cards.explain: Condensing steam releases its latent heat of vaporisation in addition to the heat of hot water.

cards.q: During a sunny day, the sea breeze blows:
cards.explain: Land heats faster; warm air over land rises and cooler air from the sea moves in.

notes.p:
Heat is a form of energy measured in **joules** (older unit: the calorie, 1 cal ≈ 4.2 J). Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles. A bathtub of warm water holds more heat than a cup of boiling water, even though its temperature is lower.

The SI unit of temperature is the **kelvin**. K = °C + 273 (more exactly 273.15).

**Example 1.** Convert 98.6 °F to Celsius: C = (98.6 − 32) × 5/9 = 66.6 × 5/9 = **37 °C**.

Liquid-in-glass thermometers rely on expansion. Mercury is opaque, conducts heat well and expands uniformly, but freezes at about −39 °C, so alcohol is used in very cold regions. A clinical thermometer usually reads from about 35 °C to 42 °C. Thermocouples and resistance thermometers measure temperature electrically, and pyrometers measure the very high temperatures of furnaces from the radiation they emit.

Q = mcΔT gives the heat needed to change temperature; Q = mL gives the heat needed to change state at constant temperature.

**Example 2.** Heat needed to turn 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 20 °C.
Step 1: Melting: 1 × 3.36 × 10⁵ = 336 000 J (using L ≈ 336 kJ/kg).
Step 2: Warming: 1 × 4200 × 20 = 84 000 J.
Step 3: Total = **420 000 J**.

Water's high specific heat makes it a good coolant in car radiators and keeps coastal climates mild.
Heat causes expansion, change of state and change in properties.
points: Gaps in rails and bridges allow for expansion
Bimetallic strips in thermostats, fire alarms and electric irons
Water densest at 4 °C: lakes freeze from the top
Evaporation causes cooling: water in an earthen pot stays cool
Boiling point rises with pressure (pressure cooker) and falls with altitude
Sublimation: camphor, naphthalene, dry ice (solid CO₂)

notes.p:
**Conduction** dominates in solids; metals are good conductors, while wood, air and plastic are insulators — which is why cooking pans have wooden handles and woollen clothes trap air. **Convection** carries heat in liquids and gases through currents: sea breeze by day, land breeze by night, and the heating of water in a pot from below. **Radiation** travels at the speed of light without a medium.

A **thermos (vacuum) flask** limits all three: the vacuum between double walls stops conduction and convection, and silvered surfaces reduce radiation.
Revise before each mock.
points: Q = mcΔT; Q = mL
Water: high specific heat; densest at 4 °C
Steam burns are worse due to latent heat
Pressure cooker raises boiling point
Conduction, convection, radiation; sea breeze by day
Thermos flask stops all three modes

cards.title: Types of waves
cards.body: **Mechanical waves** need a medium; **electromagnetic waves** (light, radio, X-rays) do not. In **transverse** waves particles move at right angles to the wave (waves on a string); in **longitudinal** waves they move along it, forming compressions and rarefactions — sound in air.

cards.title: Wave relations
points: Speed v = frequency f × wavelength λ
Time period T = 1/f
Frequency unit: hertz (Hz)

cards.title: Speed of sound
cards.body: Sound travels at roughly 330–345 m/s in air (it rises with temperature), about 1500 m/s in water and several thousand m/s in steel. It cannot travel through a vacuum, so astronauts on a spacewalk use radio.

cards.title: Characteristics of sound
points: Loudness ↔ amplitude; measured in decibels (dB)
Pitch ↔ frequency; higher frequency = shriller sound
Quality (timbre) ↔ waveform; lets us tell a flute from a violin

cards.title: Audible, infra and ultra
cards.body: Humans hear about **20 Hz to 20 kHz**. Below 20 Hz is **infrasound** (earthquakes, whales, elephants). Above 20 kHz is **ultrasound**, used by bats and dolphins and in SONAR, medical scans and cleaning delicate parts.

cards.title: Echo, SONAR and Doppler
cards.body: An echo is reflected sound. To hear it distinctly the reflector must be at least about **17 m** away (sound persists in the ear about 0.1 s). **SONAR** uses ultrasonic echoes to find depth and submarines. The **Doppler effect** is the change in observed pitch when source and listener move relative to each other.

cards.title: Musical instruments
points: Stringed (sitar, violin, guitar): pitch rises with tension, falls with length
Wind (flute, shehnai): vibrating air column; shorter column = higher pitch
Percussion (tabla, drum): vibrating stretched membrane
Resonance: forced vibration at natural frequency gives a loud sound

cards.q: Ultrasonic sound has a frequency:
cards.explain: Ultrasound is above the upper limit of human hearing, about 20 kHz.

cards.q: Sound travels fastest in:
cards.explain: Sound is fastest in solids such as steel and cannot travel in a vacuum.

cards.q: The pitch of a sound depends on its:
cards.explain: Pitch is determined by frequency.

notes.p:
A **wave** transfers energy without transferring matter. Water ripples, sound and light are all waves.

**Transverse waves** have crests and troughs (string waves, light). **Longitudinal waves** have compressions and rarefactions (sound in air). Electromagnetic waves are transverse and travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium.

The key relation is **v = fλ**. **Example 1.** A sound of frequency 500 Hz has wavelength 0.68 m. Its speed is 500 × 0.68 = **340 m/s**.

Sound travels faster in denser, more elastic media: solids > liquids > gases. In air its speed increases with temperature and humidity; at a fixed temperature it does not depend on pressure.

Lightning is seen before thunder is heard because light is enormously faster. Counting the seconds between the flash and the thunder and multiplying by about 340 m/s gives the distance of the storm: a 3-second gap means roughly 1 km.

**Example 2.** A person shouts near a cliff and hears the echo after 2 s. Speed of sound 340 m/s. Distance to cliff?
Step 1: Sound goes to the cliff and back: total path = 340 × 2 = 680 m.
Step 2: Distance = 680/2 = **340 m**.

**Example 3.** A ship's SONAR receives an echo from the sea bed 4 s after sending a pulse. Speed in water 1500 m/s.
Depth = (1500 × 4)/2 = **3000 m**.

In large halls, repeated reflections cause **reverberation**; curtains and soft boards absorb sound to reduce it.

Loudness depends on amplitude and is measured in decibels; prolonged exposure to very loud noise damages hearing. Pitch depends on frequency — women's and children's voices are usually higher-pitched than men's. Quality depends on the mix of overtones.

Infrasound (below 20 Hz) is produced by earthquakes and some large animals. Ultrasound (above 20 kHz) is used by bats for echolocation, in medical imaging (ultrasonography), in SONAR and for detecting flaws in metals.
Every instrument has a vibrating part.
points: Stringed: a tighter, shorter or thinner string gives a higher pitch (sitar, veena, violin)
Wind: shortening the air column raises pitch — closing holes on a flute changes the column length
Percussion: tightening a drum skin raises pitch (tabla, mridangam)
Resonance: a body vibrates strongly when driven at its natural frequency; soldiers break step on bridges to avoid it
The gramophone reproduces sound from vibrations traced by a needle in a groove

notes.p: Revise before each mock.
points: v = fλ; T = 1/f
Sound: solids > liquids > gases; none in vacuum
Loudness–amplitude, pitch–frequency, quality–waveform
Audible 20 Hz–20 kHz; infra below, ultra above
Echo needs ≥ about 17 m; distance = vt/2
SONAR uses ultrasound; Doppler = change in pitch with motion
Shorter/tighter string → higher pitch

chapters.title: Physics: light — mirrors, lenses & the human eye

cards.title: Light travels in straight lines
cards.body: **Rectilinear propagation** explains shadows, eclipses and the **pinhole camera**, which forms a real, inverted image. Light travels at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum and more slowly in glass or water.

cards.title: Reflection and plane mirrors
cards.body: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, and both rays and the normal lie in one plane. A plane mirror gives a **virtual, erect, same-size, laterally inverted** image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Two mirrors at angle θ form (360/θ) − 1 images.

cards.title: Mirror and lens formulas
points: Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; f = R/2
Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
Magnification: mirror m = −v/u; lens m = v/u
Power P = 1/f (f in metres), unit dioptre; convex +, concave −

cards.title: Uses of spherical mirrors
points: Concave: shaving and dentist's mirrors (magnified erect image), torch and headlight reflectors, solar cookers
Convex: rear-view mirrors and shop security mirrors — erect, diminished image with a wide field of view

cards.title: Refraction and total internal reflection
cards.body: Light bends towards the normal on entering a denser medium; refractive index n = c/v. A pool looks shallower than it is. When light goes from denser to rarer beyond the **critical angle**, it is totally reflected — diamonds sparkle, optical fibres carry signals and mirages form.

cards.title: Dispersion and scattering
cards.body: A prism splits white light into **VIBGYOR** (violet bends most). A rainbow forms by refraction, internal reflection and dispersion in raindrops. The sky is blue because air scatters short (blue) wavelengths most; sunsets look red. Stars twinkle due to atmospheric refraction.

cards.title: The human eye
cards.body: The eye lens forms a real, inverted image on the **retina**; ciliary muscles change its focal length (**accommodation**). Normal near point ≈ 25 cm, far point at infinity.
points: Myopia (short sight): concave lens
Hypermetropia (long sight): convex lens
Presbyopia: bifocal lens; cataract: cloudy lens, surgically replaced

cards.q: Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected with a:
cards.explain: A diverging (concave) lens moves the image back onto the retina.

cards.q: The mirror used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles is:
cards.explain: A convex mirror gives an erect, diminished image with a wide field of view.

cards.q: How many images are formed by two plane mirrors inclined at 60°?

notes.p:
Light is an electromagnetic wave that needs no medium. Because it travels in straight lines, opaque objects cast **shadows**, and a **pinhole camera** forms an inverted real image. A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon's shadow falls on Earth; a lunar eclipse when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

Luminous objects (the Sun, a bulb) emit light; non-luminous objects (the Moon) are seen by reflected light.

Use the **New Cartesian sign convention**: distances measured from the pole, those against the incident light negative. A concave mirror has negative f; a convex mirror positive f.

**Example 1.** An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm.
Step 1: u = −30, f = −10.
Step 2: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/10 + 1/30 = −2/30 ⇒ v = −15 cm.
Step 3: m = −v/u = −(−15)/(−30) = −0.5.
The image is **real, inverted, half-size, 15 cm in front** of the mirror.

A convex (converging) lens has positive f; a concave (diverging) lens negative f. The lens formula is 1/v − 1/u = 1/f.

**Example 2.** An object is 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 20 cm.
Step 1: u = −30, f = +20.
Step 2: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60 ⇒ v = +60 cm.
Step 3: m = v/u = 60/(−30) = −2.
The image is **real, inverted and twice the size**, 60 cm behind the lens.

**Example 3.** Power of a concave lens with f = −50 cm = 1/(−0.5) = **−2 D**.
Refraction explains many everyday observations.
points: A stick in water looks bent; a pool looks shallower (apparent depth = real depth/n)
Stars twinkle because the refractive index of moving air layers keeps changing; planets twinkle much less
The Sun is visible for a few minutes before actual sunrise and after sunset due to atmospheric refraction
Total internal reflection: optical fibres, sparkling diamonds, mirages in deserts and on hot roads
Danger signals are red because red light scatters least and is seen from far

notes.h: The human eye and its defects
notes.p:
The cornea and eye lens focus light on the retina, whose rods (dim light) and cones (colour) send signals along the optic nerve. The **iris** controls the pupil size. **Accommodation** lets a normal eye see clearly from about 25 cm to infinity.

**Myopia**: distant objects blurred; eyeball too long or lens too strong; corrected with a **concave** lens. **Hypermetropia**: near objects blurred; corrected with a **convex** lens. **Presbyopia** comes with age as accommodation weakens; bifocals help. **Astigmatism** is corrected with cylindrical lenses.
Revise before each mock.
points: Plane mirror: virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted
Images between mirrors at θ: (360/θ) − 1
Mirror 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; lens 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
P = 1/f (m); convex +, concave −
Convex mirror → rear-view; concave → shaving, headlights
Blue sky = scattering; twinkling = refraction; rainbow = dispersion + TIR
Myopia → concave; hypermetropia → convex

cards.title: Magnets
cards.body: Natural magnets (lodestone/magnetite) and artificial ones (bar, horseshoe, electromagnet) always have two poles; like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Iron, nickel and cobalt are strongly magnetic. **Soft iron** suits electromagnets; **steel** suits permanent magnets.

cards.title: Earth as a magnet
cards.body: Earth behaves like a huge bar magnet whose magnetic south pole lies near the geographic north. A freely suspended magnet points roughly north–south (**compass**). **Declination** is the angle between magnetic and geographic north; **dip** is 90° at the magnetic poles and 0° at the magnetic equator.

cards.title: Static electricity
cards.body: Rubbing two materials transfers electrons and charges them. **Conductors** (metals, salt water) let charge flow; **insulators** (rubber, glass, plastic) do not. Lightning is a huge discharge between clouds and the ground; a **lightning conductor** gives it a safe path to earth.

cards.title: Current electricity
points: Ohm's law: V = IR
R = ρL/A — longer, thinner wires resist more
Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …
Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R
1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J (1 "unit" of electricity)

cards.title: Effects of current
points: Heating: heaters, irons, fuses, filament bulbs (tungsten)
Lighting: filament, fluorescent and LED lamps
Magnetic (Oersted): electromagnets, electric bells, motors
Chemical: electrolysis, electroplating

cards.title: Cells
cards.body: A **primary cell** (e.g. the dry Leclanché cell) cannot be recharged. A **secondary cell** (lead–acid car battery, lithium-ion phone battery) can be recharged by passing current in the reverse direction. Cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy.

cards.title: X-rays
cards.body: X-rays were discovered by **Wilhelm Röntgen** in 1895. They are high-frequency electromagnetic waves that pass through soft tissue but are stopped by bone and metal — used for medical imaging, airport baggage checks and studying crystals. Excess exposure damages cells, so radiographers use lead shielding.

cards.title: Household wiring
cards.body: Household supply in India is AC at about 220–230 V and 50 Hz. A **fuse** (wire of low melting point) or an **MCB** is connected in series with the live wire and breaks the circuit on overload. **Earthing** sends leakage current safely to the ground.

cards.q: Three resistors of 6 Ω each are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:
A 1000 W heater runs for 3 hours. At ₹5 per unit, the cost is:
cards.explain: Energy = 1 kW × 3 h = 3 kWh = 3 units; cost = 3 × 5 = ₹15.

notes.p:
A magnet attracts iron and points north–south when freely suspended. Its poles cannot be separated: breaking a magnet gives two smaller magnets. Magnetism is destroyed by strong heating or hammering.

Earth's magnetism makes the **mariner's compass** possible. Magnetic field lines run from north to south pole outside a magnet; they never cross, and they are closest where the field is strongest.

Charges are of two kinds, positive and negative; like charges repel. When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, the rod loses electrons and becomes positive. A **gold-leaf electroscope** detects charge.

During a thunderstorm, charge builds up in clouds until the air breaks down and lightning strikes. A **lightning conductor** is a pointed metal rod on top of a building connected by a thick strip to a plate buried in the earth. During lightning, avoid open fields and tall isolated trees; a closed car is relatively safe.

**Example 1.** 4 Ω and 2 Ω in series across 12 V.
Step 1: R = 6 Ω, so I = 12/6 = 2 A.
Step 2: Total power = VI = 12 × 2 = **24 W**.

**Example 2.** A bulb is rated 60 W, 220 V.
R = V²/P = 48 400/60 ≈ **807 Ω**; I = P/V ≈ 0.27 A.

**Example 3.** Five 100 W bulbs run 6 hours a day for 30 days.
Energy = 0.5 kW × 6 × 30 = **90 kWh** (90 units).

In parallel, every appliance gets the full voltage and can be switched independently — which is why homes are wired in parallel.

A current produces heat (Joule heating, H = I²Rt), light, magnetism and chemical change. The magnetic effect, discovered by **Oersted**, underlies electromagnets, electric bells, relays, loudspeakers and motors. The reverse effect — **electromagnetic induction** (Faraday) — makes generators and transformers work.

The chemical effect is used in **electroplating** (chromium on taps, silver on jewellery) and in purifying metals such as copper.

Primary cells are used once; secondary cells are rechargeable. A lead–acid battery stores energy in vehicles and inverters; lithium-ion batteries power phones and laptops.

X-rays are produced when fast electrons strike a metal target. Because dense materials absorb them more, bones appear clearly on an X-ray film. CT scans combine many X-ray images. Medical staff wear lead aprons and keep exposure low because X-rays can damage living cells.
Revise before each mock.
points: Like poles repel; soft iron for electromagnets
Dip 90° at magnetic poles; compass points to magnetic north
V = IR; P = VI = I²R = V²/R
Series add R; parallel add 1/R
1 unit = 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
Fuse in series with live wire; earthing for safety
X-rays: Röntgen, 1895; primary vs secondary cells

cards.title: Simple pendulum
cards.body: For small swings, **T = 2π√(l/g)** — independent of the bob's mass and amplitude. A **seconds pendulum** has T = 2 s and length about 1 m. A pendulum clock **loses time** in summer (length increases) and on mountains (g decreases).

cards.title: Levers
points: Class I — fulcrum in the middle: seesaw, scissors, crowbar
Class II — load in the middle: nutcracker, wheelbarrow, bottle opener
Class III — effort in the middle: tongs, human forearm, fishing rod
Mechanical advantage = load/effort = effort arm/load arm

cards.title: Pulleys
cards.body: A single **fixed pulley** only changes the direction of the force (MA = 1), as on a flagpole. A single **movable pulley** gives MA = 2. A **block and tackle** combines several pulleys for larger mechanical advantage.

cards.title: Siphon and pumps
cards.body: A **siphon** moves liquid from a higher container to a lower one through a bent tube, driven by atmospheric pressure and the difference in levels; the outlet must be below the liquid surface. A **lift pump** cannot raise water more than about 10 m, because atmospheric pressure supports only a 10 m water column.

cards.title: Balloon and hydrometer
cards.body: A **balloon** rises when the weight of air it displaces exceeds its total weight — hence hot air, helium or hydrogen. A **hydrometer** floats upright and sinks deeper in less dense liquids, giving density directly; a **lactometer** checks the purity of milk.

cards.title: Optical instruments
points: Periscope: two plane mirrors (or prisms) at 45° — used in submarines and tanks
Astronomical telescope: objective of large focal length, eyepiece of short focal length
Compound microscope: objective and eyepiece both of short focal length
Pressure cooker raises the boiling point; thermos flask cuts conduction, convection and radiation

cards.title: Communication and safety devices
points: Telegraph: an electromagnet clicks to coded signals (Morse code)
Telephone: microphone turns sound into electrical signals; earpiece turns them back
Gramophone: a needle follows grooves; vibrations are amplified into sound
Mariner's compass: magnetised needle; lightning conductor: earthed pointed rod; fuse: low melting-point wire

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Questions in this area ask "which principle?" Match quickly: siphon/pump → atmospheric pressure; balloon/hydrometer → Archimedes; periscope → reflection; fuse → heating effect; compass → Earth's magnetism.

cards.q: A nutcracker is a lever of which class?
cards.explain: The load (nut) lies between the fulcrum (hinge) and the effort (hands).

cards.q: In summer, a pendulum clock:
cards.explain: The pendulum lengthens with heat, so T increases and the clock runs slow.

notes.p:
A simple pendulum is a small heavy bob on a light inextensible string. For small oscillations its period is T = 2π√(l/g).

**Example 1.** Find the length of a seconds pendulum (T = 2 s) with g = 9.8 m/s².
l = gT²/4π² = 9.8 × 4/(4 × 9.87) ≈ **0.99 m**.

Since T ∝ √l, making the string four times longer doubles the period. A girl on a swing who stands up raises her centre of mass, shortening the effective length, so the period decreases slightly. On the Moon (g about 1/6), a pendulum swings more slowly.

A **lever** is a rigid bar turning about a fulcrum. By the principle of moments, load × load arm = effort × effort arm.

**Example 2.** A crowbar with effort arm 1.2 m and load arm 0.2 m lifts a 600 N stone. Effort = 600 × 0.2/1.2 = **100 N** (MA = 6).

Class II levers always give MA > 1; Class III levers always give MA < 1 but increase speed and range of movement. In pulleys, a fixed pulley offers convenience, while movable pulleys reduce the effort needed.
Several devices rely on air or liquid pressure.
points: Siphon: used to empty tanks and in flush systems; it needs the outlet below the liquid surface
Lift (suction) pump: limited to about 10 m; deeper wells need force pumps or submersible pumps
Bicycle pump: valve allows air only into the tyre
Hydraulic press and brakes: Pascal's law
Drinking straw and syringe: atmospheric pressure pushes the liquid up

notes.p:
**Balloons** and **airships** float in air the way ships float in water: by displacing a weight of air at least equal to their own. A hydrogen balloon rises until the thinner air above no longer gives enough upthrust.

**Hydrometers** use the law of flotation; the lactometer is a hydrometer for milk.

The **pressure cooker** traps steam, raising the pressure and the boiling point of water (to roughly 120 °C), so food cooks faster. The **thermos flask** uses a vacuum and silvered double walls to keep liquids hot or cold.

A **periscope** reflects light twice at 45° so an observer can see over obstacles. A **telescope** gathers light from distant objects with a large objective lens or mirror; a **microscope** magnifies tiny nearby objects with short-focus lenses.

The **telegraph** and **telephone** use electromagnets to convert electrical signals into clicks or sound. A **fuse** melts and breaks the circuit when excess current flows. A **lightning conductor** provides a low-resistance path to earth. The **mariner's compass** has a magnetised needle that aligns with Earth's magnetic field.
Revise before each mock.
points: T = 2π√(l/g); seconds pendulum ≈ 1 m
Clock loses time in summer and on hills
Lever classes: I seesaw, II nutcracker, III tongs
Fixed pulley MA 1; movable pulley MA 2
Siphon and lift pump: atmospheric pressure; lift limit ≈ 10 m
Balloon and hydrometer: Archimedes' principle
Periscope: two mirrors at 45°; fuse: heating effect

cards.title: Matter and its changes
cards.body: Physical changes alter form, not composition (melting ice). Chemical changes create new substances (rusting, burning). Elements contain one kind of atom; compounds have elements in a fixed ratio; mixtures can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, distillation and chromatography.

cards.title: Atomic structure
cards.body: An atom has protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons around it. **Atomic number** = number of protons; **mass number** = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers (e.g. ¹²C and ¹⁴C).

cards.title: Acids, bases and pH
cards.body: Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue. pH < 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral (pure water at 25 °C), > 7 is basic. Acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation). Antacids like milk of magnesia (Mg(OH)₂) neutralise excess stomach acid.

cards.title: Everyday compounds (frequently asked)
points: Baking soda: NaHCO₃ (sodium hydrogen carbonate)
Washing soda: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O
Bleaching powder: CaOCl₂
Plaster of Paris: CaSO₄·½H₂O
Common salt: NaCl; quicklime: CaO; slaked lime: Ca(OH)₂

cards.title: Oxidation, reduction and metals
cards.body: Oxidation = gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction = the reverse. Rusting of iron is oxidation — prevented by painting, oiling or galvanisation (zinc coating). Carbon allotropes: diamond (hardest natural substance), graphite (good conductor, used in electrodes), fullerenes.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: As per the UPSC syllabus, Chemistry is about 60 marks of GAT. Class 9–10 NCERT Science covers most of it. Revise chemical names and formulas of household substances — they are near-certain marks.

cards.q: What is the chemical formula of baking soda?
cards.explain: Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃. Na₂CO₃ is the anhydrous form of washing soda.

cards.q: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
cards.explain: Pure water is neutral, with pH 7 at 25 °C.

cards.q: Galvanisation protects iron by coating it with:
cards.explain: Galvanised iron has a zinc coating that prevents rusting.

notes.p:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. It exists as **solid, liquid and gas** (plasma is often called the fourth state). A **pure substance** is either an **element** (one kind of atom: iron, oxygen) or a **compound** (elements combined chemically in a fixed ratio: water, salt). A **mixture** has components in any ratio that keep their own properties — air, sea water, alloys like brass (copper + zinc) and bronze (copper + tin).

Separation methods: **filtration** (insoluble solid from liquid), **evaporation** (salt from sea water), **distillation** (liquids with different boiling points), **fractional distillation** (crude oil, liquid air), **chromatography** (dyes in ink), **sublimation** (camphor, naphthalene, ammonium chloride) and **centrifugation** (cream from milk).

An atom has **protons** (positive) and **neutrons** (neutral) in the nucleus, with **electrons** (negative) around it. J.J. Thomson discovered the electron, Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed the nucleus, and James Chadwick discovered the neutron.

**Atomic number (Z)** = number of protons; **mass number (A)** = protons + neutrons. **Isotopes** have the same Z but different A (e.g. protium, deuterium and tritium of hydrogen; carbon-12 and carbon-14). **Isobars** have the same A but different Z.

**Mole concept:** one mole contains **6.022 × 10²³** particles (Avogadro's number).
**Example.** How many molecules in 36 g of water?
Step 1: Molar mass of H₂O = 2 + 16 = 18 g/mol.
Step 2: Moles = 36/18 = 2.
Step 3: Molecules = 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = **1.2044 × 10²⁴**.
A **balanced equation** has equal atoms of each element on both sides: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Main types:
points: Combination: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (slaking of lime, releases heat)
Decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating
Displacement: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one)
Double displacement: exchange of ions, often forming a precipitate
Redox: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain — 'OIL RIG'
Rusting of iron needs both oxygen and water; galvanisation (zinc coating) prevents it

notes.p:
**Acids** turn blue litmus red and have **pH below 7**; **bases** turn red litmus blue and have **pH above 7**; pure water is neutral at **pH 7**. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base. An acid and a base react to form salt and water (**neutralisation**) — antacids neutralise excess stomach acid (HCl).

Natural acids: citric acid (lemon), lactic acid (curd), acetic acid (vinegar), tartaric acid (tamarind), formic acid (ant sting). Hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts; temporary hardness (bicarbonates) is removed by boiling.
NDA regularly asks for common names and formulas:
points: Common salt: NaCl; Baking soda: NaHCO₃; Washing soda: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O
Bleaching powder: CaOCl₂; Plaster of Paris: CaSO₄·½H₂O; Gypsum: CaSO₄·2H₂O
Quicklime: CaO; Slaked lime: Ca(OH)₂; Limestone/marble/chalk: CaCO₃
Dry ice: solid CO₂; Laughing gas: N₂O
LPG: mainly butane and propane; CNG and biogas: mainly methane
Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature; bromine is a liquid non-metal
Carbon allotropes: diamond (hardest), graphite (conducts electricity), fullerene

notes.p: Formulas and names here are easy marks — revise them often.
points: Element, compound, mixture — know examples of each
Isotopes: same Z, different A
1 mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles
OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain
pH < 7 acid, 7 neutral, > 7 base
Baking soda NaHCO₃; washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O; PoP CaSO₄·½H₂O
Rust needs oxygen + water

chapters.title: Chemistry: atomic structure, valency & chemical weights

cards.title: Inside the atom
cards.body: An atom has a tiny, dense **nucleus** of protons (+) and neutrons (no charge), with electrons (−) in shells around it. Key discoveries: electron — J. J. Thomson (1897); nucleus — Rutherford's gold-foil experiment (1911); neutron — James Chadwick (1932).

cards.title: Atomic number and mass number
points: Atomic number Z = number of protons (= electrons in a neutral atom)
Mass number A = protons + neutrons
Isotopes: same Z, different A (¹H, ²H, ³H; ¹²C, ¹⁴C)
Isobars: same A, different Z (⁴⁰Ar, ⁴⁰Ca)
Isotones: same number of neutrons

cards.title: Electronic configuration
cards.body: Shells K, L, M, N hold at most 2n² electrons (2, 8, 18, 32), and the outermost shell holds at most 8. Sodium (11): 2, 8, 1. Chlorine (17): 2, 8, 7. Argon (18): 2, 8, 8 — a stable octet.

cards.title: Valency
cards.body: **Valency** is the combining capacity of an atom. If the outer shell has 1–4 electrons, valency = that number; if 5–8, valency = 8 − that number.
points: Na 1, Mg 2, Al 3, C 4
N 3, O 2, Cl 1
Noble gases 0

cards.title: Chemical weights
points: Molecular mass = sum of atomic masses: H₂O = 18, CO₂ = 44, H₂SO₄ = 98
Equivalent weight of an element = atomic weight/valency
Equivalent weight of an acid = molecular weight/basicity
Mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles; 1 mole of gas ≈ 22.4 L at STP

cards.title: Laws of chemical combination
points: Conservation of mass (Lavoisier)
Definite proportions (Proust): a compound always has the same composition by mass
Multiple proportions (Dalton)
Gaseous volumes (Gay-Lussac); Avogadro's law: equal volumes, equal molecules

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: For "number of neutrons" questions, subtract Z from A. For equivalent weight, divide by valency (element) or by the number of replaceable H atoms (acid). These one-line calculations are frequently asked.

cards.q: How many neutrons are there in ²³Na (atomic number 11)?
cards.explain: Neutrons = A − Z = 23 − 11 = 12.

cards.q: The equivalent weight of aluminium (atomic weight 27, valency 3) is:
Hydrogen-1 and hydrogen-2 (deuterium) are:
cards.explain: Same atomic number (1), different mass numbers — isotopes.

notes.p:
**Dalton's atomic theory** (early 1800s) treated atoms as indivisible. Later experiments showed sub-atomic particles. **Thomson** discovered the electron using cathode rays and proposed the "plum pudding" model. **Rutherford** fired alpha particles at gold foil; most passed through but a few bounced back, proving a small, dense, positive nucleus. **Bohr** placed electrons in fixed energy levels. **Chadwick** discovered the neutron.

The nucleus holds almost all the mass; the electron's mass is about 1/1836 that of a proton.

notes.h: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes
notes.p:
Z identifies the element; A counts the nucleons. Isotopes have identical chemical properties but different masses. Carbon-14 is radioactive and used in **carbon dating**; deuterium forms **heavy water** (D₂O), used as a moderator in some nuclear reactors.

**Example 1.** Chlorine is about 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl. Average atomic mass = 0.75 × 35 + 0.25 × 37 = 26.25 + 9.25 = **35.5**. This explains why atomic masses are often not whole numbers.

Electrons fill shells from the inside: K (2), L (8), M (8 for the first 20 elements). Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach a stable octet.

**Example 2.** Magnesium (12) is 2, 8, 2: it loses two electrons, so valency 2. Oxygen (8) is 2, 6: it gains two, so valency 2. Together they form MgO.

To write formulas, cross over valencies: Al (3) and O (2) give **Al₂O₃**; Ca (2) and Cl (1) give **CaCl₂**. Metals tend to lose electrons (forming positive ions) and non-metals to gain them.

**Example 3.** Molecular mass of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + 3 × 16 = **100**. The percentage of calcium = 40/100 × 100 = 40%.

**Example 4.** Equivalent weights: Mg = 24/2 = 12; Al = 27/3 = 9; H₂SO₄ (basicity 2) = 98/2 = **49**; HCl = 36.5/1 = 36.5.

One **mole** of any substance contains Avogadro's number (6.022 × 10²³) of particles and has a mass equal to its molecular mass in grams. So 18 g of water is one mole, and 44 g of CO₂ occupies about 22.4 L at STP.
The syllabus asks for these laws without numerical problems.
points: Conservation of mass: mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction
Definite proportions: water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8
Multiple proportions: in CO and CO₂, the masses of oxygen combining with fixed carbon are in the ratio 1 : 2
Gay-Lussac: reacting gas volumes are in simple whole-number ratios
Avogadro: equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure have equal numbers of molecules

notes.p: Revise before each mock.
points: Electron — Thomson; nucleus — Rutherford; neutron — Chadwick
Neutrons = A − Z
Isotopes same Z; isobars same A
Shell capacity 2n²; octet rule
Valency = outer electrons or 8 − outer electrons
Equivalent weight = atomic weight/valency
1 mole = 6.022 × 10²³; 22.4 L at STP

chapters.title: Chemistry: air, water, common gases & redox

cards.title: Air is a mixture
cards.body: Dry air is roughly **78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon** and about 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus traces of other gases and variable water vapour. It is a mixture: its composition varies, its components keep their properties and can be separated by fractional distillation of liquid air.

cards.title: Water and hardness
cards.body: Water is called the **universal solvent**. **Temporary hardness** (calcium and magnesium bicarbonates) is removed by boiling or by adding lime (Clark's method). **Permanent hardness** (chlorides and sulphates) is removed by washing soda or ion exchange. Hard water does not lather well with soap.

cards.title: Hydrogen
cards.body: Prepared by reacting zinc with dilute sulphuric acid. It is the lightest gas, burns with a "pop", and is used to make ammonia (Haber process), to harden vegetable oils into vanaspati (hydrogenation) and, as liquid hydrogen, as rocket fuel.

cards.title: Oxygen
cards.body: Prepared in the lab by heating potassium chlorate with manganese dioxide (a catalyst) or by decomposing hydrogen peroxide. It **supports combustion** but does not burn itself, and is essential for respiration. Ozone (O₃) is its allotrope.

cards.title: Nitrogen
cards.body: Fairly unreactive because of the strong N≡N triple bond. Obtained industrially from liquid air; in the lab by heating ammonium nitrite. Used to make ammonia and fertilizers, to fill food packets (prevents oxidation) and, as liquid nitrogen, for preserving biological samples.

cards.title: Carbon dioxide
cards.body: Prepared by adding dilute HCl to marble chips (CaCO₃). It turns **lime water milky** (CaCO₃ forms), does not support combustion, and is used in fire extinguishers, soda water and, as solid "dry ice", in refrigeration. It is a greenhouse gas used by plants in photosynthesis.

cards.title: Oxidation and reduction
points: Oxidation: gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, or loss of electrons
Reduction: loss of oxygen, gain of hydrogen, or gain of electrons
Both happen together — redox reactions
The oxidising agent is itself reduced
Examples: rusting, combustion, respiration

cards.q: Which gas turns lime water milky?
cards.explain: CO₂ reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate.

cards.q: Temporary hardness of water is caused by:
cards.explain: Bicarbonates decompose on boiling, so this hardness is "temporary".

cards.q: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, the substance oxidised is:
cards.explain: Hydrogen gains oxygen to form water, so H₂ is oxidised; CuO is reduced.

notes.h: Air: composition and evidence it is a mixture
notes.p: Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour and traces of neon, helium and other gases. Evidence that air is a **mixture** and not a compound: its composition varies from place to place; no heat or light is produced when its gases are mixed; each gas keeps its own properties; and the components can be separated physically by **fractional distillation** of liquefied air (nitrogen boils off before oxygen).

Pure water is neutral and boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. It dissolves more substances than any other common liquid, which is why it is rarely found pure in nature.

**Hard water** contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. With soap it forms an insoluble **scum** instead of lather, and it leaves scale in boilers and kettles.
points: Temporary hardness: Ca(HCO₃)₂ and Mg(HCO₃)₂ — removed by boiling or by lime
Permanent hardness: CaCl₂, MgCl₂, CaSO₄, MgSO₄ — removed by washing soda or ion-exchange (permutit) resins
Heavy water (D₂O) is used as a moderator in some nuclear reactors

notes.p:
**Hydrogen**: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Colourless, odourless, lightest gas; burns in air with a pale blue flame and a "pop"; forms water. Uses: ammonia manufacture, hydrogenation of oils, fuel cells and rocket fuel.

**Oxygen**: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ (heated, with MnO₂ as catalyst). Colourless, slightly heavier than air, supports burning — a glowing splinter rekindles in it. Uses: hospitals and high-altitude breathing, welding (oxy-acetylene flame), steel making and rocket propulsion.

**Nitrogen**: NH₄NO₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O on heating. It neither burns nor supports burning, which makes it useful as an inert atmosphere in food packaging and in electric bulbs. Nitrogen is fixed into the soil by lightning and by bacteria in the root nodules of legumes.

**Carbon dioxide**: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Heavier than air, so it smothers fires. Passing excess CO₂ through milky lime water makes it clear again because soluble calcium bicarbonate forms.

In **2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO**, magnesium gains oxygen and is oxidised. In **CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O**, copper oxide loses oxygen (reduced) while hydrogen gains oxygen (oxidised); H₂ is the **reducing agent** and CuO the **oxidising agent**.

In electron terms, oxidation is loss and reduction is gain — remember **OIL RIG**. Everyday redox processes include rusting of iron, burning of fuels, respiration in cells and the bleaching action of chlorine. Rusting needs both air and moisture and is prevented by painting, oiling or galvanising.
Revise before each mock.
points: Air ≈ 78% N₂, 21% O₂, 0.9% Ar, 0.04% CO₂; a mixture
Temporary hardness: bicarbonates; permanent: chlorides/sulphates
H₂: Zn + dil H₂SO₄; burns with a pop
O₂: KClO₃ + MnO₂; supports combustion
N₂: inert; food packaging, ammonia
CO₂: marble + HCl; turns lime water milky
OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain (of electrons)

chapters.title: Chemistry: acids, bases, salts, carbon & fertilizers

cards.title: Acids
cards.body: Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red and release H⁺ ions in water. Strong acids: HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃. Weak acids: acetic, citric, carbonic.
points: Vinegar — acetic; lemon — citric; curd — lactic
Tamarind — tartaric; ant sting — formic (methanoic)
Tomato — oxalic; apple — malic

cards.title: Bases and neutralisation
cards.body: Bases taste bitter, feel soapy and turn red litmus blue. Soluble bases are **alkalis** (NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂). **Acid + base → salt + water** (neutralisation). Antacids such as magnesium hydroxide neutralise excess stomach acid.

cards.title: pH and indicators
cards.body: pH runs from 0 to 14: 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, above 7 basic. Human blood is about 7.4. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base.

cards.title: Salts you must know
points: Common salt — NaCl
Baking soda — NaHCO₃
Washing soda — Na₂CO₃·10H₂O
Bleaching powder — CaOCl₂
Plaster of Paris — CaSO₄·½H₂O; gypsum — CaSO₄·2H₂O

cards.title: Forms of carbon
cards.body: **Diamond**: each carbon bonded to four others in 3D — hardest natural substance, does not conduct electricity. **Graphite**: layers of hexagons — soft, slippery, conducts electricity; used in pencils and as a lubricant and electrode. **Fullerenes** (C₆₀) and **graphene** are other allotropes. Coal, charcoal and coke are impure (amorphous) forms.

cards.title: Natural fertilizers
cards.body: Farmyard manure, compost, vermicompost and green manure add nutrients and improve soil structure. **Biofertilizers** use living organisms: *Rhizobium* in legume root nodules and free-living *Azotobacter* fix nitrogen; blue-green algae help in paddy fields.

cards.title: Chemical fertilizers
points: Nitrogen: urea (about 46% N), ammonium sulphate, calcium ammonium nitrate
Phosphorus: superphosphate of lime, DAP (diammonium phosphate)
Potassium: muriate of potash (KCl)
NPK fertilizers supply all three; overuse harms soil and water

cards.q: The chemical formula of Plaster of Paris is:
cards.explain: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate; gypsum is the dihydrate.

cards.q: The "lead" in a pencil is actually:
cards.explain: Pencil cores are graphite mixed with clay.

cards.q: Which acid is present in an ant sting?
cards.explain: Ants inject formic (methanoic) acid; rubbing a mild base like baking soda gives relief.

notes.p:
An **acid** produces H⁺ (H₃O⁺) ions in water; a **base** produces OH⁻ ions. Mineral acids such as hydrochloric, sulphuric and nitric acid are strong and corrosive; organic acids in food are weak.

Neutralisation releases heat: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Everyday uses: antacids for acidity, baking soda for bee or ant stings, and lime (calcium hydroxide) to reduce the acidity of soil. When diluting a concentrated acid, always add acid to water slowly, never water to acid.

**Example.** 10 mL of an acid solution is exactly neutralised by 10 mL of a base solution of the same strength. Adding a few drops of phenolphthalein to the base makes it pink; as the acid is added, the colour disappears exactly at the neutral point — this is the principle of a **titration**.
The **pH scale** measures acidity: each step is a tenfold change in H⁺ concentration.
points: Stomach juice (HCl): strongly acidic, roughly pH 1.5–3
Lemon juice and vinegar: acidic
Pure water: 7 (at 25 °C)
Blood: about 7.4 (slightly basic)
Milk of magnesia, soap solution: basic
Acid rain: pH below about 5.6

notes.p: **Baking soda** (NaHCO₃) releases CO₂ when heated or mixed with acid, making cakes rise; it is also an antacid. **Washing soda** (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) softens hard water and is used in cleaning and glass making. **Bleaching powder** (CaOCl₂) disinfects drinking water and bleaches textiles. **Plaster of Paris** sets into gypsum when mixed with water and is used for casts and statues. **Common salt** is the raw material for caustic soda, chlorine and baking soda.

Carbon forms more compounds than any other element because of **tetravalency** (four bonds) and **catenation** (bonding to itself in long chains and rings).

Its allotropes differ only in the arrangement of atoms. Diamond is used for cutting tools and jewellery; graphite in pencils, dry cells and as a moderator in some reactors; activated charcoal adsorbs gases in gas masks and water filters; coke is used as a reducing agent in extracting iron. Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are its main oxides — CO is poisonous because it binds strongly to haemoglobin.

Plants need **N, P and K** in large amounts. Nitrogen promotes leafy growth, phosphorus root development and flowering, and potassium overall vigour and disease resistance.

Natural sources (manure, compost, green manure, biofertilizers) are cheap and improve soil texture but release nutrients slowly. Chemical fertilizers act fast and are nutrient-specific. Overuse leads to soil acidity and water pollution; runoff rich in nitrates and phosphates causes **eutrophication** (algal blooms) in lakes. Balanced use guided by **soil testing** is recommended.
Revise before each mock.
points: Acid: sour, blue litmus → red; base: bitter, red → blue
pH 7 neutral; blood ≈ 7.4
Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in base
NaHCO₃ baking soda; Na₂CO₃·10H₂O washing soda; CaOCl₂ bleaching powder
PoP CaSO₄·½H₂O; gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O
Diamond hard non-conductor; graphite soft conductor
Urea ≈ 46% N; DAP for P; muriate of potash for K

chapters.title: Chemistry: soap, glass, cement, paper, ink, paints, matches & gunpowder

cards.title: Soap and detergents
cards.body: **Saponification**: oil or fat + sodium hydroxide → soap + glycerol. Sodium soaps are hard; potassium soaps are soft. Soap forms scum with hard water, whereas **synthetic detergents** (sulphonates) lather even in hard water.
