cards.title: Glass
cards.body: Ordinary **soda-lime glass** is made by fusing sand (silica), soda ash (Na₂CO₃) and limestone, then cooling slowly (**annealing**). Glass is an amorphous solid. **Borosilicate (Pyrex)** glass resists heat; lead (flint) glass is used for lenses and cut-glass; cobalt oxide colours glass blue.

cards.title: Cement and concrete
cards.body: **Portland cement** is made by heating limestone and clay in a rotary kiln to form **clinker**, then grinding it with a little **gypsum**, which slows down setting. Concrete = cement + sand + gravel + water; reinforced cement concrete (RCC) adds steel bars.

cards.title: Paper
cards.body: Paper is mainly **cellulose** fibre from wood pulp, bamboo, bagasse (sugarcane waste) or rags. The pulp is cooked with chemicals, bleached, mixed with sizing agents (such as rosin and alum) so ink does not spread, and pressed into sheets.

cards.title: Ink
cards.body: Ink is a dye or pigment dispersed in a liquid. Traditional blue-black ink used iron salts with tannic or gallic acid. Printing ink uses carbon black (lamp black) in oil. Election (indelible) ink contains **silver nitrate**, which stains the skin.

cards.title: Paints and varnish
points: Pigment — gives colour and covering power (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, white lead)
Vehicle/binder — a drying oil such as linseed oil
Thinner — turpentine
Drier — speeds up drying
Varnish: resin in a solvent, without pigment

cards.title: Safety matches and gunpowder
cards.body: A safety match head carries **potassium chlorate** and antimony trisulphide; the striking surface on the box has **red phosphorus** and powdered glass, so it lights only on the box. **Gunpowder** is about 75% potassium nitrate, 15% charcoal and 10% sulphur.

cards.q: Soap is a sodium or potassium salt of:
cards.explain: Soaps are salts of long-chain fatty acids formed by saponification of oils and fats.

cards.q: Gunpowder is a mixture of:
cards.explain: Classic black powder is potassium nitrate, charcoal and sulphur.

cards.q: Gypsum is added to cement clinker to:
cards.explain: Gypsum controls (retards) the setting time of cement.

notes.p:
A soap molecule has a long hydrocarbon tail that dissolves in oil and grease and an ionic head that dissolves in water. In water, soap molecules form **micelles** that trap grease and wash it away.

Soap is made by boiling oils (coconut, palm, groundnut) or animal fats with caustic soda; glycerol is a valuable by-product. In hard water, calcium and magnesium ions form insoluble scum with soap, wasting it. **Detergents** do not form scum, but some older detergents are not biodegradable and cause foaming in rivers.

**Glass** is made by melting sand, soda ash and limestone at high temperature and cooling slowly to remove internal stresses. Adding metal oxides gives colour; replacing soda with boric oxide gives heat-resistant **borosilicate glass** used in laboratory ware; adding lead oxide gives brilliant **flint glass** for optical lenses.

**Cement** sets by reacting with water (hydration) and gains strength over weeks, which is why concrete is kept wet (**curing**). Gypsum is added to the clinker so that the cement does not set too quickly to work with.

Paper making follows clear steps.
Step 1: Pulping — wood chips, bamboo or bagasse are broken down to free the cellulose fibres.
Step 2: Bleaching — the pulp is whitened.
Step 3: Sizing and loading — rosin and alum stop ink spreading; fillers like clay improve smoothness.
Step 4: Sheet forming — the pulp is spread, pressed and dried.

Inks combine a colourant with a liquid carrier and a binder. Writing inks use dyes; printing inks use carbon black and oils. The indelible ink used in Indian elections contains silver nitrate, which darkens on exposure to light and cannot be washed off easily.

A **paint** protects and decorates surfaces. The drying oil (linseed) reacts with oxygen to form a tough film; the pigment gives colour and hides the surface; the thinner adjusts flow. Titanium dioxide has largely replaced toxic white lead as a white pigment.

In **safety matches**, the reactive red phosphorus is kept on the box, not on the match head, reducing accidental fires. Striking produces friction heat that converts a trace of red phosphorus to white phosphorus, which ignites and lights the potassium chlorate mixture.

**Gunpowder** burns rapidly because potassium nitrate supplies oxygen to the charcoal and sulphur; it is used in fireworks and in mining and quarrying.
A quick map of raw materials to products.
points: Soap: oils/fats + caustic soda (NaOH)
Glass: sand + soda ash + limestone
Cement: limestone + clay (+ gypsum)
Paper: cellulose from wood, bamboo, bagasse, rags
Paint: pigment + linseed oil + turpentine
Match head: KClO₃ + Sb₂S₃; box: red phosphorus
Gunpowder: KNO₃ + charcoal + sulphur

notes.p: Revise before each mock.
points: Saponification: fat + NaOH → soap + glycerol
Detergents work in hard water
Soda-lime glass; Pyrex = borosilicate; cobalt → blue
Gypsum slows setting of cement
Paper = cellulose; sizing stops ink spreading
Election ink contains silver nitrate
Gunpowder ≈ 75% KNO₃, 15% charcoal, 10% sulphur

cards.title: Cell — the unit of life
cards.body: All living organisms are made of cells. Key organelles: **nucleus** (controls the cell, holds DNA), **mitochondria** (powerhouse, makes ATP), ribosomes (protein synthesis), chloroplasts (photosynthesis, only in plants). Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose; animal cells do not.

cards.title: Human body systems
cards.body: Digestion starts in the mouth (salivary amylase) and absorption mainly happens in the small intestine. The heart has four chambers. Insulin, made by the pancreas, controls blood sugar — its deficiency causes diabetes. Kidneys filter blood through nephrons.
points: Largest gland: liver
Smallest bone: stapes (in the ear)

cards.title: Vitamins and deficiency diseases
points: Vitamin A — night blindness
Vitamin B1 — beriberi
Vitamin C — scurvy
Vitamin D — rickets
Vitamin K — poor blood clotting

cards.title: Blood groups
cards.body: The ABO system has groups A, B, AB and O. Group **O** has no A/B antigens, so O-negative is the universal donor; **AB** has no anti-A/anti-B antibodies, so AB-positive is the universal recipient. Rh factor decides positive or negative.

cards.title: Diseases and their causes
cards.body: Bacterial: tuberculosis, typhoid, cholera. Viral: COVID-19, measles, polio, dengue, AIDS. Protozoan: malaria (Plasmodium, spread by female Anopheles mosquito). Vaccines train the immune system before infection.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: As per the UPSC syllabus, General Science is about 40 marks in GAT. Focus on human body, nutrition, diseases and basic plant biology from NCERT Class 6–10 Science. Make one table of disease → pathogen → vector.

cards.q: Deficiency of vitamin C causes:
cards.explain: Vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy (bleeding gums, weak tissue).

cards.q: Insulin is secreted by the:
cards.explain: Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas.

cards.q: Malaria is caused by:
cards.explain: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and spread by the female Anopheles mosquito.

notes.p:
The **cell** is the basic structural and functional unit of life (cell theory: Schleiden and Schwann). **Prokaryotic** cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus; **eukaryotic** cells (plants, animals, fungi) do.

Organelles you must know: **nucleus** (controls the cell, holds DNA), **mitochondria** ("powerhouse", aerobic respiration makes ATP), **ribosomes** (protein synthesis), **endoplasmic reticulum** and **Golgi body** (transport and packaging), **lysosomes** ("suicide bags", digestive enzymes). Plant cells also have a **cell wall** of cellulose, **chloroplasts** (photosynthesis) and a large **vacuole**.

Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll. The oxygen released comes from water.

A balanced diet contains carbohydrates and fats (energy), proteins (growth and repair), vitamins and minerals (protection), water and roughage. Vitamins A, D, E and K are **fat-soluble**; B and C are **water-soluble**.
points: Vitamin A — night blindness
Vitamin B1 (thiamine) — beriberi
Vitamin C — scurvy (bleeding gums)
Vitamin D — rickets in children (made in skin with sunlight)
Vitamin K — needed for blood clotting
Iodine — goitre; Iron — anaemia; Calcium — weak bones and teeth
Protein deficiency — kwashiorkor; protein-energy deficiency — marasmus

notes.p:
**Blood:** red blood cells carry oxygen using **haemoglobin**; white blood cells fight infection; platelets help clotting. In the ABO system, **O negative** is the universal donor for red cells and **AB positive** the universal recipient. The **heart** has four chambers; normal adult blood pressure is about **120/80 mmHg**. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins towards it (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — a classic trick question).

**Digestion:** saliva contains amylase (starch digestion begins in the mouth); the stomach secretes HCl and pepsin; the **liver** is the largest gland and makes bile; most absorption happens in the **small intestine** (villi). The **kidneys** filter blood through nephrons.

An adult has **206 bones**; the **femur** is the longest and the **stapes** (in the ear) the smallest. Humans have **46 chromosomes** (23 pairs); a baby's sex is decided by whether the father's sperm carries X or Y.

**Hormones:** insulin (pancreas) controls blood sugar — its deficiency causes diabetes; thyroxine (thyroid) controls metabolism; adrenaline prepares the body for "fight or flight".
Grouping diseases by cause makes them easy to remember:
points: Bacterial: tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, diphtheria, leprosy
Viral: COVID-19, polio, measles, rabies, AIDS (HIV), dengue, chickenpox, influenza
Protozoan: malaria (Plasmodium, spread by female Anopheles mosquito), kala-azar
Fungal: ringworm, athlete's foot
Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses
BCG vaccine protects against tuberculosis
Dengue is spread by the Aedes mosquito

notes.p: Don't confuse "vaccine" (prevents) with "antibiotic" (treats bacterial infection). Penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic, was discovered by **Alexander Fleming**; the smallpox vaccine came from **Edward Jenner**. Remember that malaria is caused by a protozoan, not a virus or bacterium — the mosquito is only the carrier (vector).
These lines answer a large share of NDA biology questions.
points: Mitochondria = powerhouse; ribosomes = protein synthesis
Vit A night blindness, B1 beriberi, C scurvy, D rickets, K clotting
O− universal donor; AB+ universal recipient
206 bones; femur longest; stapes smallest
46 chromosomes; father's chromosome decides sex
Malaria — Plasmodium via female Anopheles
Insulin from pancreas; deficiency → diabetes

cards.title: Living vs non-living
cards.body: Living things show **nutrition, respiration, growth from within, reproduction, excretion, response to stimuli** and are made of cells. Non-living things may grow by adding material from outside (crystals) but show no metabolism. **Viruses** are borderline: they reproduce only inside a host cell and can be crystallised outside it.

cards.title: Discovery of the cell
cards.body: **Robert Hooke** (1665) coined "cell" after seeing cork under a microscope. **Leeuwenhoek** first observed living cells. **Schleiden and Schwann** proposed the cell theory (1838–39), and **Virchow** added that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

cards.title: Prokaryotes and eukaryotes
cards.body: **Prokaryotic** cells (bacteria, blue-green algae) lack a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles. **Eukaryotic** cells (plants, animals, fungi, protists) have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.

cards.title: Cell organelles
points: Nucleus — control centre; holds DNA in chromosomes
Mitochondria — "powerhouse"; make ATP by respiration
Chloroplasts — photosynthesis (plants)
Ribosomes — protein synthesis
Golgi body — packaging and secretion; lysosomes — "suicide bags"
Endoplasmic reticulum — transport network

cards.title: Plant vs animal cells
cards.body: Plant cells have a rigid **cellulose cell wall**, **chloroplasts** and a large central vacuole. Animal cells lack a cell wall and chloroplasts, have small vacuoles, and have **centrioles** that help in cell division.

cards.title: Protoplasm
cards.body: **Protoplasm** is the living substance of the cell (cytoplasm + nucleoplasm), a term introduced by Purkinje; T. H. Huxley called it the "physical basis of life". It is mostly water with proteins, fats, carbohydrates, nucleic acids and salts.

cards.title: Plant tissues
points: Meristematic — dividing tissue at root/shoot tips (apical), sides (lateral) and nodes (intercalary)
Simple permanent — parenchyma (storage), collenchyma (flexible support), sclerenchyma (hard support, e.g. husk of coconut)
Complex — xylem carries water and minerals upward; phloem carries food

cards.title: Animal tissues
points: Epithelial — covering and lining (skin, gut lining)
Connective — blood, bone, cartilage; ligament joins bone to bone, tendon joins muscle to bone
Muscular — striated (voluntary), smooth (involuntary), cardiac (heart)
Nervous — neurons carry impulses

cards.q: Which organelle is called the "powerhouse of the cell"?
cards.explain: Mitochondria release energy as ATP through cellular respiration.

cards.q: A tendon connects:
cards.explain: Tendons join muscles to bones; ligaments join bones to bones.

notes.p:
All living organisms share a set of features: they are made of **cells**, obtain and use energy (**nutrition** and **respiration**), **grow** by building new material inside their bodies, **reproduce**, **excrete** wastes and **respond** to their surroundings. Plants also move — leaves turn to light and tendrils coil — but more slowly than animals.

The **virus** is a well-known exception: outside a host it behaves like a chemical particle; inside a host cell it uses the cell's machinery to multiply.

notes.h: The cell: basic unit of life
notes.p:
The cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all life processes. Unicellular organisms (Amoeba, Paramecium, bacteria) do everything with a single cell; multicellular organisms divide labour among specialised cells.

The **plasma membrane** is selectively permeable: it allows some substances in and out but not others. Water moves across it by **osmosis**, from a dilute to a concentrated solution. Placing raisins in water makes them swell; placing a plant cell in strong salt solution makes it shrink (**plasmolysis**).

The largest single cell is the ostrich egg; nerve cells are among the longest cells in the human body.
Think of the cell as a factory.
points: Nucleus: the head office holding instructions (DNA, genes, chromosomes)
Mitochondria: the power plant, with their own DNA
Ribosomes: assembly lines for proteins
Endoplasmic reticulum: internal roads; rough ER has ribosomes, smooth ER makes lipids
Golgi apparatus: packing and dispatch
Lysosomes: waste disposal with digestive enzymes
Plastids: chloroplasts (green), chromoplasts (coloured), leucoplasts (storage)

notes.p:
**Meristems** are regions of active cell division. Apical meristem increases length; lateral meristem (cambium) increases girth; intercalary meristem at nodes helps grasses regrow after grazing.

Permanent tissues have stopped dividing. **Parenchyma** stores food; **collenchyma** gives flexible support to young stems and leaf stalks; **sclerenchyma** has thick, dead cells that make husks and seed coats hard. **Xylem** (vessels and tracheids) carries water and minerals from the roots upward; **phloem** (sieve tubes) carries food in both directions. Annual rings in a tree trunk are layers of xylem.

**Epithelium** forms the skin and lines organs. **Connective tissue** binds and supports: blood is a fluid connective tissue; bone is hard because of calcium phosphate; cartilage at the nose tip and ear is flexible. **Muscle** tissue contracts: skeletal (striated) muscles are under our control, smooth muscles in the gut are not, and cardiac muscle works rhythmically without tiring. **Nervous tissue** is made of neurons with dendrites, a cell body and an axon. **Blood** carries oxygen, food, hormones and wastes; **lymph** returns tissue fluid to the blood and helps in immunity.
Revise before each mock.
points: Hooke named the cell (1665); cell theory — Schleiden & Schwann
Prokaryotes lack a nuclear membrane
Mitochondria — powerhouse; ribosomes — proteins; lysosomes — suicide bags
Plant cell: wall, chloroplasts, big vacuole
Xylem — water up; phloem — food
Ligament: bone–bone; tendon: muscle–bone
Protoplasm: "physical basis of life"

chapters.title: Biology: growth & reproduction in plants and animals

cards.title: Vegetative propagation
cards.body: New plants grow from roots, stems or leaves.
points: Potato — stem tuber; ginger — rhizome; onion — bulb
Sweet potato — root; Bryophyllum — buds on leaf margins
Artificial: cutting (rose), layering, grafting (mango, citrus), tissue culture

cards.title: Asexual reproduction in simple organisms
points: Binary fission — Amoeba, bacteria
Multiple fission — Plasmodium
Budding — Hydra, yeast
Fragmentation — Spirogyra
Spores — Rhizopus (bread mould), ferns
Regeneration — Planaria

cards.title: The flower
cards.body: The **stamen** (anther + filament) is male and makes pollen. The **pistil/carpel** (stigma, style, ovary) is female. **Pollination** moves pollen to the stigma — by wind, insects, water or birds. After fertilisation the **ovary becomes the fruit** and the **ovule becomes the seed**.

cards.title: Double fertilisation
cards.body: In flowering plants, one male gamete fuses with the egg to form the zygote (embryo), and the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form the **endosperm**, the food store of the seed. This double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms.

cards.title: Plant hormones
points: Auxin — cell elongation; bending towards light (phototropism)
Gibberellin — stem elongation, seed germination
Cytokinin — cell division; delays ageing
Abscisic acid — stress hormone; dormancy, closes stomata
Ethylene — fruit ripening (a gas)

cards.title: Reproduction in animals
cards.body: Sexual reproduction joins a sperm and an egg. Fertilisation is **external** in most fish and frogs and **internal** in reptiles, birds and mammals. **Oviparous** animals lay eggs (birds, most reptiles); **viviparous** animals give birth to young (most mammals).

cards.title: Human reproduction
cards.body: Testes make sperm and testosterone; ovaries release an egg about once a month and make oestrogen and progesterone. **Fertilisation** normally occurs in the **fallopian tube (oviduct)**; the embryo implants in the uterus and is nourished through the **placenta**. Pregnancy lasts about nine months.

cards.title: Growth and metamorphosis
cards.body: In frogs, the tadpole changes into an adult under the control of **thyroxine**. Insects such as butterflies pass through egg → larva → pupa → adult. In humans, **growth hormone** from the pituitary controls growth; too little causes dwarfism and too much gigantism.

cards.q: Which plant hormone promotes fruit ripening?
cards.explain: Ethylene, a gaseous hormone, speeds ripening.

cards.q: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the:
cards.explain: The sperm meets the egg in the fallopian tube (oviduct).

notes.p:
Asexual reproduction needs only one parent and produces genetically identical offspring (clones). It is fast and useful when conditions are stable.

Single-celled organisms divide by **fission** — Amoeba splits into two, while the malaria parasite Plasmodium splits into many. **Budding** forms an outgrowth that detaches (Hydra, yeast). **Spores** are light and survive harsh conditions; bread mould spreads this way. Planaria can regrow a complete body from a small piece (**regeneration**).
Many crops are grown from vegetative parts because the new plants are identical to the parent and mature faster.
points: Natural: potato eyes (buds on a stem tuber), ginger rhizome, onion bulb, Bryophyllum leaf buds
Cutting: sugarcane, rose and money plant grow from stem pieces
Layering: a branch is bent into soil and roots before separation (jasmine)
Grafting: a scion of a good variety is joined to a hardy stock (mango, apple, citrus)
Tissue culture (micropropagation): many plants from a few cells, used for orchids and bananas

notes.p:
A complete flower has sepals, petals, stamens and pistil. Pollen lands on the stigma and grows a **pollen tube** down the style to the ovule. **Double fertilisation** then forms the zygote and the endosperm.

After fertilisation the petals fall, the ovary ripens into the **fruit** and the ovules into **seeds**. Seeds are dispersed by wind (winged or hairy seeds such as cotton), water (coconut), animals (hooked seeds) or by bursting fruits (balsam). A seed **germinates** when it gets water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.

Plant growth is controlled by hormones (phytohormones). **Auxins** collect on the shaded side of a stem, making it grow faster there, so the stem bends towards light. **Gibberellins** make stems elongate and are used to increase the size of grapes. **Cytokinins** promote cell division. **Abscisic acid** inhibits growth and helps plants survive drought. **Ethylene** is used commercially to ripen fruits such as bananas and mangoes; calcium carbide, sometimes misused for ripening, is harmful and banned for this purpose.

notes.h: Reproduction and growth in animals and humans
notes.p:
Animals that reproduce sexually produce **gametes** by a special cell division (meiosis) that halves the chromosome number; fertilisation restores it. Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) in body cells and 23 in each gamete.

The sex of a child depends on the father's sperm: an X-bearing sperm gives a girl (XX) and a Y-bearing sperm gives a boy (XY). The **placenta** supplies oxygen and nutrients to the foetus and removes its wastes. Growth in animals is controlled by hormones such as growth hormone and thyroxine; in frogs, thyroxine triggers metamorphosis, and iodine deficiency can delay it.
Revise before each mock.
points: Potato — stem tuber; ginger — rhizome; onion — bulb
Amoeba — binary fission; Hydra, yeast — budding
Ovary → fruit; ovule → seed
Double fertilisation → zygote + endosperm
Auxin — phototropism; ethylene — ripening; ABA — stress
Fertilisation in the fallopian tube; placenta nourishes the foetus
Father's sperm (X or Y) decides the sex of the child

cards.title: Digestive system
points: Mouth: salivary amylase starts starch digestion
Stomach: HCl and pepsin digest proteins
Liver: largest gland; bile emulsifies fats
Pancreas: digestive enzymes and insulin
Small intestine: completes digestion; villi absorb food
Large intestine: absorbs water

cards.title: Respiratory system
cards.body: Air passes nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → **alveoli**, where oxygen enters the blood and CO₂ leaves. The **diaphragm** contracts to draw air in. During heavy exercise muscles respire anaerobically and form **lactic acid**, causing cramps.

cards.title: Heart and circulation
cards.body: The human heart has **four chambers**: two atria and two ventricles. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins towards it — the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein are the exceptions in oxygen content.

cards.title: Blood
points: RBCs: carry O₂ with haemoglobin; live about 120 days; made in bone marrow
WBCs: fight infection
Platelets: help clotting
Normal adult BP is about 120/80 mm Hg; resting pulse about 72 per minute
O negative — universal donor; AB positive — universal recipient

cards.title: Excretory system
cards.body: The **kidneys** filter blood through about a million **nephrons** each, forming urine that flows via ureters to the bladder. **Urea** is made in the liver from excess amino acids. When kidneys fail, **dialysis** filters the blood artificially.

cards.title: Nervous system
points: Cerebrum — thinking, memory, voluntary actions
Cerebellum — balance and coordination
Medulla oblongata — involuntary actions: heartbeat, breathing
Spinal cord — reflex actions
Neuron — the basic unit; synapse — gap between neurons

cards.title: Endocrine glands
points: Pituitary — "master gland"; growth hormone
Thyroid — thyroxine; iodine deficiency → goitre
Adrenal — adrenaline ("fight or flight")
Pancreas (islets of Langerhans) — insulin; deficiency → diabetes
Testes/ovaries — sex hormones

cards.title: Skeleton
cards.body: An adult human has **206 bones**. The **femur** (thigh bone) is the longest and the **stapes** in the middle ear is the smallest. Joints include ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (knee, elbow) and pivot (neck).

cards.q: The largest gland in the human body is the:
cards.explain: The liver is the largest gland; it secretes bile.

cards.q: Which part of the brain maintains balance and posture?
cards.explain: The cerebellum coordinates muscular activity and balance.

notes.p: Digestion breaks large food molecules into small ones the body can absorb. Starch digestion begins in the mouth (amylase). In the stomach, **hydrochloric acid** kills germs and activates **pepsin** for proteins. In the small intestine, bile from the liver emulsifies fats, and pancreatic and intestinal enzymes finish the job — carbohydrates to glucose, proteins to amino acids, fats to fatty acids and glycerol. Finger-like **villi** greatly increase the surface for absorption. The large intestine absorbs water and forms faeces.

**Breathing** is the physical movement of air; **respiration** is the release of energy from food in cells. Aerobic respiration (with oxygen) gives carbon dioxide, water and much energy; anaerobic respiration gives less energy and, in muscles, lactic acid.

The lungs contain millions of alveoli with thin walls and a rich blood supply. Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries most of the oxygen. Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen.

Humans have **double circulation**: blood passes through the heart twice in each full circuit — once to the lungs (pulmonary) and once to the body (systemic). Valves keep blood flowing one way; their closing makes the "lub-dub" sounds heard with a stethoscope.

Blood groups (A, B, AB, O) were discovered by **Karl Landsteiner**. The Rh factor adds positive or negative. Group O negative can donate to all groups in an emergency; AB positive can receive from all. Blood pressure is measured with a **sphygmomanometer**.

Kidneys remove urea and excess salts and water, keeping the blood's composition steady. Lungs excrete CO₂; skin removes some salts and water as sweat.

The **nervous system** gives fast responses through electrical impulses. A **reflex action**, like pulling your hand from a hot object, is controlled by the spinal cord before the brain is aware.

The **endocrine system** gives slower, longer-lasting control through hormones in the blood. Insulin lowers blood sugar; adrenaline raises heart rate in emergencies; thyroxine controls the rate of metabolism.

The skeleton supports the body, protects organs (skull — brain, ribs — heart and lungs), makes blood cells in the bone marrow and stores calcium. A newborn has more bones than an adult because some fuse during growth.
points: Longest bone: femur; smallest: stapes (ear)
Ball-and-socket joint: shoulder, hip — movement in all directions
Hinge joint: knee, elbow — one plane
Pivot joint: between the first two neck vertebrae
Muscles work in pairs, e.g. biceps and triceps

notes.p: Revise before each mock.
points: Liver — largest gland, bile; pancreas — insulin
Alveoli — gas exchange; diaphragm — breathing
Four-chambered heart; double circulation
RBC life about 120 days; O− universal donor; AB+ universal recipient
Nephron — unit of kidney; urea made in liver
Cerebellum — balance; medulla — involuntary actions
206 bones; femur longest; stapes smallest

cards.title: Kinds of disease
cards.body: **Communicable** diseases spread through pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi, worms). **Non-communicable** diseases (diabetes, heart disease, cancer) do not spread from person to person. Others are **deficiency** diseases or **genetic** disorders such as haemophilia, colour blindness and sickle-cell anaemia.

cards.title: Bacterial diseases
points: Tuberculosis — Mycobacterium tuberculosis; BCG vaccine
Cholera — Vibrio cholerae; contaminated water
Typhoid — Salmonella typhi; Widal test
Diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus — DPT vaccine
Leprosy, plague

cards.title: Viral diseases
cards.body: Common cold, influenza, measles, mumps, chickenpox, polio, hepatitis, rabies, dengue, chikungunya, AIDS (caused by HIV) and COVID-19 (caused by SARS-CoV-2). **Antibiotics do not work against viruses**; prevention relies on vaccines, hygiene and some antiviral drugs.

cards.title: Protozoan and fungal diseases
points: Malaria — Plasmodium; spread by female Anopheles mosquito
Kala-azar — Leishmania; spread by sandfly
Amoebic dysentery — Entamoeba histolytica
Sleeping sickness — Trypanosoma; tsetse fly
Fungal: ringworm, athlete's foot

cards.title: Vectors to remember
points: Female Anopheles — malaria
Aedes — dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever
Culex — filariasis (elephantiasis)
Rat flea — plague
Housefly — carries germs of cholera, typhoid, dysentery

cards.title: Endemic, epidemic, pandemic
cards.body: An **endemic** disease is always present in a region. An **epidemic** is a sudden rise in cases in a community or region. A **pandemic** is an epidemic spreading across many countries or continents, such as COVID-19.

cards.title: Prevention and treatment
cards.body: **Vaccination** trains the immune system; Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine (1796). **Penicillin**, the first widely used antibiotic, was discovered by Alexander Fleming (1928). Safe water, sanitation, mosquito control, hand washing and isolation of patients break the chain of infection.

cards.title: Milestones
cards.body: The WHO declared smallpox eradicated worldwide in 1980. India was certified polio-free by the WHO in 2014. For current disease-control programmes and targets, check the latest Ministry of Health and WHO releases.

cards.q: Malaria is transmitted by the:
cards.explain: The Plasmodium parasite is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito.

cards.q: BCG vaccine protects against:
cards.explain: BCG (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin) is given against tuberculosis.

notes.p:
The WHO defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease. Diseases may be **acute** (short, like a cold) or **chronic** (long-lasting, like diabetes).

Communicable diseases spread by air (TB, influenza), water and food (cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A), contact (ringworm), body fluids (HIV, hepatitis B) or vectors (malaria, dengue). Knowing the route tells you the prevention: masks for air, boiled water for water-borne diseases, nets and repellents for vectors.
Learn the cause together with the disease.
points: Bacteria: TB, cholera, typhoid, diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, leprosy, plague, pneumonia (often)
Viruses: polio, measles, mumps, rabies, hepatitis, influenza, dengue, chikungunya, AIDS, COVID-19
Protozoa: malaria, kala-azar, amoebic dysentery, sleeping sickness
Fungi: ringworm, athlete's foot, some skin and lung infections
Worms: roundworm, tapeworm, filaria

notes.p:
An **epidemic** occurs when many people in an area fall ill with the same disease within a short time, often after floods (water-borne diseases) or during the monsoon (mosquito-borne diseases). Crowding, poor sanitation and lack of immunity make outbreaks worse.

To control an epidemic, health authorities trace and isolate cases, treat patients, vaccinate where possible, chlorinate water, remove stagnant water where mosquitoes breed and spread awareness. **Quarantine** keeps exposed but healthy people apart until it is clear they are not infected.

A **vaccine** contains a killed or weakened pathogen, or a part of it, which teaches the immune system to recognise the real pathogen. Childhood vaccines in India cover diseases such as TB (BCG), polio, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, measles and hepatitis B; check the current Universal Immunisation Programme for the full list.

**Antibiotics** kill or stop bacteria. Misusing them — taking them for viral infections or stopping the course early — encourages **antibiotic resistance**. **ORS** (oral rehydration solution) saves lives in diarrhoea and cholera by replacing lost water and salts.

**Immunity** is the body's ability to resist infection. **Innate** immunity is present from birth: skin, mucus, stomach acid, tears and white blood cells that engulf germs. **Acquired** immunity develops after exposure to a pathogen or a vaccine, when lymphocytes make **antibodies** and remember the invader. **Active** immunity is produced by one's own body (after infection or vaccination) and lasts long; **passive** immunity comes from ready-made antibodies, such as those passed from mother to baby through breast milk, and is short-lived. HIV damages helper T-cells, weakening the whole immune system.

Lifestyle factors drive many non-communicable diseases: tobacco (cancers, heart disease), excess salt (high blood pressure), lack of exercise and high sugar intake (type 2 diabetes). Regular exercise, a balanced diet and avoiding tobacco and alcohol reduce the risk.

**Haemophilia** (blood does not clot properly) and **colour blindness** are X-linked and more common in males. **Sickle-cell anaemia** changes the shape of red blood cells. **Down syndrome** results from an extra copy of chromosome 21.
Revise before each mock.
points: TB, cholera, typhoid — bacteria; polio, dengue, AIDS — viruses
Malaria — Plasmodium — female Anopheles
Dengue/chikungunya — Aedes; filaria — Culex
BCG — TB; Widal test — typhoid
Antibiotics do not work on viruses
Smallpox eradicated (1980); India polio-free (2014)
Epidemic = regional outbreak; pandemic = worldwide

cards.title: Food as fuel
cards.body: Food supplies energy, materials for growth and repair, and substances that regulate body processes. Energy values: carbohydrates and proteins give about **4 kcal (≈ 17 kJ) per gram**; fats give about **9 kcal (≈ 37 kJ) per gram** — more than twice as much.

cards.title: Seven constituents of food
points: Carbohydrates — main energy source (cereals, potatoes, sugar)
Proteins — body building and repair (pulses, milk, eggs, meat)
Fats — concentrated energy, insulation (oils, butter, nuts)
Vitamins and minerals — protective and regulatory
Water — transport, temperature control
Roughage (dietary fibre) — prevents constipation

cards.title: Proteins and their deficiency
cards.body: Proteins are made of **amino acids** and form enzymes, hormones, antibodies and muscles. Severe protein deficiency in children causes **kwashiorkor** (swollen belly, oedema); a lack of both protein and energy causes **marasmus** (extreme wasting).

cards.title: Vitamins and deficiency diseases
points: A — night blindness (carrots, green leaves, milk)
B1 (thiamine) — beriberi; B3 (niacin) — pellagra; B12 — pernicious anaemia
C — scurvy, bleeding gums (citrus, amla)
D — rickets in children (sunlight, fish oil)
K — needed for blood clotting
Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K; water-soluble: B group, C

cards.title: Minerals
points: Iron — haemoglobin; deficiency → anaemia
Iodine — thyroxine; deficiency → goitre
Calcium and phosphorus — bones and teeth
Sodium and potassium — nerve function, water balance
Fluoride — strong teeth (excess causes fluorosis)

cards.title: Balanced diet
cards.body: A **balanced diet** contains all nutrients in the right amounts for a person's age, sex, body size and activity. A soldier in training needs more energy than a person at a desk; growing children and pregnant women need extra protein, iron and calcium.

cards.title: Simple food tests
points: Starch: iodine solution turns blue-black
Protein: biuret test gives violet colour
Fat: leaves a translucent grease spot on paper
Glucose: Benedict's solution gives a brick-red colour on heating

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Vitamin–disease pairs are among the most frequently asked GK questions. Learn them as a table and revise weekly; also note which vitamins are fat-soluble (A, D, E, K), since the body stores these.

cards.q: Night blindness is caused by a deficiency of:
cards.explain: Vitamin A is needed to form the visual pigment in the retina.

cards.q: Which nutrient gives the most energy per gram?
cards.explain: Fat gives about 9 kcal/g, more than twice carbohydrates or proteins.

notes.p:
Food provides **energy** for every activity, **materials** for growth and repair, and **protective** substances that keep the body working properly. The energy value of food is measured in kilocalories (kcal) or kilojoules (kJ). A physically active young adult needs considerably more energy each day than an inactive one; exact needs vary, so check standard dietary guidelines (such as those from ICMR–NIN) for figures.

**Example.** 10 g of fat supplies about 90 kcal, while 10 g of sugar supplies about 40 kcal — which is why fried snacks are so energy-dense.

**Carbohydrates** include sugars (glucose, sucrose), starch and cellulose. Humans cannot digest cellulose, but it acts as roughage that keeps the gut healthy.

**Fats** store energy, cushion organs, insulate the body and help absorb fat-soluble vitamins. Excess saturated and trans fats raise the risk of heart disease.

**Proteins** are needed in larger amounts during growth, pregnancy and recovery from injury. Pulses with cereals (dal–rice, dal–roti) together provide a better mix of amino acids than either alone.
Vitamins are needed in tiny amounts, but their absence causes specific deficiency diseases.
points: Vitamin A (retinol): healthy eyes and skin; deficiency — night blindness, xerophthalmia
Vitamin B1: beriberi (weak nerves and muscles); common where diets rely on polished rice
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid): scurvy; destroyed by prolonged cooking
Vitamin D: absorption of calcium; deficiency — rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults); made in skin in sunlight
Vitamin E: antioxidant
Vitamin K: blood clotting; made partly by gut bacteria

notes.p:
**Iron** deficiency anaemia is widespread in India, especially among women and children; green leafy vegetables, jaggery and pulses provide iron, and vitamin C improves its absorption. **Iodised salt** prevents goitre. **Calcium** from milk and ragi builds bones.

**Water** makes up roughly 60% of adult body weight. It dissolves nutrients, carries wastes and controls temperature through sweating. Dehydration during long marches or hot weather can be dangerous, so regular drinking is essential. **Roughage** from whole grains, fruits and vegetables prevents constipation.

A balanced plate includes cereals or millets for energy, pulses, milk, eggs or meat for protein, vegetables and fruits for vitamins, minerals and fibre, and a small amount of fats and sugar.

**Example.** A cadet's breakfast of poha with peanuts, a boiled egg, a glass of milk and a banana provides carbohydrates, protein, fats, calcium, potassium and fibre — a good balance before physical training.

Malnutrition includes both **undernutrition** (deficiencies) and **overnutrition** (obesity). Food adulteration — such as mixing starch in milk or coloured sawdust in spices — reduces quality and can harm health.
Revise before each mock.
points: Carbs and proteins ≈ 4 kcal/g; fats ≈ 9 kcal/g
Kwashiorkor — protein; marasmus — protein + energy
A night blindness; B1 beriberi; C scurvy; D rickets; K clotting
Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K
Iron — anaemia; iodine — goitre
Iodine test: starch → blue-black
Balanced diet depends on age, sex and activity

chapters.title: The solar system, meteors, comets & eclipses

cards.title: The solar system
cards.body: The Sun, eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and meteoroids. The Sun holds about 99.8% of the system's mass. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union reclassified **Pluto** as a **dwarf planet**.

cards.title: Order of planets
cards.body: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four are small, rocky **terrestrial** planets; the outer four are **giant** planets made mostly of gas and ice. Mnemonic: "My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles".

cards.title: Planet facts often asked
points: Mercury — smallest, closest to the Sun
Venus — hottest and brightest planet; rotates east to west; "morning/evening star"
Mars — "Red Planet" (iron oxide); Olympus Mons
Jupiter — largest; Great Red Spot
Saturn — prominent rings; least dense
Uranus — rotates on its side; Neptune — farthest

cards.title: The Moon
cards.body: Earth's only natural satellite is about 3.84 lakh km away. We always see the same face because it rotates once in the time it takes to orbit Earth. It has almost no atmosphere, so there is no sound or weather, and temperatures swing widely.

cards.title: Asteroids, comets and meteors
cards.body: **Asteroids** are rocky bodies, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter. **Comets** are balls of ice and dust; near the Sun they develop a tail that points **away from the Sun**. Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years. **Meteors** ("shooting stars") burn up in the atmosphere; pieces that reach the ground are **meteorites**.

cards.title: Solar eclipse
cards.body: The **Moon comes between the Sun and Earth**, on a **new moon** day. It can be total, partial or **annular** (when the Moon is farther away and a ring of the Sun remains visible). Never look at the Sun directly; use certified solar filters.

cards.title: Lunar eclipse
cards.body: **Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon**, on a **full moon** night. The Moon often looks reddish because Earth's atmosphere bends red light into the shadow. Eclipses do not occur every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's.

cards.title: Stars and distances
cards.body: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth. A **light-year** is the distance light travels in a year (about 9.46 × 10¹² km) — a unit of distance, not time. The nearest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away.

cards.q: Which planet is called the "Red Planet"?
cards.explain: Iron oxide (rust) on its surface makes Mars look red.

cards.q: A lunar eclipse can occur only on a:
cards.explain: Earth must be between the Sun and the Moon, which happens at full moon.

notes.p:
The **Sun** is a medium-sized star powered by **nuclear fusion** of hydrogen into helium in its core. Its gravity holds the solar system together.

Planets move in elliptical orbits in the same direction around the Sun. Mercury has the shortest year (about 88 days); Neptune the longest (about 165 Earth years). Venus has an extremely thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun. Jupiter is so large that more than a thousand Earths could fit inside it.

Earth is the only planet known to support life, thanks to liquid water, a protective atmosphere and a suitable distance from the Sun. It rotates once in about 24 hours (day and night) and revolves once in about 365¼ days (the year).

The Moon shows **phases** because we see different portions of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth — new moon, crescent, half, gibbous, full and back. The Moon's gravity, together with the Sun's, causes **tides**. India's lunar missions (the Chandrayaan series) have studied the Moon; check ISRO's official site for the latest mission details.

notes.h: Small bodies: asteroids, comets and meteors
notes.p:
**Asteroids** range from pebbles to hundreds of kilometres across; Ceres, the largest object in the main belt, is now classed as a dwarf planet.

**Comets** come from the cold outer solar system. As they approach the Sun, ice turns to gas and releases dust, forming a glowing head (coma) and a long tail pushed outward by sunlight and the solar wind.

**Meteor showers** occur when Earth passes through debris left by a comet. Most meteoroids burn up high in the atmosphere due to friction; a rare large one can survive as a meteorite.
Eclipses are caused by shadows and depend on alignment.
points: Solar eclipse: Sun–Moon–Earth in line; occurs at new moon; seen only from places within the Moon's shadow
Total solar eclipse: the Sun's corona becomes visible
Annular solar eclipse: Moon too far to cover the Sun fully; a "ring of fire" remains
Lunar eclipse: Sun–Earth–Moon in line; occurs at full moon; visible from the whole night side of Earth
Eclipses are not monthly because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbit

notes.p: Stars are huge balls of hot gas. Their colour shows their temperature: blue stars are hottest, red stars cooler. A **constellation** is a recognisable pattern of stars, such as Ursa Major (Saptarishi) and Orion. The **Pole Star** (Dhruva) lies almost above Earth's north pole, so it appears fixed and has guided travellers and sailors for centuries. Distances to stars are measured in light-years.
Revise before each mock.
points: Eight planets; Pluto a dwarf planet since 2006

Mars red; Saturn rings; Uranus rotates on its side
Comet tail points away from the Sun; Halley about 76 years
Meteor burns up; meteorite reaches the ground
Solar eclipse — new moon; lunar eclipse — full moon
Light-year is a unit of distance

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Questions usually pair a scientist with a discovery or an Indian institution. Make a three-column table — name, field, key achievement — and add one line whenever a scientist appears in the news (anniversaries, awards).

cards.q: C. V. Raman received the Nobel Prize in Physics in:
cards.explain: Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for the Raman effect; National Science Day (28 February) marks its discovery.

cards.q: Penicillin was discovered by:
cards.explain: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.

notes.p:
India has a long scientific tradition. **Aryabhata** wrote the *Aryabhatiya* and proposed that Earth rotates on its axis; India's first satellite (1975) was named after him. **Brahmagupta** gave rules for operations with zero and negative numbers. The decimal place-value system with zero spread from India to the wider world.

In medicine, **Charaka** wrote on diagnosis and treatment, and **Sushruta** described surgical procedures, including early plastic surgery of the nose. **Bhaskara II** wrote *Lilavati*, a popular mathematics text.
The twentieth century produced world-class Indian scientists working with limited resources.
points: C. V. Raman discovered the scattering effect named after him (announced on 28 February 1928) — now celebrated as National Science Day
J. C. Bose showed that plants respond to stimuli and built sensitive instruments such as the crescograph
S. N. Bose's work with Einstein led to Bose–Einstein statistics
Homi Bhabha and Vikram Sarabhai built India's atomic energy and space programmes
A. P. J. Abdul Kalam led work on SLV-3 and the missile programme, and later became President (2002–2007)
Ramanujan, largely self-taught, made deep contributions to number theory

notes.p: **Isaac Newton** unified falling apples and orbiting planets with the law of gravitation. **Galileo** used the telescope to discover Jupiter's four largest moons and showed that falling bodies accelerate equally (ignoring air resistance). **Michael Faraday** discovered electromagnetic induction, the basis of generators. **Albert Einstein** gave the theories of relativity and E = mc²; his Nobel Prize was for explaining the photoelectric effect. **Marie Curie** was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. **Ernest Rutherford** discovered the nucleus and **Niels Bohr** modelled electron orbits.

**Charles Darwin** explained evolution by natural selection after his voyage on HMS Beagle. **Gregor Mendel** discovered the basic laws of heredity using pea plants. **Louis Pasteur** disproved spontaneous generation and developed pasteurisation and a rabies vaccine. **Robert Koch** identified the bacteria causing tuberculosis and cholera. **Edward Jenner** pioneered vaccination against smallpox. **Alexander Fleming** discovered penicillin. **Karl Landsteiner** discovered blood groups. **Watson and Crick**, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, proposed the double-helix structure of DNA.
A few methods make this topic easy.
points: Group scientists by field and by country

Check anniversaries in the news; they often prompt questions

cards.title: Indus Valley Civilisation
cards.body: A Bronze Age urban civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE at its mature phase). Known for planned cities, grid streets, covered drains and standard weights. Key sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro (Great Bath), **Lothal** (dockyard), Dholavira, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi.

cards.title: Vedic age, Buddhism and Jainism
cards.body: The Rigveda is the oldest Veda. In the 6th century BCE, Gautama Buddha (Buddhism) and Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara (Jainism), challenged ritualism. Buddha gave his first sermon at Sarnath.

cards.title: Mauryas and Guptas
cards.body: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire with Chanakya's guidance. **Ashoka** turned to Buddhism after the Kalinga War and spread dhamma through edicts. The Gupta period is called a golden age for art, science and literature — Aryabhata and Kalidasa belong to this era.

cards.title: Delhi Sultanate and Mughals
cards.body: The Delhi Sultanate began in 1206 with Qutb-ud-din Aibak. **Babur** founded Mughal rule after the First Battle of Panipat (1526) against Ibrahim Lodi. Akbar's policies included Sulh-i-kul (tolerance) and the mansabdari system. Shivaji founded the Maratha state in the 17th century.

cards.title: Battles to remember
points: First Battle of Panipat (1526): Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi
Second Battle of Panipat (1556): Akbar's forces defeated Hemu
Third Battle of Panipat (1761): Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas
Battle of Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764): British gain power in Bengal

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: As per the UPSC syllabus, History & Freedom Movement is about 80 marks in GAT, with emphasis on culture and civilisation. Use NCERT Class 6–8 (Our Pasts) and Class 12 Themes in Indian History. Make timelines — UPSC often asks chronological order.

cards.q: Which Harappan site is known for its dockyard?
cards.explain: Lothal in Gujarat had a dockyard, showing maritime trade.

cards.q: The First Battle of Panipat (1526) was fought between:
cards.explain: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in 1526, founding Mughal rule in India.

cards.q: Ashoka embraced Buddhism after which war?
cards.explain: The bloodshed of the Kalinga War moved Ashoka to adopt Buddhism and the policy of dhamma.

notes.h: Indus Valley and the Vedic age
notes.p:
The **Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilisation** was a Bronze Age urban culture. **Harappa** was excavated by Daya Ram Sahni (1921) and **Mohenjo-daro** by R.D. Banerji (1922). Its hallmarks were planned cities with grid streets, covered drains, standard burnt bricks and weights, and seals (often with a unicorn-like animal). Site facts NDA likes: the **Great Bath** at Mohenjo-daro, the **dockyard** at Lothal (Gujarat), ploughed fields at Kalibangan (Rajasthan) and the water-management system of **Dholavira** (Gujarat). The Harappan script has **not been deciphered**.

The **Vedic period** followed. The **Rigveda** is the oldest Veda; the four Vedas are Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva. Early Vedic society was largely pastoral, with assemblies called the **sabha** and **samiti**. The Gayatri Mantra is from the Rigveda.

**Gautama Buddha** was born at **Lumbini**, attained enlightenment at **Bodh Gaya**, gave his first sermon at **Sarnath** and attained mahaparinirvana at **Kushinagar**. His teachings include the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. **Mahavira** was the 24th Jain tirthankara; Jainism stresses ahimsa and the three jewels (right faith, right knowledge, right conduct).

The **Maurya Empire** was founded by **Chandragupta Maurya** with the guidance of **Chanakya (Kautilya)**, author of the **Arthashastra**. Megasthenes, the Greek envoy of Seleucus, described the court in **Indica**. **Ashoka** turned to Buddhism after the bloody **Kalinga war** and spread the message of **dhamma** through rock and pillar edicts, mostly in the Brahmi script, first deciphered by James Prinsep. The Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath is India's national emblem.

The **Gupta period** is often called a "classical age". **Samudragupta**'s conquests are recorded in the **Prayag (Allahabad) pillar inscription** composed by Harisena. **Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)** was a patron of the arts; the Chinese pilgrim **Fa-Hien** visited in his reign. **Kalidasa** (Abhijnanashakuntalam) and the mathematician-astronomer **Aryabhata** belong to this era.

**Harshavardhana** ruled in the 7th century; **Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang)** studied at **Nalanda**, and Banabhatta wrote the **Harshacharita**.

In the South, the **Pallavas** built the rock-cut rathas of **Mahabalipuram**, and the **Cholas** built a powerful navy. **Rajaraja I** built the **Brihadeeswara temple** at Thanjavur, and **Rajendra I** led naval expeditions to Southeast Asia.

The Sultanate began in **1206** with **Qutb-ud-din Aibak**. Its five dynasties in order: **Slave (Mamluk), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi** — remember "**S**ome **K**ings **T**ake **S**ilver **L**ands".
points: Iltutmish consolidated the Sultanate; Razia Sultan was its first woman ruler
Alauddin Khalji introduced market price controls and resisted Mongol raids
Muhammad bin Tughlaq tried token currency and shifted the capital to Daulatabad
Timur invaded Delhi in 1398
Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka; Krishnadevaraya was its greatest ruler; it was defeated at Talikota in 1565

notes.h: The Mughals, Marathas and Bhakti–Sufi movements
notes.p:
**Babur** defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)**. The Mughal sequence: **Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb** — "**B**ig **H**orses **A**re **J**umping **S**o **A**ctively". Humayun lost his throne to **Sher Shah Suri**, who introduced the silver **rupiya** and improved the road later called the Grand Trunk Road, before Humayun regained Delhi in 1555.

**Akbar** won the **Second Battle of Panipat (1556)** against Hemu, set up the **mansabdari** system and promoted tolerance (Din-i-Ilahi, Sulh-i-kul). The Battle of **Haldighati (1576)** was fought against Maharana Pratap. **Shah Jahan** built the Taj Mahal. **Shivaji** was crowned at Raigad in **1674**. The **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)** saw Ahmad Shah Abdali defeat the Marathas.

**Bhakti and Sufi** saints — Kabir, Guru Nanak, Mirabai, Tulsidas, and the Chishti saints Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer) and Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi) — preached devotion and equality.

Trap: don't mix up the three Panipat battles — match each year with its winner.
Dates and pairs here are frequent one-mark questions.

chapters.title: History: freedom movement & the modern world

cards.title: Early phase (1857–1905)
cards.body: The **Revolt of 1857** ended Company rule; the Crown took over in 1858. The Indian National Congress was founded in **1885** (A.O. Hume helped found it; W.C. Bonnerjee presided over the first session in Bombay). Moderates used petitions and dialogue.

cards.title: Swadeshi to Gandhi (1905–1919)
cards.body: Partition of Bengal (1905) sparked the Swadeshi movement. The Muslim League formed in 1906; Congress split at Surat in 1907. Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and led Champaran (1917). The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar.

cards.title: Mass movements timeline
points: Non-Cooperation: 1920–22, withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (1922)
Simon Commission boycott: 1928
Purna Swaraj resolution: Lahore session, 1929
Dandi March / Civil Disobedience: 1930
Quit India: 8 August 1942 ('Do or Die')
Independence: 15 August 1947

cards.title: Revolutionaries and the INA
cards.body: Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were executed in 1931. Subhas Chandra Bose led the **Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj)** with the slogan 'Delhi Chalo'. The INA trials at the Red Fort (1945–46) stirred nationwide anger against British rule.

cards.title: Forces that shaped the modern world
cards.body: The NDA syllabus also covers world history: the Renaissance, Industrial Revolution, American (1776) and French (1789) revolutions, the two World Wars (1914–18 and 1939–45), and the founding of the United Nations (1945). Know causes and outcomes, not just dates.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Learn the freedom movement as a story of cause → event → result. Also revise post-independence topics in the syllabus: Five Year Plans, Panchayati Raj, Bhoodan, Sarvodaya and the Constitution.

cards.q: Who presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress (1885)?
cards.explain: W.C. Bonnerjee presided over the first session in Bombay; A.O. Hume helped found the Congress.

cards.q: The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn after:
cards.explain: Gandhi called off the movement in 1922 after violence at Chauri Chaura.

cards.q: The Quit India Movement was launched in:
cards.explain: It was launched on 8 August 1942 at the Bombay session of the AICC.

notes.p:
The East India Company's power grew after the **Battle of Plassey (1757)**, where Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, and the **Battle of Buxar (1764)**, after which the Company gained the **Diwani** (revenue rights) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa (1765).

The **Revolt of 1857** began at **Meerut on 10 May 1857** (Mangal Pandey's protest at Barrackpore came earlier that year). Leaders: Bahadur Shah Zafar (Delhi), Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Nana Saheb and Tantia Tope (Kanpur), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow) and Kunwar Singh (Bihar). After the revolt, the **Government of India Act 1858** ended Company rule and India came under the British Crown.

The **Indian National Congress** was founded in **1885**, with A.O. Hume's help; its first session was in Bombay under **W.C. Bonnerjee**. Early "moderates" (Dadabhai Naoroji — the drain theory, Gokhale) used petitions; "extremists" (Lal-Bal-Pal) demanded swaraj.
points: 1905: Partition of Bengal by Curzon → Swadeshi and Boycott movement (annulled in 1911)
1906: All-India Muslim League founded at Dhaka
1907: Surat split between moderates and extremists
1909: Morley–Minto Reforms introduced separate electorates
1915: Gandhi returns from South Africa
1917–18: Champaran (indigo), Kheda and Ahmedabad satyagrahas

notes.p:
**1919:** the Rowlatt Act led to protests; on **13 April 1919** General Dyer ordered firing at **Jallianwala Bagh**, Amritsar. Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood.

**1920–22: Non-Cooperation Movement** (with the Khilafat issue) — boycott of schools, courts and foreign cloth. Gandhi withdrew it after the violence at **Chauri Chaura (February 1922)**.

**1928:** the all-British **Simon Commission** was met with "Simon Go Back"; Lala Lajpat Rai died after a lathi charge. **December 1929:** the Lahore Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru declared **Purna Swaraj**, and **26 January 1930** was celebrated as Independence Day — the reason 26 January was chosen for the Constitution.

**1930:** the **Dandi March** (12 March–6 April) launched **Civil Disobedience**. **1931:** Gandhi–Irwin Pact; Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference. **1932:** **Poona Pact** between Gandhi and Ambedkar. **1935:** Government of India Act (provincial autonomy).

**1942:** after the failed Cripps Mission, the **Quit India Movement** began on **8 August 1942** with the call "**Do or Die**". Subhas Chandra Bose led the **Indian National Army** ("Dilli Chalo") from Southeast Asia. **1946:** Cabinet Mission. **3 June 1947:** Mountbatten Plan for partition; independence on **15 August 1947**.
NDA's history section also covers world events. Keep a simple timeline:
points: 1776: American Declaration of Independence (4 July)
1789: French Revolution — Liberty, Equality, Fraternity; storming of the Bastille
18th–19th century: Industrial Revolution begins in Britain (textiles, steam power)
1914–1918: First World War; Treaty of Versailles 1919; League of Nations 1920
1917: Russian Revolution led by Lenin and the Bolsheviks
1939–1945: Second World War; atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945)
24 October 1945: United Nations founded; Cold War follows; Berlin Wall falls 1989; USSR dissolves 1991

notes.p:
Learn the movements as a chain — each one is a **reaction** to a British act: Partition of Bengal → Swadeshi; Rowlatt Act → Jallianwala → Non-Cooperation; Simon Commission → Purna Swaraj → Civil Disobedience; Cripps failure → Quit India. Knowing the cause helps you order events in "arrange chronologically" questions.

Common traps: confusing the Lahore session (1929, Purna Swaraj) with the Lucknow Pact (1916, Congress–League unity); mixing up the Poona Pact (1932) with the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931); and placing the 1857 start at Barrackpore instead of Meerut.
If you can say each line in one breath, you are ready.

cards.title: Religions and reform movements
cards.body: **Buddhism** (Gautama Buddha: Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path) and **Jainism** (Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara: three jewels, non-violence) arose in the 6th century BCE. The **Bhakti** movement (Kabir, Mirabai, Chaitanya, Guru Nanak) and **Sufi** saints (Moinuddin Chishti, Nizamuddin Auliya) preached devotion and equality.

cards.title: Classical dances
points: Bharatanatyam — Tamil Nadu
Kathak — North India
Kathakali and Mohiniyattam — Kerala
Kuchipudi — Andhra Pradesh; Odissi — Odisha
Manipuri — Manipur; Sattriya — Assam

cards.title: Music
cards.body: Indian classical music has two streams: **Hindustani** (north) and **Carnatic** (south). **Tansen** was a famous musician at Akbar's court; **Purandara Dasa** is called the father of Carnatic music. Amir Khusrau is linked with the qawwali tradition.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Questions pair a monument with its builder or dynasty, or a dance with its state. Make two tables — monument → dynasty, dance → state — and revise them along with UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India.

cards.q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was built under the:
cards.explain: It was carved under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I in the 8th century.

cards.q: Kathakali is a classical dance of:
cards.explain: Kathakali is from Kerala.

notes.p:
The **Harappan** cities show remarkable planning: streets on a grid, baked-brick houses and covered drains. Under the **Mauryas**, polished sandstone pillars carried Ashoka's edicts; the **Lion Capital** at Sarnath, with the wheel (chakra) on its base, became India's national emblem.

Buddhist art produced **stupas** (Sanchi, Bharhut), **chaityas** (prayer halls) and **viharas** (monasteries). The **Gandhara** school blended Greek and Indian styles; the **Mathura** school was more Indian in form. The **Ajanta** paintings, mostly from the Gupta–Vakataka period, are world-famous.
Hindu temples developed three regional styles.
points: Nagara: a beehive-shaped shikhara over the sanctum — Khajuraho, Lingaraja (Bhubaneswar), Konark
Dravida: tall gateways (gopurams) and pyramidal towers (vimanas) — Brihadeeswara (Thanjavur), Meenakshi (Madurai)
Vesara: a blend of the two, seen in Chalukya and Hoysala temples
Pallava rock-cut rathas and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram
Jain temples of Dilwara (Mount Abu) are famous for marble carving

notes.p:
From the 13th century, arches, domes and minarets came into Indian building. The **Qutub Minar** and Alai Darwaza in Delhi date from the Sultanate. Regional kingdoms added their own monuments — Gol Gumbaz in Bijapur and Charminar in Hyderabad (Qutb Shahi).

Mughal architecture reached its peak under **Shah Jahan** with the **Taj Mahal** in Agra, the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid in Delhi. Akbar built **Fatehpur Sikri**, whose Buland Darwaza commemorates his Gujarat campaign. Mughal gardens followed the four-part **charbagh** plan.

Sanskrit literature includes the **Vedas**, **Upanishads**, the epics and the **Puranas**. Classical poets and playwrights include Kalidasa, Bhasa and Banabhatta (Harshacharita). Tamil **Sangam** poems describe life in the early south. **Nalanda** and **Takshashila** were great centres of learning.

In medieval times, Persian histories such as Abul Fazl's *Akbarnama* and *Ain-i-Akbari* recorded court life. Bhakti poets wrote in regional languages — Kabir's dohas, Tulsidas's *Ramcharitmanas* in Awadhi, Surdas in Braj — which helped these languages grow.

In the modern period, **Rabindranath Tagore** won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for *Gitanjali* and composed the national anthem, *Jana Gana Mana*; **Bankim Chandra Chatterjee** wrote *Vande Mataram* in his novel *Anandamath*.

Buddhism and Jainism challenged ritualism and spread ideas of non-violence. The **Bhakti** saints rejected caste barriers; **Guru Nanak** founded Sikhism; **Sufi** orders such as the Chishtis built bridges between communities through music and devotion.

The classical dances recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi include Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam and Sattriya (check the Akademi's current list). Hindustani music forms include dhrupad and khayal; Carnatic music centres on kriti compositions by composers such as Tyagaraja.
Revise before each mock.

chapters.title: Modern India: British expansion, 1857 & reform movements

cards.title: Europeans arrive
cards.body: **Vasco da Gama** reached Calicut in 1498, opening the sea route from Europe. The Portuguese, Dutch, English (East India Company, chartered in 1600) and French set up trading posts. Anglo-French rivalry ended in British dominance after the Carnatic Wars.

cards.title: Decisive battles
points: Plassey (1757) — Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah
Buxar (1764) — British defeated Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II
Treaty of Allahabad (1765) — Company got the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
Anglo-Mysore Wars — Tipu Sultan killed in 1799
Anglo-Maratha and Anglo-Sikh Wars completed British control

cards.title: Tools of expansion
points: Subsidiary Alliance — Lord Wellesley
Doctrine of Lapse — Lord Dalhousie (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur annexed)
Permanent Settlement (1793) — Lord Cornwallis, Bengal
Ryotwari system — Thomas Munro, Madras
Mahalwari system — North-Western Provinces and Punjab

William Bentinck — abolished sati (1829); first Governor-General of India (1833)
Dalhousie — first railway line (1853), telegraph, postal reforms
Canning — first Viceroy (1858)

cards.title: The Revolt of 1857
cards.body: The revolt broke out at **Meerut on 10 May 1857**. The immediate cause was the **greased cartridges** of the Enfield rifle; deeper causes were annexations, economic hardship and resentment of foreign rule. Earlier, **Mangal Pandey** had attacked officers at Barrackpore.

cards.title: Leaders of 1857
points: Delhi — Bahadur Shah Zafar (symbolic leader)
Jhansi — Rani Lakshmibai
Kanpur — Nana Sahib and Tantia Tope
Lucknow — Begum Hazrat Mahal
Bihar (Jagdishpur) — Kunwar Singh

cards.title: Social and religious reformers
points: Raja Ram Mohan Roy — Brahmo Samaj (1828); campaign against sati
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar — widow remarriage (Act of 1856)
Swami Dayananda Saraswati — Arya Samaj (1875)
Swami Vivekananda — Ramakrishna Mission (1897); Chicago address (1893)

cards.q: The Battle of Plassey was fought in:
cards.explain: Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah at Plassey in 1757.

cards.q: The Doctrine of Lapse is associated with:
cards.explain: Dalhousie used it to annex states such as Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur.

cards.q: The Brahmo Samaj was founded by:
cards.explain: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828.

notes.p:
The East India Company came to trade, but the decline of Mughal authority after Aurangzeb (d. 1707) let it play off regional rulers against each other. Victory at **Plassey (1757)** made it kingmaker in Bengal; victory at **Buxar (1764)** made it the real power. Under the **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)**, the Mughal emperor granted the Company the **Diwani** (right to collect revenue) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

By the mid-19th century, after wars with Mysore, the Marathas and the Sikhs, most of India was either directly ruled by the British or bound to them by treaty.

notes.h: Methods of expansion and land revenue
notes.p: The British used both war and diplomacy.
points: Subsidiary Alliance: an Indian ruler kept British troops at his own cost and could not deal with other powers without British approval — Hyderabad was among the first to accept
Doctrine of Lapse: a state whose ruler died without a natural heir passed to the British
Permanent Settlement: zamindars paid a fixed revenue forever; peasants suffered
Ryotwari: revenue directly from peasants (ryots)
Mahalwari: revenue settled with the village community

notes.p:
The revolt began with sepoys at Meerut, who marched to Delhi and proclaimed **Bahadur Shah Zafar** emperor. It spread across north and central India, with leaders such as **Rani Lakshmibai**, **Nana Sahib**, **Tantia Tope**, **Begum Hazrat Mahal** and **Kunwar Singh**.

It failed because it lacked unified leadership and a common plan, the south and Punjab largely stayed out, and the British had superior resources. Yet it was a turning point: the **Government of India Act 1858** ended Company rule and transferred power to the Crown, and Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised non-interference in religion. Historians debate whether it was a "sepoy mutiny" or a "first war of independence".

Several Governors-General introduced lasting changes. **Warren Hastings** organised the revenue and judicial system. **Cornwallis** reformed the civil services and introduced the Permanent Settlement. **Bentinck** abolished sati with Ram Mohan Roy's support and, under Macaulay's influence, promoted English education (1835). **Dalhousie** introduced railways (Bombay–Thane, 1853), the telegraph and a modern postal system — tools that also helped the British control the country.

Reformers used reason and scripture to fight social evils. **Ram Mohan Roy** opposed sati and idol worship. **Vidyasagar** campaigned for widow remarriage and girls' education. **Dayananda Saraswati** called for a return to the Vedas ("Back to the Vedas") and opposed caste rigidity. **Vivekananda** spread Vedanta worldwide and stressed service to the poor. **Jyotiba and Savitribai Phule** opened schools for girls and lower castes in Pune. **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** founded the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh. These movements laid the ground for modern nationalism.
Revise before each mock.

chapters.title: Freedom struggle: Congress sessions & constitutional acts

cards.title: The Indian National Congress
cards.body: Founded in **1885** with the help of **A. O. Hume**. The first session at Bombay was presided over by **W. C. Bonnerjee**. The 1907 **Surat** session split Moderates and Extremists. The **Lahore session (1929)** under Jawaharlal Nehru adopted **Purna Swaraj**; 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day.

Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919)

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Arrange events in a single timeline and learn them in decades. Many questions simply ask you to put four events in chronological order — a timeline answers these in seconds.

cards.q: The Purna Swaraj resolution was passed at the Congress session of:
cards.explain: The Lahore session (1929), presided over by Nehru, adopted complete independence as the goal.

cards.q: Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced by the:
cards.explain: The Morley–Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909) introduced them.

cards.q: Who presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress?
cards.explain: W. C. Bonnerjee presided over the 1885 Bombay session.

notes.p: British Parliament gradually took control over the Company. The **Regulating Act (1773)** created the post of Governor-General of Bengal and a Supreme Court at Calcutta. **Pitt's India Act (1784)** set up a Board of Control in London. The **Charter Act of 1813** allowed missionaries and set aside money for education; the **1833 Act** made the Governor-General of Bengal the **Governor-General of India** (Bentinck) and ended the Company's commercial functions. The **1853 Act** introduced open competition for the civil services.
After 1858, reforms slowly widened Indian participation, often with "divide and rule" features.
points: 1861 and 1892: Indians nominated to legislative councils; limited debate on the budget
1909 (Morley–Minto): elected element increased; separate electorates for Muslims
1919 (Montagu–Chelmsford): dyarchy — provincial subjects split into "transferred" and "reserved"; bicameral central legislature
1935: provincial autonomy, an all-India federation (never formed), and a Federal Court; much of it shaped the later Constitution
1947: India and Pakistan created as dominions from 15 August 1947

notes.p: The **Moderates** (Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta) used petitions and exposed economic exploitation — Naoroji's "drain theory". The **Extremists** (Lal-Bal-Pal: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal) demanded Swaraj and used boycott and Swadeshi after the **Partition of Bengal (1905)**. The two groups split at **Surat (1907)** and reunited at **Lucknow (1916)**, where the Congress–League pact was also signed. The **Jallianwala Bagh massacre** at Amritsar under General Dyer turned many moderates against British rule.

**Gandhi** returned from South Africa in 1915 and turned the movement into a mass struggle.

The **Non-Cooperation Movement** (1920–22), linked with the Khilafat issue, was called off after violence at **Chauri Chaura**. The all-white **Simon Commission** (1928) was boycotted. The **Civil Disobedience Movement** began with the **Dandi March** to break the salt law. After the Gandhi–Irwin Pact, Gandhi attended the **Second Round Table Conference** (1931). The **Quit India Movement** (1942) saw mass arrests and widespread protest. Meanwhile, **Subhas Chandra Bose** led the **Indian National Army** from Southeast Asia, and the RIN mutiny (1946) showed the loyalty of Indian forces was no longer certain.

The **Cabinet Mission (1946)** proposed a federal plan and a Constituent Assembly. The Muslim League's "Direct Action Day" (16 August 1946) led to communal violence. **Lord Mountbatten's plan (3 June 1947)** proposed partition, and the **Indian Independence Act** gave effect to it. India became independent on **15 August 1947**. The Constituent Assembly, which had first met in December 1946, completed the Constitution, adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950.
Revise before each mock.
