chapters.title: Forces shaping the modern world: Renaissance to Russian Revolution

cards.title: The Renaissance
cards.body: A cultural "rebirth" from the 14th to 16th centuries that began in **Italy** (Florence). It revived classical learning and stressed **humanism** — the worth of the individual. Artists: Leonardo da Vinci (Mona Lisa, The Last Supper), Michelangelo (Sistine Chapel ceiling), Raphael. **Gutenberg's printing press** (c. 1440s) spread new ideas fast.

cards.title: The Reformation
cards.body: In **1517 Martin Luther** posted his Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences, starting the Protestant Reformation. The Catholic Church responded with the Counter-Reformation; the **Jesuit** order spread education and missionary work, including in India (Francis Xavier).

cards.title: Exploration and discovery
points: Fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans (1453) pushed Europeans to seek new sea routes
Columbus reached the Americas (1492)
Vasco da Gama reached India by sea (1498)
Magellan's expedition completed the first circumnavigation (1519–22)
Compass, better ships and maps made long voyages possible

cards.title: American War of Independence
cards.body: Thirteen British colonies rebelled against taxes imposed without their consent — **"No taxation without representation"**. Boston Tea Party (1773); war began 1775; **Declaration of Independence, 4 July 1776** (drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson); George Washington led the army; Treaty of Paris (1783) recognised independence.

cards.title: French Revolution (1789)
cards.body: Causes: royal debt, unfair taxes on the Third Estate, and Enlightenment ideas of **Rousseau** (The Social Contract), **Voltaire** and **Montesquieu** (separation of powers). The **storming of the Bastille (14 July 1789)** began the revolution. Slogan: **Liberty, Equality, Fraternity**. Louis XVI was executed (1793); Napoleon later rose to power.

cards.title: Industrial Revolution
cards.body: It began in **Britain** in the mid-18th century, shifting production from hand to machine.
points: Spinning jenny (Hargreaves), water frame (Arkwright), power loom (Cartwright)
James Watt's improved steam engine
Stephenson's locomotive; railways
Effects: factories, cities, a new working class, demand for colonies as markets and raw-material sources

cards.title: Russian Revolution (1917)
cards.body: In **February 1917** Tsar Nicholas II abdicated. In **October 1917** the **Bolsheviks** under **Lenin** seized power with the slogan "Peace, Land and Bread", creating the first communist state; the USSR was formed in 1922. Its ideas came from **Karl Marx** and Friedrich Engels.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Link each revolution to one slogan, one thinker and one year: American — "No taxation without representation", Jefferson, 1776; French — "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity", Rousseau, 1789; Russian — "Peace, Land and Bread", Lenin, 1917.

cards.q: The American Declaration of Independence was adopted in:
cards.explain: It was adopted on 4 July 1776.

cards.q: "The Social Contract" was written by:
cards.explain: Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote The Social Contract (1762).

notes.p:
The **Renaissance** marked the shift from medieval to modern Europe. Wealthy Italian city-states like Florence and Venice sponsored artists and scholars; the fall of Constantinople sent Greek scholars and manuscripts westward. Thinkers questioned blind faith and valued observation — **Copernicus** proposed that Earth moves around the Sun, and **Galileo** supported this with telescope observations.

The **Reformation** split Western Christianity. Luther translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it, helped by printing. Protestant churches spread across northern Europe, weakening the political power of the Pope.
Spain and Portugal led the early voyages, followed by the Dutch, English and French.
points: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope (1488)
Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean (1492)
Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (1498)
Magellan's fleet sailed around the world (1519–22); Magellan himself died on the way
Results: colonial empires, the Atlantic slave trade, exchange of crops (potato, maize, chilli reached Asia) and the growth of world trade

notes.p:
The **American Revolution** created a republic based on a written constitution (1787) and a Bill of Rights. It showed that colonies could overthrow an imperial power and that government rests on the consent of the governed.

The **French Revolution** abolished feudal privileges and issued the **Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen** (1789). It passed through radical phases — the Reign of Terror under Robespierre — before **Napoleon** took power and spread its legal ideas (the Napoleonic Code) across Europe. Its ideas of nationalism, democracy and equality inspired movements worldwide, including in India.

Britain had coal and iron, capital from trade, colonies and an agricultural revolution that freed labour. Textile machines and steam power created factories; railways and steamships cut transport costs.

The effects were mixed. Production and wealth rose, but early factory workers, including children, faced long hours and poor conditions in crowded cities. This led to trade unions, labour laws and socialist ideas. Industrial nations sought colonies for raw materials such as cotton and for markets — India's handloom industry suffered as cheap British cloth flooded in.

Russia under the Tsars was autocratic, with poor peasants and harsh factory conditions. Defeats and shortages in the First World War broke the system. After the February Revolution a provisional government took over but continued the war. Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in October, withdrew Russia from the war, redistributed land and nationalised industry. A civil war followed, and the **Union of Soviet Socialist Republics** was formed in 1922. The revolution inspired communist movements across the world and shaped the 20th century until the USSR dissolved in **1991**.
Revise before each mock.
points: Renaissance — Italy; humanism; Leonardo, Michelangelo; printing press
Reformation — Luther, 1517
Columbus 1492; Vasco da Gama 1498; Magellan 1519–22
American independence — 4 July 1776; Treaty of Paris 1783
French Revolution — Bastille, 14 July 1789; Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Industrial Revolution — Britain; Watt's steam engine
Russian Revolution — 1917; Lenin; USSR 1922–1991

chapters.title: World wars, the UN, Panchsheel & India's role

cards.title: Two world wars
points: WWI (1914–18): triggered by the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo; ended with the Treaty of Versailles (1919); League of Nations formed (1920)
WWII (1939–45): began with Germany's invasion of Poland (1 Sept 1939); USA entered after Pearl Harbor (1941); atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945)

cards.title: The United Nations
cards.body: The UN was founded on **24 October 1945** (UN Day); its Charter was signed at San Francisco in June 1945 and its headquarters is in **New York**. India was a founding member. Main organs: General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, Trusteeship Council (inactive since 1994), International Court of Justice (The Hague) and Secretariat.

cards.title: Security Council
cards.body: It has **15 members**: **5 permanent members with veto power** (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. India has served several non-permanent terms and seeks a permanent seat.

cards.title: Specialised agencies
points: WHO — Geneva; ILO — Geneva
UNESCO — Paris; FAO — Rome
IMF and World Bank — Washington, D.C.
UNICEF — New York
ICJ — The Hague

cards.title: Panchsheel
cards.body: The **Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence**, set out in the 1954 India–China agreement on Tibet (Nehru and Zhou Enlai): mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty; non-aggression; non-interference in internal affairs; equality and mutual benefit; peaceful coexistence.

cards.title: Non-Aligned Movement
cards.body: Newly independent countries refused to join either Cold War bloc. After the **Bandung Conference (1955)**, NAM was founded at **Belgrade in 1961**. Founding leaders: **Nehru** (India), **Nasser** (Egypt), **Tito** (Yugoslavia), **Sukarno** (Indonesia) and **Nkrumah** (Ghana).

cards.title: Democracy, socialism and communism
points: Democracy — government of, by and for the people (Lincoln)
Socialism — social ownership/control of key resources; reducing inequality
Communism — Marx and Engels (Communist Manifesto, 1848); classless, stateless society as the goal
Capitalism — private ownership and free markets
Cold War: USA-led bloc vs USSR-led bloc, roughly 1947–1991

cards.title: One world and India's role
cards.body: Science and technology — from vaccines to the internet — have made nations interdependent; problems like climate change, pandemics and terrorism need global cooperation. India's ideal of **"Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam"** (the world is one family) reflects this. India is a major contributor to UN peacekeeping and is active in groupings like the G20 and BRICS.

cards.q: How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?
cards.explain: USA, UK, France, Russia and China.

cards.q: The Panchsheel agreement of 1954 was signed between India and:
cards.explain: It was part of the 1954 India–China agreement on trade with Tibet.

notes.p:
The **First World War** grew out of rival alliances, militarism, imperial competition and nationalism in the Balkans. It was fought largely in trenches and killed millions. Over a million Indian soldiers served abroad; the India Gate in Delhi commemorates many who died. The **Treaty of Versailles** punished Germany harshly, sowing resentment.

The **Second World War** followed the rise of Hitler in Germany, Mussolini in Italy and militarism in Japan. It was the deadliest conflict in history and included the Holocaust. It ended with Germany's surrender in May 1945 and Japan's in August 1945, after the atomic bombings.

The failure of the **League of Nations** to stop aggression led to the stronger **United Nations**. Its aims are to maintain international peace and security, develop friendly relations, promote cooperation on economic, social and humanitarian problems and protect human rights.
points: General Assembly: every member state has one vote
Security Council: primary responsibility for peace; decisions on substantive matters can be blocked by a permanent member's veto
ICJ: settles legal disputes between states
Secretariat: headed by the Secretary-General
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted on 10 December 1948 (Human Rights Day)

notes.p:
Under **Jawaharlal Nehru**, India chose **non-alignment**: keeping independence of judgement rather than joining the US-led or Soviet-led blocs. This was not neutrality — India took positions on issues such as colonialism and apartheid.

**Panchsheel** expressed the same spirit of peaceful coexistence. The 1962 war with China showed its limits, but the principles remain part of India's stated foreign-policy values. NAM gave newly independent nations of Asia, Africa and Latin America a collective voice.

**Democracy** rests on free elections, rule of law and protection of rights. **Socialism** seeks to reduce inequality through public ownership or regulation of key sectors and welfare measures. **Communism**, based on Marx's ideas, aims at a classless society; in practice communist states were run by a single party. **Capitalism** relies on private enterprise and markets.

India combined parliamentary democracy with a **mixed economy** — public and private sectors together — and the Preamble describes India as a "socialist, secular, democratic republic" (the words socialist and secular were added in 1976).

Science and technology have transformed society: better medicine has raised life expectancy, the Green Revolution increased food production, and communication technology has made information available instantly. They also bring challenges — nuclear weapons, pollution, cyber threats and job displacement.

The idea of **one world** recognises that no country can solve global problems alone. India participates in climate negotiations, disaster relief, peacekeeping and vaccine supply. For India's current positions and memberships, check recent official sources such as the Ministry of External Affairs.
Revise before each mock.
points: UN founded 24 October 1945; HQ New York
Security Council: 15 members, 5 permanent with veto
WHO Geneva; UNESCO Paris; FAO Rome; ICJ The Hague
Panchsheel 1954 — India–China, Nehru–Zhou Enlai
NAM — Belgrade 1961; Nehru, Nasser, Tito, Sukarno, Nkrumah
"Socialist" and "secular" added to the Preamble in 1976

chapters.title: Planning, Panchayati Raj, co-operatives & Gandhian ideas

cards.title: Five Year Plans
cards.body: The **Planning Commission** was set up in **1950** with the Prime Minister as chairman. The **First Plan (1951–56)** stressed agriculture and irrigation; the **Second (1956–61)**, based on the **Mahalanobis** model, stressed heavy industry. India had twelve plans, the last ending in 2017.

cards.title: NITI Aayog
cards.body: On **1 January 2015** the Planning Commission was replaced by **NITI Aayog** (National Institution for Transforming India), a policy think tank chaired by the Prime Minister. It promotes "cooperative federalism" with states rather than allocating funds through five-year plans.

cards.title: Community Development
cards.body: The **Community Development Programme** began on 2 October 1952 to improve rural life through local participation, followed by the National Extension Service (1953). Its weak results led to the **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957)**, which recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj.

cards.title: Panchayati Raj
cards.body: First inaugurated at **Nagaur, Rajasthan, on 2 October 1959**. The **73rd Amendment (1992)** gave it constitutional status:
points: Gram Sabha and three tiers: village, block, district
Elections every five years by a State Election Commission
At least one-third of seats reserved for women
State Finance Commission; 11th Schedule lists 29 subjects
74th Amendment does the same for urban local bodies (12th Schedule, 18 subjects)

cards.title: Co-operatives
cards.body: A co-operative is a voluntary association that pools members' resources for mutual benefit. The Co-operative Credit Societies Act came in 1904. **Amul** (Anand, Gujarat), led by **Verghese Kurien**, powered **Operation Flood** — the White Revolution. The **97th Amendment (2011)** gave co-operatives constitutional status.

cards.title: Bhoodan and Sarvodaya
cards.body: **Vinoba Bhave** began the **Bhoodan** (land gift) movement in **1951** at Pochampally (now in Telangana), asking landlords to give land to the landless; it grew into **Gramdan** (village gift). **Sarvodaya** — "the welfare of all" — was Gandhi's term, inspired by Ruskin's *Unto This Last*; Jayaprakash Narayan later joined the movement.

cards.title: Gandhi's core teachings
points: Satya (truth) and ahimsa (non-violence)
Satyagraha — non-violent resistance
Swaraj (self-rule) and swadeshi (self-reliance)
Trusteeship — the rich hold wealth in trust for society
Nai Talim (basic education through work); Hind Swaraj (1909)

cards.title: Welfare state and national integration
cards.body: The **Directive Principles** aim at a **welfare state** that secures social and economic justice. **National integration** means unity amid diversity of language, religion and region; communalism, casteism and regionalism threaten it. A National Integration Council was first set up in 1961.

cards.q: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in:
cards.explain: NITI Aayog was set up on 1 January 2015.

cards.q: The Bhoodan movement was started by:
cards.explain: Vinoba Bhave began Bhoodan in 1951.

notes.p:
After independence India chose planned development within a **mixed economy**. The Planning Commission drew up Five Year Plans that set targets and allocated resources. The First Plan focused on agriculture and recovery from partition; the Second, guided by P. C. Mahalanobis, built steel plants and heavy industry; later plans addressed self-reliance, poverty removal, employment and, from the Eleventh Plan, "inclusive growth".

There were breaks in planning — annual plans from 1966 to 1969 (the "plan holiday") and in 1990–92. **NITI Aayog** (2015) replaced the Commission and works more as an adviser and coordinator with states.

The **Community Development Programme** (1952) tried to improve agriculture, health, education and roads at the block level, but people's participation was low. The **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee** recommended democratic decentralisation through elected panchayats.

Rajasthan was the first state to adopt Panchayati Raj (1959), followed by Andhra Pradesh. However, elections were irregular in many states until the **73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992)** made the system mandatory. 24 April is celebrated as **National Panchayati Raj Day**, marking the date the amendment came into force (1993). Many states now reserve 50% of panchayat seats for women — check the specific state law for details.
Co-operatives help small farmers, workers and consumers gain bargaining power.
points: Credit co-operatives provide loans to farmers
Dairy co-operatives (the Anand pattern) collect milk village by village; Operation Flood began in 1970 and made India a leading milk producer
Marketing and consumer co-operatives cut out middlemen
The 97th Amendment (2011) added the right to form co-operative societies to Article 19(1)(c) and inserted Part IX-B
The Union Ministry of Co-operation was created in 2021

notes.p:
Gandhi's philosophy joined politics with ethics. **Satyagraha** meant resisting injustice by willingly accepting suffering, without hatred. **Swadeshi** encouraged Indian goods and the charkha; **trusteeship** asked the wealthy to use their wealth for society; the **constructive programme** included removal of untouchability, Hindu–Muslim unity, khadi and village industries. His **Nai Talim** (1937) linked education with productive work.

After independence, **Vinoba Bhave** carried these ideas into Bhoodan and Gramdan, collecting several lakh acres of land, though much of it was not distributed effectively. **Jayaprakash Narayan** later led the "Total Revolution" movement (1974).

A **welfare state** takes responsibility for citizens' basic needs — education, health, work and social security. The Directive Principles (Part IV) guide the government towards it, for example through equal pay for equal work, free legal aid and village panchayats.

**National integration** is strengthened by the Constitution's single citizenship, an integrated judiciary, all-India services, national symbols and shared institutions such as the armed forces, which draw personnel from every region and community.
Revise before each mock.
points: Planning Commission 1950; First Plan 1951–56; Mahalanobis — Second Plan
NITI Aayog — 1 January 2015
Community Development — 2 October 1952
Panchayati Raj — Nagaur, 2 October 1959; 73rd Amendment 1992
One-third seats for women; 11th Schedule 29 subjects
Amul — Kurien — Operation Flood; 97th Amendment 2011
Bhoodan — Vinoba Bhave 1951; Sarvodaya — Gandhi (Ruskin)

cards.title: Earth's motions and time
cards.body: Earth rotates west to east once in about 24 hours (day and night) and revolves around the Sun in about 365¼ days (seasons). 360° of longitude = 24 hours, so **1° = 4 minutes** and 15° = 1 hour. Indian Standard Time is based on **82.5° E** longitude.

cards.title: Latitudes
cards.body: The Equator (0°) divides Earth into hemispheres. Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N) and Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S) mark the limits of the overhead sun. Arctic and Antarctic Circles are at 66.5°. The Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 Indian states.

cards.title: Interior and rocks
cards.body: Earth has a crust, mantle and core (outer core liquid, inner core solid). Rocks are **igneous** (from magma, e.g. granite, basalt), **sedimentary** (layers, e.g. sandstone, limestone; contain fossils) and **metamorphic** (changed by heat/pressure, e.g. marble from limestone, slate from shale).

cards.title: Atmosphere
cards.body: Layers from bottom: troposphere (weather happens here), **stratosphere** (ozone layer, absorbs UV), mesosphere, thermosphere (ionosphere reflects radio waves), exosphere. Nitrogen (~78%) and oxygen (~21%) make up most of the air.

cards.title: Winds, currents and hazards
cards.body: Planetary winds: trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies, deflected by the Coriolis effect. Warm currents (e.g. Gulf Stream) raise coastal temperatures; cold currents (e.g. Labrador) lower them. Earthquakes and volcanoes cluster along plate boundaries such as the Pacific 'Ring of Fire'.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: As per the UPSC syllabus, Geography is about 80 marks in GAT. Use NCERT Class 11 'Fundamentals of Physical Geography' and an atlas. Time-zone calculations (4 minutes per degree) are easy marks.

cards.q: Indian Standard Time is based on which longitude?
cards.explain: IST is based on 82.5° E, which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

cards.q: The ozone layer lies mainly in the:
cards.explain: Ozone is concentrated in the stratosphere, where it absorbs harmful UV radiation.

cards.q: Marble is formed from limestone. Marble is therefore a/an:
cards.explain: Heat and pressure change limestone (sedimentary) into marble, a metamorphic rock.

notes.p:
The Earth has three main layers: the **crust** (thin outer layer; continental crust is rich in silica and aluminium — "SIAL", oceanic crust in silica and magnesium — "SIMA"), the **mantle**, and the **core** (iron and nickel — "NIFE"). The **outer core is liquid** and the inner core is solid; we know this because **S-waves cannot pass through liquids**. The **Mohorovičić (Moho) discontinuity** separates crust and mantle; the **Gutenberg discontinuity** separates mantle and core.

Rocks are of three types. **Igneous** rocks form from cooled magma (granite, basalt). **Sedimentary** rocks form in layers and may contain fossils (sandstone, limestone, shale). **Metamorphic** rocks form under heat and pressure: limestone → **marble**, sandstone → **quartzite**, shale → **slate**, granite → gneiss.

The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, i.e. **15° per hour** or **1° every 4 minutes**. Places to the east are ahead in time.

**Example 1.** It is 12 noon at Greenwich (0°). What is the local time at 90°E?
Step 1: 90° × 4 minutes = 360 minutes = 6 hours.
Step 2: East is ahead, so the time is **6 pm**.

**Example 2.** India's Standard Meridian is **82°30′E**. IST is 82.5 × 4 = 330 minutes = **5 h 30 min ahead of GMT**.

**Rotation** causes day and night; **revolution** with the axis tilted about 23½° causes **seasons**. Summer solstice ~21 June (Sun over the Tropic of Cancer), winter solstice ~22 December; equinoxes around 21 March and 23 September, when day and night are nearly equal everywhere.
Air is about **78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen**, nearly 1% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide. Layers from the ground up:
points: Troposphere: all weather happens here; temperature falls with height
Stratosphere: contains the ozone layer; calm air preferred by jet aircraft
Mesosphere: coldest layer; meteors burn up here
Thermosphere (with the ionosphere): reflects radio waves; auroras
Exosphere: outermost, merges with space

notes.p:
Air moves from high to low pressure. The **Coriolis effect** deflects winds to the **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and to the left in the Southern. Planetary winds: **trade winds** (towards the equator), **westerlies** (mid-latitudes) and **polar easterlies**. The calm equatorial belt is the **doldrums**.

Tropical cyclones rotate **anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere**. They are called hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the north-west Pacific and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.

Local winds NDA asks: **Loo** (hot, dry, north India in summer), **Chinook** (Rockies, "snow eater"), **Foehn** (Alps), **Sirocco** (Sahara to the Mediterranean), **Harmattan** (West Africa, called "the doctor" for its dryness).

Ocean currents: warm — **Gulf Stream**, **Kuroshio**; cold — **Labrador**, **Humboldt (Peru)**, **Benguela**, **California**. Where warm and cold currents meet (Grand Banks near Newfoundland) there are rich fishing grounds.

Each agent creates typical shapes. **Rivers:** V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, meanders, **ox-bow lakes**, deltas. **Glaciers:** U-shaped valleys, cirques, **moraines**. **Wind:** mushroom rocks, **barchans** (crescent dunes). **Sea:** cliffs, sea caves, stacks, beaches. **Volcanoes and earthquakes** cluster along plate boundaries, especially the **Pacific "Ring of Fire"**.

Trap: in time questions, people forget that moving **east adds** time. Draw a quick arrow before calculating.
Revise these with a world map open.
points: Moho: crust–mantle; Gutenberg: mantle–core; outer core liquid
Limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite; shale → slate
15° = 1 hour; 1° = 4 minutes; east is ahead
IST meridian 82°30′E = GMT + 5:30
Ozone in the stratosphere; weather in the troposphere
Coriolis: right in the Northern Hemisphere
Humboldt, Labrador, Benguela = cold currents

cards.title: Physiographic divisions
cards.body: India has six physiographic divisions: the Himalayas, the Northern Plains, the Peninsular Plateau, the Indian Desert, the Coastal Plains and the Islands (Andaman & Nicobar in the Bay of Bengal, Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea).

cards.title: Rivers
cards.body: Himalayan rivers (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra) are perennial. Most peninsular rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi) flow east into the Bay of Bengal and form deltas. **Narmada and Tapi** flow west through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea and form estuaries.
points: Godavari is the longest peninsular river

cards.title: Monsoon and climate
cards.body: India has a tropical monsoon climate. The south-west monsoon (roughly June–September) brings most of the rainfall; it reaches Kerala first, around early June. The north-east (retreating) monsoon gives winter rain to Tamil Nadu. Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya receive very heavy rainfall.

cards.title: Soils and crops
cards.body: **Alluvial** soil is the most widespread (Northern Plains). **Black (regur)** soil of the Deccan holds moisture — ideal for cotton. Red and laterite soils occur in high-rainfall, high-temperature areas.
points: Kharif (sown with monsoon): rice, maize, cotton, jowar
Rabi (sown in winter): wheat, barley, gram, mustard

cards.title: Quick facts
points: Tropic of Cancer states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram
Palk Strait separates India and Sri Lanka
Southernmost point: Indira Point (Great Nicobar)
Standard meridian: 82.5° E

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Practise with a blank map of India: mark rivers, mountain passes, national parks and states on the Tropic of Cancer. UPSC repeatedly asks map-based matching questions.

cards.q: Which river flows westward through a rift valley into the Arabian Sea?
cards.explain: The Narmada (and the Tapi) flow west through rift valleys and form estuaries, not deltas.

cards.q: Black (regur) soil is best suited for:
cards.explain: Black soil retains moisture and is rich in lime and magnesium, making it ideal for cotton.

cards.q: Which of these is a rabi crop?
cards.explain: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring — a rabi crop.

notes.p:
India lies entirely in the Northern and Eastern hemispheres, between roughly **8°4′N and 37°6′N** latitude and **68°7′E and 97°25′E** longitude. With an area of about **3.28 million km²**, it is the **seventh-largest** country in the world. The **Tropic of Cancer** passes through eight states: **Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram**. The Standard Meridian (82°30′E) passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.

Boundary lines: **Radcliffe Line** (India–Pakistan and India–Bangladesh), **McMahon Line** (India–China in the east), and the **Durand Line** (Pakistan–Afghanistan, not an Indian border). India shares its longest land border with **Bangladesh**. The **Palk Strait** separates India from Sri Lanka.
India has six major physical divisions:
points: The Himalayas: three parallel ranges — Himadri (Greater), Himachal (Lesser) and Shiwaliks (outer)
The Northern Plains: built by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; very fertile alluvium
The Peninsular Plateau: oldest landmass; Deccan Plateau, with the Western and Eastern Ghats
The Indian Desert (Thar): west of the Aravallis
The Coastal Plains: western (Konkan, Malabar) and eastern (Coromandel, Northern Circars)
The Islands: Andaman & Nicobar (Bay of Bengal) and Lakshadweep (coral, Arabian Sea)

notes.p:
**Himalayan rivers** (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra) are **perennial** — fed by both rain and snowmelt. The Ganga is formed at **Devprayag** where the **Bhagirathi** and **Alaknanda** meet. The Brahmaputra is called the Tsangpo in Tibet and enters India in Arunachal Pradesh; **Majuli** in Assam is a large river island on it.

**Peninsular rivers** are mostly rain-fed. The **Godavari** is the longest peninsular river ("Dakshin Ganga"). Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Mahanadi flow **east** into the Bay of Bengal and form **deltas**. The **Narmada and Tapi** flow **west** through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea and form **estuaries** — a very common NDA question.

Mountain passes: **Zoji La** (Srinagar–Leh), **Shipki La** (Himachal–Tibet), **Nathu La** (Sikkim–Tibet), **Bomdi La** (Arunachal).

India has a **monsoon** climate. The **south-west monsoon** usually reaches Kerala around **1 June** and brings most of the country's rain from June to September. As it retreats (October–December), the **north-east monsoon** gives **Tamil Nadu** much of its rain. **Mawsynram** and **Cherrapunji** in Meghalaya receive some of the world's heaviest rainfall. In winter, **western disturbances** bring rain to north-west India, which helps the rabi wheat crop. Pre-monsoon showers: "mango showers" (Kerala, Karnataka) and **Kalbaisakhi** (West Bengal, Assam).

Soils: **alluvial** (most widespread, Northern Plains), **black/regur** (Deccan lava region, ideal for cotton), **red** (iron oxide gives colour), **laterite** (heavy rainfall areas, leached; good for cashew and tea with manure).

Crops: **kharif** (sown with the monsoon — rice, maize, cotton, soybean), **rabi** (sown in winter — wheat, mustard, gram), **zaid** (short summer season — watermelon, cucumber).

The **Ten Degree Channel** separates the Andaman group from the Nicobar group. **Barren Island** in the Andaman Sea is India's only active volcano. **Indira Point** on Great Nicobar is India's southernmost point. Lakshadweep's capital is Kavaratti; the capital of Andaman & Nicobar, Port Blair, was renamed **Sri Vijaya Puram** in 2024.

Traps: Narmada and Tapi make estuaries, not deltas; the Tropic of Cancer does **not** pass through Odisha, Bihar or Uttar Pradesh; and Tamil Nadu gets more rain in winter than in July.
Use a blank map of India while revising these points.
points: Area ≈ 3.28 million km²; seventh largest
Tropic of Cancer: 8 states, from Gujarat to Mizoram
Ganga = Bhagirathi + Alaknanda at Devprayag
Narmada and Tapi flow west through rift valleys
SW monsoon reaches Kerala around 1 June
Black soil = cotton; alluvial = most widespread
Barren Island = only active volcano; Ten Degree Channel splits Andaman and Nicobar

chapters.title: Geography: the Earth, latitudes, longitudes & time

cards.title: Origin and age
cards.body: The universe is explained by the **Big Bang** theory. The solar system is thought to have formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust (the **nebular hypothesis**, associated with Kant and Laplace). Earth is about **4.6 billion years** old.

cards.title: Shape and size
cards.body: Earth is an **oblate spheroid** (a "geoid") — slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator. Equatorial radius ≈ 6378 km, polar radius ≈ 6357 km; equatorial circumference ≈ 40,000 km. Evidence: ships disappearing hull-first, Earth's curved shadow in lunar eclipses, satellite images.

cards.title: Latitudes
cards.body: Latitudes measure distance north or south of the equator (0°–90°). Parallels are all parallel circles that get smaller towards the poles.
points: Tropic of Cancer 23½° N; Tropic of Capricorn 23½° S
Arctic Circle 66½° N; Antarctic Circle 66½° S
1° of latitude ≈ 111 km
The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states

cards.title: Longitudes and time
cards.body: Longitudes (meridians) run pole to pole. The **Prime Meridian (0°)** passes through Greenwich. Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so **15° = 1 hour** and **1° = 4 minutes**. Places east of Greenwich are ahead in time. **IST** is based on **82½° E**, so it is **5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT**.

cards.title: International Date Line
cards.body: Roughly along the **180° meridian**, zig-zagging to avoid land. A traveller crossing it **eastward** (from Asia towards America) sets the calendar back by one day; crossing **westward** adds a day.

cards.title: Rotation
cards.body: Earth rotates **west to east** in about 24 hours (23 h 56 min relative to the stars). Effects: day and night, the apparent east-to-west movement of the Sun, and the **Coriolis force**, which deflects winds and currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

cards.title: Revolution and seasons
cards.body: Earth orbits the Sun in about **365¼ days** with its axis tilted 23½° from the perpendicular (66½° to the orbital plane). This tilt causes seasons.
points: 21 June: Sun overhead at Tropic of Cancer — longest day in the Northern Hemisphere
22 December: Sun overhead at Tropic of Capricorn
21 March and 23 September: equinoxes — Sun overhead at the equator
Perihelion (nearest the Sun) in early January; aphelion in early July

cards.q: When it is 12 noon at Greenwich, the local time at 90° E is:
cards.explain: 90° × 4 min = 360 min = 6 hours ahead, so 6 p.m.

cards.q: The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer on about:
cards.explain: 21 June is the summer solstice for the Northern Hemisphere.

cards.q: Earth rotates through 1° of longitude in:
cards.explain: 360° in 24 hours = 1440 minutes, so 1° takes 4 minutes.

notes.h: Origin, shape and size of the Earth
notes.p:
Most scientists explain the formation of the solar system by the collapse of a rotating cloud of gas and dust; the Sun formed at the centre and planets from the surrounding disc. Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago, cooled and developed a crust, oceans and an atmosphere.

Earth is not a perfect sphere: rotation makes it bulge at the equator, so the equatorial diameter is about 43 km more than the polar diameter. The highest point is Mount Everest (about 8,849 m) and the deepest the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench (roughly 11 km).

A **latitude** is the angle north or south of the equator measured at Earth's centre; a **longitude** is the angle east or west of the Prime Meridian. Together they locate any place — New Delhi lies at about 28.6° N, 77.2° E.

The distance between parallels is nearly constant (about 111 km per degree), but the distance between meridians shrinks from about 111 km at the equator to zero at the poles. The equator is the only **great circle** among parallels; every meridian with its opposite forms a great circle.

Because Earth turns 15° each hour, local time changes by 4 minutes per degree.

**Example 1.** It is noon at Greenwich. What is the local time at 75° W?
Step 1: 75 × 4 = 300 min = 5 hours.
Step 2: West is behind, so the time is **7 a.m.**

**Example 2.** The local time at a place is 2:00 p.m. when it is 8:00 a.m. at Greenwich. Find its longitude.
Step 1: Difference = 6 hours = 360 minutes.
Step 2: 360/4 = 90°. It is ahead, so the place is at **90° E**.

India spans roughly 68° E to 97° E, about 29° or nearly 2 hours of local-time difference, which is why a single **standard time** (82½° E) is used.

notes.h: International Date Line and time zones
notes.p:
The world is divided into time zones roughly 15° wide, adjusted to political borders. At the 180° meridian, the time difference from Greenwich is 12 hours either way, so a day must change there.

The Date Line bends to keep island groups and countries on one side — for example, it swings east around some Pacific island nations. Ships and aircraft adjust their calendars when they cross it.

Rotation causes day and night, tides' daily rhythm and the Coriolis effect. Revolution, combined with the tilted axis, causes **seasons** and the changing length of days.

At the **summer solstice** (about 21 June) the North Pole tilts towards the Sun: northern days are longest and the region north of the Arctic Circle has 24-hour daylight. At the **equinoxes** day and night are nearly equal everywhere. Seasons are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere — Australia has summer in December. Seasons are caused by tilt, not by distance from the Sun: Earth is actually nearest the Sun in January.
Revise before each mock.
points: Earth: oblate spheroid; about 4.6 billion years old
Tropics 23½°; polar circles 66½°
15° = 1 hour; 1° = 4 minutes; east is ahead
IST: 82½° E = GMT + 5:30
Crossing the IDL eastward: subtract a day
21 June — Sun over Cancer; 22 Dec — Capricorn; equinoxes 21 Mar, 23 Sep
Coriolis: right in the north, left in the south

cards.title: Earth's interior
cards.body: Three layers: **crust** (thin; continental SIAL — silica + alumina; oceanic SIMA — silica + magnesium), **mantle** (thickest) and **core** (NIFE — nickel + iron), with a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. The Moho discontinuity separates crust and mantle; the Gutenberg discontinuity separates mantle and core.

cards.title: Three types of rock
points: Igneous — from cooled magma; granite (intrusive), basalt (extrusive); "primary rocks"
Sedimentary — layers of deposited material; sandstone, limestone, shale; contain fossils and coal
Metamorphic — changed by heat and pressure; limestone → marble, sandstone → quartzite, shale → slate, granite → gneiss

cards.title: Weathering
cards.body: **Weathering** breaks rocks in place. **Physical**: frost wedging in cold regions; exfoliation (onion-like peeling) in deserts with big daily temperature ranges. **Chemical**: oxidation (rusting), carbonation (dissolving limestone into caves), hydration and solution. **Biological**: roots and burrowing animals.

cards.title: Earthquakes
cards.body: The point of origin underground is the **focus (hypocentre)**; the point directly above on the surface is the **epicentre**. **P-waves** are fastest and pass through solids and liquids; **S-waves** pass only through solids; **surface waves** cause most damage. Magnitude is measured on the **Richter** scale; intensity on the **Mercalli** scale.

cards.title: Volcanoes
cards.body: Volcanoes may be **active**, **dormant** or **extinct**. Shapes: **shield** (gentle slopes, fluid basalt — Hawaii), **composite/strato** (steep, layered — Fuji, Vesuvius) and cinder cones. **Barren Island** in the Andaman Sea is India's only confirmed active volcano. About two-thirds of active volcanoes lie on the Pacific **Ring of Fire**.

cards.title: Plate tectonics
cards.body: Alfred **Wegener** proposed **continental drift** (1912): continents were once joined as **Pangaea**. Plate tectonics explains it: rigid plates move over the mantle. Collisions build fold mountains — the **Himalayas** formed as the Indian plate pushed into the Eurasian plate — and plate boundaries are the main earthquake and volcano zones.

cards.title: Landforms by agents
points: Rivers: V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, meanders, ox-bow lakes, deltas
Glaciers: U-shaped valleys, cirques, moraines
Wind: sand dunes, crescent-shaped barchans, mushroom rocks
Sea: cliffs, caves, arches, stacks, beaches
Groundwater (limestone): stalactites hang from the roof; stalagmites rise from the floor

cards.q: S-waves cannot travel through:
cards.explain: S-waves are shear waves and cannot pass through liquids; this is how the liquid outer core was detected.

cards.q: India's only confirmed active volcano is located on:
cards.explain: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is active; Narcondam is generally regarded as dormant.

cards.q: Stalactites are formed by:
options: deposition by groundwater in limestone caves, hanging from the roof
cards.explain: Dripping water deposits calcium carbonate that grows downward from cave roofs.

notes.p:
We know the interior mainly from **seismic waves**. P-waves slow down and S-waves disappear at the core boundary, showing that the outer core is liquid. Temperature and pressure rise with depth.

The **crust** is thickest under mountains and thinnest under oceans. The **mantle** contains the semi-molten **asthenosphere**, on which the rigid **lithospheric plates** move. The **core**, mostly iron and nickel, produces Earth's magnetic field through the movement of its liquid outer part.

Rocks keep changing form in the **rock cycle**: igneous rocks weather into sediments, sediments harden into sedimentary rocks, heat and pressure turn either into metamorphic rocks, and melting returns them to magma.
points: Igneous: granite (coarse crystals, cooled slowly underground); basalt (fine, cooled quickly; forms the Deccan Traps)
Sedimentary: formed in layers (strata); limestone and coal are of organic origin
Metamorphic: marble (from limestone) is used in the Taj Mahal; slate (from shale) splits into thin sheets
Most minerals of economic value are linked to particular rock types — coal in sedimentary rocks, many metallic ores in igneous and metamorphic rocks

notes.p:
**Weathering** breaks rock in place; **erosion** removes and transports the pieces by running water, wind, ice and waves. Weathering forms soil and also loosens material for landslides.

In hot deserts, rocks expand by day and contract by night until outer layers peel off (**exfoliation**). In cold mountains, water freezing in cracks expands and splits rocks (**frost action**). In humid limestone regions, rainwater containing carbon dioxide dissolves rock, forming caves, sinkholes and **karst** landscapes.

Earthquakes occur when stress along faults is released suddenly. Each whole number on the Richter scale represents about a tenfold increase in wave amplitude. India's Himalayan belt and the northeast are among its highest-risk seismic zones; check the current Bureau of Indian Standards seismic zoning map for details. Undersea earthquakes can generate **tsunamis**, like the one in December 2004.

Volcanoes erupt where magma reaches the surface — mostly at plate boundaries and some hot spots. Volcanic ash enriches soils (the black soils of the Deccan formed from basalt), but eruptions can destroy settlements and affect climate.

Each agent of erosion creates typical shapes. A **river** cuts V-shaped valleys and waterfalls in its youthful stage, winds in **meanders** in its middle course and builds **deltas** at its mouth — the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta is the world's largest. **Glaciers** carve U-shaped valleys. **Wind** shapes dunes and mushroom rocks in deserts like the Thar. **Waves** form cliffs, sea caves and stacks along coasts.
Revise before each mock.
points: Crust–mantle–core; outer core liquid
Igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (limestone, coal), metamorphic (marble, slate)
Exfoliation — deserts; carbonation — limestone caves
Focus vs epicentre; P-waves fastest; S-waves not in liquids
Richter = magnitude; Mercalli = intensity
Barren Island — India's active volcano; Ring of Fire — Pacific
Wegener — continental drift; Himalayas — Indian–Eurasian collision

cards.title: The oceans
cards.body: The **Pacific** is the largest and deepest (Mariana Trench); the **Atlantic** is second largest and S-shaped; then the **Indian**, **Southern** and **Arctic** (smallest). The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country.

cards.title: Ocean floor relief
points: Continental shelf — shallow, rich in fish and oil (e.g. Bombay High)
Continental slope — steep drop to the deep sea
Abyssal plain — flat deep-ocean floor
Mid-ocean ridges — underwater mountain chains
Trenches — deepest parts, near subduction zones

cards.title: Salinity
cards.body: Average ocean salinity is about **35 parts per thousand**. It is higher in enclosed seas of hot, dry regions with high evaporation (such as the Red Sea) and lower where rivers or melting ice add fresh water (such as the Baltic Sea).

cards.title: What drives currents
cards.body: Ocean currents are moved by **planetary winds**, differences in **temperature** and **salinity** (density), the **Coriolis force** and the shape of coastlines. **Warm currents** flow from the equator towards the poles; **cold currents** flow from the poles towards the equator.

cards.title: Currents to remember
points: Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift (warm) — keep north-west European ports ice-free
Kuroshio (warm) — off Japan
Labrador and Oyashio (cold)
Humboldt/Peru (cold) — rich fisheries; dry Atacama coast
Benguela (cold) — Namib Desert; Canaries and California (cold)

cards.title: Tides
cards.body: Tides are the rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the **Moon's gravity**, with help from the Sun. Most coasts get two high tides and two low tides in about 24 hours 50 minutes. **Spring tides** (highest) occur at **new and full moon**; **neap tides** (lowest range) at the **quarter moons**.

cards.title: El Niño
cards.body: **El Niño** is an unusual warming of the eastern Pacific off Peru. It disrupts fisheries there and is often associated with a weaker south-west monsoon in India, though not every El Niño year brings drought. La Niña is the opposite, cooler phase.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Where a warm and a cold current meet, fog forms and plankton thrive, creating rich fishing grounds — the Grand Banks off Newfoundland (Gulf Stream + Labrador) and the waters off Japan (Kuroshio + Oyashio) are classic examples.

cards.q: Spring tides occur on:
options: new moon and full moon days
cards.explain: The Sun, Moon and Earth are in line at new and full moon, so their pulls add up.

cards.q: The Humboldt (Peru) current is a:
options: cold current in the Indian Ocean
cards.explain: It is a cold current flowing north along the coast of Peru and Chile.

notes.p: Oceans cover about 71% of Earth's surface. The ocean floor has mountains, plains and trenches just like land. The **continental shelf** is the gently sloping edge of a continent under shallow sea; its width varies greatly from coast to coast, and it holds most of the world's fishing grounds and offshore oil fields, such as Bombay High. Mid-ocean ridges mark where plates move apart and new ocean floor forms; trenches mark where one plate sinks beneath another.
Surface water is warmest near the equator and coldest near the poles; temperature also falls with depth. Salinity depends on evaporation, precipitation, river inflow and freezing.
points: High salinity: Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Mediterranean (high evaporation, little river inflow)
Low salinity: Baltic Sea, polar seas (river inflow, melting ice)
Inland water bodies such as the Dead Sea are far saltier than the open ocean
Salt water is denser than fresh water, so ships float slightly higher in the sea

notes.p:
Currents move huge amounts of heat. The **Gulf Stream** and its extension, the **North Atlantic Drift**, warm the coasts of Britain and Norway so their ports stay open in winter. Cold currents cool the air above them, which then holds little moisture — this helps explain coastal deserts such as the Atacama (Humboldt current) and the Namib (Benguela current).

In the northern Indian Ocean, currents reverse direction with the **monsoon winds** — a feature unique to this ocean.

The Moon pulls the ocean on the side nearest to it; on the far side, water bulges outward too. As Earth rotates, a place passes through two bulges each day. When Sun and Moon pull together (new and full moon), **spring tides** give the greatest range; when they pull at right angles, **neap tides** give the least.

Tides help ships enter shallow harbours and river ports, flush out pollutants and can generate electricity. The Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kutch are often cited as having tidal-energy potential in India.

notes.h: El Niño, La Niña and the monsoon
notes.p: Normally, trade winds push warm water westward across the Pacific, and cold water wells up off Peru. During **El Niño** the trade winds weaken and warm water spreads east. This changes global circulation; in India, many El Niño years have seen below-normal monsoon rainfall, though other factors such as the **Indian Ocean Dipole** also matter. **La Niña** strengthens the normal pattern and is often linked to good Indian monsoons. The IMD's seasonal forecasts discuss these conditions each year.
Revise before each mock.
points: Pacific largest and deepest; Arctic smallest
Average salinity ≈ 35 ‰; Red Sea high, Baltic low
Warm currents poleward; cold currents equatorward
Gulf Stream/North Atlantic Drift — ice-free NW Europe
Cold currents → coastal deserts (Atacama, Namib)
Spring tides — new/full moon; neap — quarter moons
El Niño often linked to weak Indian monsoon

chapters.title: Geography: atmosphere, winds, rainfall & natural regions

cards.title: Layers of the atmosphere
points: Troposphere — all weather; about 8 km thick at the poles, 18 km at the equator
Stratosphere — ozone layer; calm, used by jet aircraft
Mesosphere — meteors burn up
Thermosphere (ionosphere) — reflects radio waves
Exosphere — outermost layer

cards.title: Temperature
cards.body: Temperature normally falls with height by about **6.5 °C per km** (normal lapse rate). It depends on latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents and relief. Coastal places have a moderate (maritime) climate; interiors have an extreme (continental) climate.

cards.title: Pressure belts
points: Equatorial low — the calm "doldrums"
Subtropical highs (about 30°) — "horse latitudes"
Subpolar lows (about 60°)
Polar highs
Belts shift north and south with the overhead Sun

cards.title: Planetary and local winds
cards.body: Winds blow from high to low pressure, deflected by the Coriolis force.
points: Trade winds: subtropical highs → equator (NE in the north, SE in the south)
Westerlies: 30°–60°; "Roaring Forties" in the Southern Hemisphere
Polar easterlies: from the poles
Local: Loo (hot, N India), Chinook (Rockies, "snow eater"), Foehn (Alps), Sirocco (Sahara), Mistral (cold, France), Harmattan (W Africa, "the doctor")

cards.title: Cyclones and anticyclones
cards.body: A **cyclone** is a low-pressure system with winds spiralling inward — **anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere**. Tropical cyclones are called hurricanes (Atlantic), typhoons (W Pacific) and cyclones (Indian Ocean). **Temperate cyclones** bring **western disturbances** — winter rain and snow to north-west India. **Anticyclones** are high-pressure systems with fair, dry weather.

cards.title: Humidity and precipitation
cards.body: **Relative humidity** is the moisture in air as a percentage of what it can hold at that temperature. Air cooled to its **dew point** condenses into dew, fog or clouds. Rain types: **convectional** (equatorial afternoons), **orographic** (windward side of mountains, with a **rain-shadow** on the leeward side) and **cyclonic/frontal**.

cards.title: Major natural regions
points: Equatorial — hot, wet all year; rainforests (Amazon, Congo)
Savanna — tropical grasslands (East Africa)
Hot desert — Sahara, Thar, Atacama
Mediterranean — dry summers, winter rain; grapes, citrus
Temperate grasslands — prairies, pampas, steppes, veld, downs
Taiga (coniferous forest) and tundra (mosses, lichens)

cards.q: The "Roaring Forties" are:
options: trade winds in the Northern Hemisphere
cards.explain: Strong westerlies blow between about 40° and 50° S over open ocean.

cards.q: A rain-shadow area lies on the:
cards.explain: Air descends and warms on the leeward side, so it gives little rain.

cards.q: Mediterranean regions receive most of their rain in:
cards.explain: Westerlies bring rain in winter; summers are hot and dry.

notes.p:
The atmosphere is a mixture of gases (mainly nitrogen and oxygen), water vapour and dust. Water vapour and dust are concentrated in the **troposphere**, which is why weather happens there. The **ozone layer** in the stratosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation; chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damaged it, and the **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phased them out.

The atmosphere is heated mostly from below: the Sun heats the ground, which then heats the air. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap outgoing heat — the basis of the greenhouse effect and global warming.

Unequal heating creates a pattern of pressure belts and winds. Air rises at the hot equator (low pressure), sinks near 30° (high pressure) and flows back towards the equator as the **trade winds**. From the subtropical highs, the **westerlies** blow towards the subpolar lows; from the polar highs, the **polar easterlies** blow outward.

The trade winds bring rain to the eastern sides of continents in the tropics, while the western sides near 20°–30° are dry — the location of most hot deserts. The westerlies give rain to the western sides of continents in middle latitudes, such as Britain and British Columbia.

**Tropical cyclones** form over warm seas (roughly 27 °C or more) and draw energy from water vapour. The calm centre is the **eye**. They weaken over land. In India, the Bay of Bengal sees more cyclones than the Arabian Sea, especially in the post-monsoon season, affecting Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal. Cyclone names are assigned from a list prepared by countries of the region; the IMD issues warnings.

**Temperate cyclones** form where warm and cold air masses meet along fronts. **Anticyclones** have sinking air, clear skies and light winds; winds circulate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.

Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. When air rises and cools, its relative humidity rises; at the dew point condensation begins. Forms of condensation include dew, frost, fog, mist and clouds.

**Orographic rain** explains India's rainfall pattern: the south-west monsoon gives very heavy rain on the windward Western Ghats (Mumbai, Mangaluru) but far less to the rain-shadow Deccan plateau (Pune, Bengaluru region). **Convectional rain** falls almost daily in equatorial regions in the afternoon, often with thunder. **Frontal rain** occurs in temperate cyclones.
Similar climates produce similar vegetation and ways of life, forming **natural regions**.
points: Equatorial: rubber, cocoa; dense forests; few seasons
Tropical monsoon: wet summer, dry winter — India, Myanmar, Bangladesh
Savanna: tall grass and scattered trees; large herbivores
Hot deserts: under about 25 cm of rain; oases; date palms
Mediterranean: "orchard lands" of the world — grapes, olives, citrus
Temperate grasslands: "granaries of the world" — wheat, ranching
Taiga: softwood forests for timber and paper; tundra: reindeer, permafrost

notes.p: Revise before each mock.
points: Troposphere — weather; stratosphere — ozone
Lapse rate ≈ 6.5 °C per km
Doldrums at the equator; horse latitudes near 30°
Trade winds → equator; westerlies 30°–60°
Cyclone: low pressure, anticlockwise in the NH
Rain shadow on the leeward side
Mediterranean — winter rain; prairies/pampas/steppes — temperate grasslands

chapters.title: India: natural vegetation, minerals & power resources

cards.title: Forest types of India
points: Tropical evergreen — Western Ghats, NE, Andamans; over 200 cm rain; ebony, mahogany, rosewood
Tropical deciduous (monsoon) — the most widespread; teak, sal
Thorn and scrub — Rajasthan, Gujarat; under 70 cm; acacia, babool, cactus
Montane — Himalaya; oak, deodar, pine, then alpine meadows
Mangroves — deltas; Sundarbans named after the sundari tree

cards.title: Conservation
cards.body: India protects wildlife through **national parks**, **wildlife sanctuaries** and **biosphere reserves**. **Project Tiger** began in 1973 and **Project Elephant** in 1992. For current forest-cover figures, check the latest India State of Forest Report (Forest Survey of India).

cards.title: Iron ore
cards.body: India has large reserves of high-grade **haematite** and **magnetite**. Major belts: Odisha–Jharkhand, **Bailadila** (Chhattisgarh), Ballari–Chitradurga (Karnataka), **Kudremukh** (Karnataka) and Goa. Ore is exported through ports such as Mormugao, Paradip and Visakhapatnam.

cards.title: Other important minerals
points: Manganese — Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka
Bauxite (aluminium ore) — Odisha, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Chhattisgarh
Mica — Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan; used in electrical industry
Copper — Khetri (Rajasthan), Malanjkhand (MP), Singhbhum (Jharkhand)
Gold — Hutti (Karnataka); Kolar fields were historically famous

cards.title: Coal
cards.body: Most Indian coal is **Gondwana** coal from the Damodar, Mahanadi and Godavari valleys. **Jharia** (Jharkhand) is the major coking-coal field; **Raniganj** (West Bengal) is the oldest worked field. Younger **Tertiary** coal occurs in the north-east, and **lignite** is mined at **Neyveli** (Tamil Nadu).

cards.title: Petroleum and natural gas
points: Digboi (Assam) — oil field with one of the world's oldest refineries (1901)
Mumbai High — offshore field discovered in 1974
Ankleshwar and Cambay basin — Gujarat
Krishna–Godavari basin — gas
Barmer (Rajasthan) — onshore oil

cards.title: Power resources
points: Thermal power (mainly coal) supplies the largest share
Hydro: Bhakra Nangal (Sutlej); Tehri (Bhagirathi) — India's highest dam
Nuclear: Tarapur (first, 1969), Rawatbhata, Kalpakkam, Narora, Kakrapar, Kaiga, Kudankulam
Renewables: solar (e.g. Bhadla, Rajasthan) and wind (Tamil Nadu, Gujarat) growing fast

cards.q: The Sundarbans are named after the:
cards.explain: The sundari tree is the characteristic mangrove species there.

cards.q: India's first nuclear power station was set up at:
cards.explain: Tarapur in Maharashtra began operation in 1969.

cards.q: Neyveli in Tamil Nadu is known for:
cards.explain: Neyveli has large lignite (brown coal) deposits used for power generation.

notes.p:
The type of natural vegetation depends mainly on rainfall and temperature, and also on relief and soil. **Tropical deciduous forests**, which shed leaves in the dry season, cover the largest area and provide valuable timber like teak and sal. **Evergreen forests** in the wettest regions are dense and multi-layered. In the Himalaya, vegetation changes with altitude — from tropical forest in the foothills through temperate conifers to alpine grasslands and finally snow.

**Mangroves** grow in salty, tidal coastal swamps of the Ganga–Brahmaputra, Mahanadi, Godavari and Krishna deltas and the Andamans; they protect coasts from storms and erosion.
Forests supply timber, fuel, fodder and medicines, regulate rainfall and prevent soil erosion. India's National Forest Policy aims at one-third of the geographical area under forest or tree cover.
points: National parks give the highest protection; sanctuaries allow some regulated activities
Biosphere reserves protect whole ecosystems with core and buffer zones
Project Tiger (1973) — tiger reserves across India
Project Elephant (1992)
Kaziranga (one-horned rhinoceros) and Gir (Asiatic lion) are well-known protected areas

notes.p:
Most of India's minerals occur in old crystalline rocks of the **Peninsular plateau**. The **Chota Nagpur plateau** (Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal) is the richest mineral belt, with coal, iron ore, manganese, bauxite and mica. A second belt runs through Karnataka and Goa (iron ore, manganese, gold), and a third through Rajasthan (copper, zinc, lead, marble). Petroleum is found in sedimentary basins — Assam, Gujarat, Mumbai offshore and the Krishna–Godavari basin.

State rankings in production change over time; check the Indian Bureau of Mines or Ministry of Mines for the latest figures.

Coal-based thermal plants are concentrated near coalfields (Singrauli, Korba, Talcher) or ports. **Hydroelectric** projects depend on fast-flowing rivers — the Himalaya and Western Ghats have the most potential. **Nuclear** power uses uranium, mined at Jaduguda (Jharkhand), and India plans to use its large thorium reserves in later stages of its nuclear programme.

**Renewable energy** — solar, wind, small hydro and biomass — is expanding rapidly; Rajasthan and Gujarat have large solar parks and Tamil Nadu and Gujarat lead in wind power. Check the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy for current capacity figures and targets.

Heavy industries tend to locate near raw materials: steel plants such as Jamshedpur, Rourkela, Bokaro, Bhilai and Durgapur lie in or near the coal–iron ore belt. Aluminium smelters need bauxite and cheap power (Hirakud, Renukoot). Refineries are located at ports or near oil fields (Jamnagar, Mumbai, Digboi, Barauni).
Revise before each mock.
points: Deciduous forests most widespread; evergreen in >200 cm rain
Sundarbans — sundari tree; mangroves in deltas
Project Tiger 1973; Project Elephant 1992
Iron ore: Odisha–Jharkhand, Bailadila, Kudremukh, Goa
Jharia — coking coal; Raniganj — oldest; Neyveli — lignite
Digboi — old refinery (1901); Mumbai High — offshore (1974)
Tarapur — first nuclear plant (1969); Tehri — highest dam

chapters.title: India: agriculture & industries — location and distribution

cards.title: Cropping seasons
points: Kharif — sown with the monsoon (June–July), harvested Sept–Oct: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, groundnut, soybean
Rabi — sown Oct–Dec, harvested Mar–Apr: wheat, barley, gram, mustard
Zaid — short summer season: watermelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder

cards.title: Food crops
points: Rice — needs high temperature and over 100 cm rain or irrigation; West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab among leaders
Wheat — cool growing season, 50–75 cm rain; Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh
Millets — jowar, bajra (Rajasthan), ragi (Karnataka); hardy, drought-tolerant
Pulses — gram, tur; Madhya Pradesh a major producer

cards.title: Cash and plantation crops
points: Cotton — black soil of the Deccan; Gujarat, Maharashtra
Jute ("golden fibre") — West Bengal, Assam
Sugarcane — Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra
Tea — Assam, Darjeeling, Nilgiris; well-drained hill slopes
Coffee — Karnataka; rubber and spices — Kerala

cards.title: Agricultural revolutions
points: Green Revolution (1960s) — high-yielding wheat and rice, irrigation, fertilizers; M. S. Swaminathan in India, Norman Borlaug globally
White Revolution — milk (Operation Flood, Verghese Kurien)
Blue Revolution — fisheries
Yellow Revolution — oilseeds

cards.title: What decides where industry goes
cards.body: Raw materials, power, labour, transport, markets, water, capital and government policy. Industries using heavy, weight-losing raw materials (steel, cement, sugar) locate near the raw material; light, high-value industries (electronics, IT) locate near skilled labour and markets.

cards.title: Iron and steel
points: TISCO, Jamshedpur (1907) — first large private steel plant
Bhilai (with USSR help), Rourkela (West Germany), Durgapur (UK), Bokaro (USSR)
Visakhapatnam (RINL) — coastal plant
Most plants lie in the Chota Nagpur coal–iron belt

cards.title: Other major industries
points: Cotton textiles — Mumbai ("Cottonopolis"), Ahmedabad ("Manchester of India"), Coimbatore
Jute mills — Hooghly belt near Kolkata
IT and software — Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, NCR
Automobiles — Chennai, Pune, Gurugram–Manesar

cards.q: The Bhilai steel plant was set up with the help of:
cards.explain: Bhilai (Chhattisgarh) was built with Soviet collaboration.

cards.q: Jute, called the "golden fibre", is grown mainly in:
cards.explain: West Bengal is the leading jute-growing and jute-milling state.

cards.q: TISCO was established at Jamshedpur in:
cards.explain: The Tata Iron and Steel Company was founded in 1907.

notes.p:
Agriculture employs a large share of India's workforce, though its share of GDP has fallen over the decades. Much of it still depends on the monsoon, which is why irrigation — canals in the north, tanks in the south and tube wells in many regions — is crucial. Indian farming ranges from **subsistence farming** on small holdings to **commercial** and **plantation** agriculture.

Crops are matched to climate and soil: rice in high-rainfall alluvial plains and deltas, wheat in the cooler north-west, cotton on black soil, tea on hill slopes with heavy rain and good drainage, and millets in dry regions.
Leading states change with time, so learn the main belts.
points: Rice: the Ganga plain, the eastern and southern deltas, irrigated Punjab–Haryana
Wheat: the Indo-Gangetic plain and central India
Sugarcane: Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka
Cotton: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana
Tea: Assam (Brahmaputra valley), West Bengal (Darjeeling, Dooars), Nilgiris
Coffee: Karnataka (Kodagu, Chikkamagaluru), Kerala, Tamil Nadu
For current production rankings, check the latest Ministry of Agriculture estimates

notes.p:
In the mid-1960s, India faced food shortages. **High-yielding varieties** of wheat (and later rice), together with irrigation, chemical fertilizers and pesticides, sharply increased output, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. India became self-sufficient in food grains.

The revolution had costs: regional inequality, falling water tables, soil degradation and heavy chemical use. Today the focus includes crop diversification, micro-irrigation, soil-health testing and sustainable practices. **Operation Flood** similarly transformed dairying through village co-operatives.

**Example (iron and steel).** Steel making needs iron ore, coking coal, limestone and manganese. Because several tonnes of raw material make one tonne of steel, plants are built close to the ores — Jamshedpur lies near the iron ore of Odisha–Jharkhand and the coal of Jharia, with water from the Subarnarekha.

**Example (cotton textiles).** Mumbai grew as a textile centre because of nearby cotton-growing areas, a port for importing machinery, a humid climate that suits spinning, capital and labour. Later, mills spread to cotton-growing areas such as Ahmedabad and Coimbatore.

The **IT industry** needs skilled people and good communications rather than raw materials, which explains Bengaluru's rise.

India's main industrial regions include the **Mumbai–Pune** belt, the **Hooghly** belt near Kolkata, the **Bengaluru–Chennai** region, the **Gujarat** belt (Ahmedabad–Vadodara–Surat–Jamnagar), the **Chota Nagpur** plateau, and the **NCR** around Delhi. Special Economic Zones and industrial corridors aim to spread industry more widely.
Revise before each mock.
points: Kharif — rice, cotton; rabi — wheat, gram, mustard; zaid — summer crops
Cotton — black soil; tea — hill slopes; jute — West Bengal

cards.title: Roads

cards.title: Railways
cards.body: India's first passenger train ran from **Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853**. Indian Railways is among the world's largest networks under single management. Broad gauge is 1.676 m; most lines are being converted to it. Dedicated freight corridors and high-speed rail are under development — check current status.

cards.title: Main imports
cards.body: India's largest import by value is **crude petroleum and petroleum products**. Other major imports include electronic goods, gold and precious stones, machinery, coal, chemicals, edible oils and fertilizers.

cards.title: Main exports
cards.body: Major exports include **refined petroleum products**, **engineering goods**, **gems and jewellery**, **pharmaceuticals**, textiles and garments, chemicals, rice and marine products. India is also a large exporter of **software and IT services**. For current values and top partners, check the Ministry of Commerce data.

cards.q: Which port is known as the deepest landlocked and protected port of India?
cards.explain: Visakhapatnam has a deep harbour protected by surrounding hills.

cards.explain: It ran from Bombay (Bori Bunder) to Thane on 16 April 1853.

cards.explain: NW-1 runs on the Ganga–Bhagirathi–Hooghly system from Prayagraj to Haldia.

notes.p: Transport links producers with markets, carries raw materials to factories and moves people. India's transport network includes roads, railways, waterways, airways and pipelines. Each suits different needs: roads for short distances and door-to-door delivery, railways for bulk goods and long-distance passengers, waterways for heavy and non-perishable goods, airways for speed, and pipelines for oil and gas (for example, from Gujarat ports to northern refineries).

India has one of the largest road networks in the world. National Highways form a small share of total length but carry a large share of traffic. The **Golden Quadrilateral** connects the four metros; the **North–South and East–West corridors** cross the country.

Railways carry bulk freight such as coal, iron ore, food grains, cement and fertilizers. Railway density is high in the northern plains and low in hilly, desert and forest regions. The **Konkan Railway** (along the west coast, through difficult terrain) and mountain railways such as the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway are engineering landmarks.

About 95% of India's trade by volume is often cited as moving by sea (check the latest Ministry of Ports figures). India has about a dozen **major ports** under the Central Government and many non-major ports under state governments, including large private ports such as Mundra.
points: Kandla was developed after partition to serve north-west India after Karachi went to Pakistan
Mumbai and JNPT handle much of the west coast's container traffic
Mormugao and Paradip export iron ore
Kolkata is a riverine port that needs constant dredging; Haldia was built downstream to help
Port Blair serves the Andaman and Nicobar Islands

notes.p:
Inland waterways are cheap and fuel-efficient but need navigable rivers year-round. Besides NW-1, NW-2 and NW-3, many more waterways have been declared national waterways; check the Inland Waterways Authority of India for the current list.

Air transport connects remote areas such as the north-east, Ladakh and the islands. Air India, nationalised in 1953, was returned to the Tata group in 2022. Regional connectivity schemes like **UDAN** aim to make flying affordable from smaller towns.

India's **balance of trade** in goods has usually been in deficit, mainly because of large oil and gold imports; strong exports of IT and business services help the overall balance of payments. Trade policy aims to diversify exports and partners.

Major trading partners have included the USA, China, the UAE, Saudi Arabia and the European Union, but rankings change from year to year — always check the latest official data before an exam.
Revise before each mock.

cards.title: Making of the Constitution
cards.body: The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on **26 November 1949** (now Constitution Day); it came into force on **26 January 1950** (Republic Day). Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee; Dr Rajendra Prasad was the Assembly's President.

cards.title: Preamble
cards.body: India is declared a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**. The Preamble promises Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.

cards.title: Key parts and articles
points: Part III (Art. 12–35): Fundamental Rights
Art. 32: Right to Constitutional Remedies — Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul'
Part IV (Art. 36–51): Directive Principles of State Policy
Part IV-A (Art. 51A): Fundamental Duties (added by the 42nd Amendment)
Art. 352, 356, 360: National, State (President's rule) and Financial emergencies

cards.title: Union government
cards.body: The **President** is the constitutional head and the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces; real executive power lies with the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. Parliament = President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha. The Supreme Court is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution.

cards.title: Local self-government
cards.body: The **73rd Amendment (1992)** gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj (three tiers: village, block, district) and the **74th** to urban local bodies. One-third of seats are reserved for women.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: As per the UPSC syllabus, NDA asks an 'elementary study of the Indian Constitution'. NCERT Class 9 Civics and Class 11 'Indian Constitution at Work' are enough. Memorise article numbers only for the top 15–20 articles.

cards.q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by the:
cards.explain: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Part IV-A, Article 51A, on Fundamental Duties.

cards.q: Who is the Supreme Commander of India's Armed Forces?
cards.explain: Article 53 vests the supreme command of the Defence Forces in the President.

cards.q: Which Article provides the Right to Constitutional Remedies?
cards.explain: Article 32 lets citizens move the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights.

notes.p:
The **Constituent Assembly** first met on **9 December 1946**. **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was its President and **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** chaired the **Drafting Committee**. The Constitution was adopted on **26 November 1949** (celebrated as Constitution Day) and came into force on **26 January 1950** (Republic Day), the anniversary of the 1930 Purna Swaraj celebration.

The **Preamble** declares India a **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic**. "Socialist", "Secular" and "Integrity" were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**. Article 1 says "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."

Borrowed features (a favourite question): parliamentary system and rule of law — **UK**; Fundamental Rights and judicial review — **USA**; Directive Principles — **Ireland**; federation with a strong centre — **Canada**; Concurrent List — **Australia**; suspension of rights during emergency — **Germany (Weimar)**.
**Fundamental Rights** are in **Part III (Articles 12–35)** and are enforceable in court. There are six:
points: Right to Equality (Arts 14–18) — Art 17 abolishes untouchability
Right to Freedom (Arts 19–22) — Art 21: life and personal liberty; Art 21A: education for ages 6–14 (86th Amendment, 2002)
Right against Exploitation (Arts 23–24)
Right to Freedom of Religion (Arts 25–28)
Cultural and Educational Rights (Arts 29–30)
Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art 32) — Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution
Right to Property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment (1978); it is now a legal right under Art 300A

notes.p:
**Directive Principles of State Policy** (Part IV, Articles 36–51) are guidelines for the government — such as equal pay for equal work and a uniform civil code — but they are **not enforceable** in court.

**Fundamental Duties** (Part IVA, **Article 51A**) were added by the 42nd Amendment on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. There are now **11** — the eleventh, about providing education opportunities to children aged 6–14, was added by the 86th Amendment.

**President (Art 52):** elected by an electoral college of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the state Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry). Minimum age 35, term five years; removed by impeachment (Art 61). The **Vice-President** is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

**Prime Minister and Council of Ministers:** collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha** (Art 75).

**Parliament:** the Lok Sabha currently has **543** elected seats; the Rajya Sabha can have up to **250** members (238 elected, 12 nominated), is a permanent House, and one-third of its members retire every two years. A **Money Bill** (Art 110) can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Speaker certifies it. A **joint sitting** (Art 108) is presided over by the Speaker.

**Judiciary:** Supreme Court under Art 124. Writs can be issued by the Supreme Court (Art 32) and High Courts (Art 226): **habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto**. The **basic structure doctrine** comes from the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).
Know these article numbers cold:
points: Art 352 National Emergency; Art 356 President's Rule; Art 360 Financial Emergency (never imposed so far)
Art 368 — amendment of the Constitution
Art 324 Election Commission; Art 148 CAG; Art 76 Attorney General; Art 280 Finance Commission; Art 315 UPSC
73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) — panchayats and municipalities
61st Amendment — voting age lowered from 21 to 18
Tenth Schedule — anti-defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985); Seventh Schedule — Union, State and Concurrent Lists

notes.p: Article numbers are the easiest marks in polity — drill them.
points: Adopted 26 Nov 1949; in force 26 Jan 1950
42nd Amendment: socialist, secular, integrity; Fundamental Duties
Six Fundamental Rights; Art 32 = constitutional remedies
DPSP from Ireland; not justiciable
Money Bill only in Lok Sabha (Art 110)
Five writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto
