chapters.title: Polity: Union & State government and administration

cards.title: The President
cards.body: Elected **indirectly** by an electoral college of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the state Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry). Term five years; minimum age 35. Removed by **impeachment** (Article 61). Supreme Commander of the armed forces; can issue **ordinances** (Article 123) and grant **pardons** (Article 72).

cards.title: Vice-President and Prime Minister
cards.body: The **Vice-President** is elected by members of both Houses and is the ex-officio **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**. The **Prime Minister** heads the Council of Ministers, which is **collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha**. The 91st Amendment limits the Council's size to 15% of the Lok Sabha's strength.

cards.title: Parliament
cards.body: Parliament = President + **Lok Sabha** + **Rajya Sabha**.
points: Lok Sabha: directly elected; five-year term unless dissolved; presided over by the Speaker
Rajya Sabha: permanent body; one-third of members retire every two years; up to 12 nominated members
Money Bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha (Article 110); the Speaker certifies them
Joint sitting to resolve deadlock: Article 108, presided over by the Speaker

cards.title: The judiciary
cards.body: The **Supreme Court** (Article 124) has original, appellate and advisory (Article 143) jurisdiction and issues writs under **Article 32**; **High Courts** issue writs under **Article 226**. Supreme Court judges retire at 65 and High Court judges at 62. Judges can be removed only by Parliament through a special majority.

cards.title: State government
cards.body: The **Governor** is appointed by the President (Article 155) for a five-year term, held at the President's pleasure. The **Chief Minister** heads the state Council of Ministers, responsible to the Legislative Assembly. Only a few states have a Legislative Council (bicameral legislature) — check the current list.

cards.title: Constitutional bodies
points: Election Commission — Article 324
Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) — Article 148
Union Public Service Commission — Article 315
Finance Commission — Article 280
Attorney General — Article 76

cards.title: Administration
cards.body: **All India Services** (IAS, IPS, Indian Forest Service) serve both Centre and states (Article 312). The **Cabinet Secretary** is the senior-most civil servant. In a district, the **District Collector/Magistrate** coordinates administration, revenue and law and order.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Article numbers are asked often. Learn a short core list — 14, 19, 21, 32, 72, 110, 123, 226, 280, 324, 352, 356, 360, 368 — with one line each, and revise it weekly.

cards.q: A Money Bill can be introduced in:
cards.explain: Article 110 and Article 109 provide that Money Bills originate only in the Lok Sabha.

cards.q: The ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is the:
cards.explain: The Vice-President presides over the Rajya Sabha.

notes.p:
India has a **parliamentary system**: the President is the constitutional head, but real executive power lies with the **Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister** (Article 74 — the President acts on their advice). The President appoints the PM, usually the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha, and other ministers on the PM's advice.

The President's powers include summoning and proroguing Parliament, dissolving the Lok Sabha, assenting to bills, appointing governors and judges, and declaring emergencies on the Cabinet's written advice. In a vacancy, the Vice-President acts as President.
An ordinary bill passes through three readings in each House and then goes to the President, who may assent, withhold assent or (except for Money Bills) return it once for reconsideration.
points: Lok Sabha: up to 550 elected members under Article 81; currently 543 constituencies
Rajya Sabha: up to 250 members — 238 elected by state and UT legislatures and 12 nominated for expertise in literature, science, art and social service
The Lok Sabha controls finance: the Rajya Sabha can only delay a Money Bill by 14 days
No-confidence motions can be moved only in the Lok Sabha
Constitutional amendments follow Article 368 and need special majorities in both Houses

notes.p:
India has a single integrated judiciary: the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in the states, and subordinate courts below. The Supreme Court is the guardian of the Constitution and of Fundamental Rights; through **judicial review** it can strike down laws that violate the Constitution. Its advisory opinion can be sought by the President under Article 143.

The **five writs** — habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto — protect rights. High Courts can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for other legal rights, so their writ jurisdiction is wider.

States mirror the Union: the **Governor** is the constitutional head; the **Chief Minister** and Council of Ministers hold real power. The Governor can reserve certain bills for the President's consideration and reports to the President when constitutional machinery fails (leading to **President's Rule**, Article 356).

Below the state, districts are the key unit of administration. Panchayati Raj institutions (73rd Amendment) and urban local bodies (74th Amendment) handle local governance.
Constitutional bodies are created by the Constitution itself; statutory bodies by an Act of Parliament.
points: Election Commission conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President
CAG audits government accounts — "guardian of the public purse"
UPSC recruits for All India and Central services, including the NDA examination
Finance Commission is constituted every five years
Statutory examples: National Human Rights Commission, National Green Tribunal

notes.p: Revise before each mock.

cards.title: What NDA asks
cards.body: As per the UPSC syllabus, current events are about 40 marks in GAT: important recent events in India and the world, prominent personalities, awards, sports, defence exercises, appointments, summits and schemes. Most questions cover the 6–12 months before the exam.

cards.title: Use trusted, free sources
cards.body: Read one national newspaper daily. For official facts use the **Press Information Bureau (pib.gov.in)** — every government scheme, appointment and defence press release appears there. Ministry of Defence releases cover military exercises and inductions.

cards.title: Make topic-wise notes, not date-wise
cards.body: Keep separate pages for: defence (exercises, inductions, missions), awards, sports, international summits, schemes, science & space, and appointments. Topic-wise notes are much easier to revise than a daily diary.

cards.title: Linking static with current
cards.body: If a news item mentions a joint military exercise with a country, also note that country's capital and where the exercise was held. One news item then gives you 2–3 possible questions.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Revise your notes every weekend and do one monthly compilation quiz. In the last month, focus on the previous 8–10 months only — older events are rarely asked.

cards.q: Which official source publishes Government of India press releases?
cards.explain: The Press Information Bureau (pib.gov.in) is the government's official source for press releases.

cards.q: The most effective way to organise current affairs notes is:
options: Memorising one magazine cover to cover
cards.explain: Topic-wise notes group related facts together and make revision faster.

notes.p:
As per the UPSC syllabus, current events carry around **40 marks** in the GAT's General Knowledge part. Questions usually come from the **6–12 months before the exam**: national and international events, prominent personalities, awards, sports, defence exercises and inductions, appointments, summits, government schemes, and science and space missions.

The good news: current affairs reward **consistency, not intelligence**. Thirty focused minutes a day beat a frantic week of cramming. Because exact facts change constantly, always confirm them from official sources rather than forwarded messages or social media.
Keep sources few and reliable:
points: One national newspaper daily — read for 30–40 minutes, skipping political gossip
Press Information Bureau (pib.gov.in) for official releases: schemes, appointments, defence
Ministry of Defence and PIB Defence wing for exercises, inductions and missions
ISRO's website for space missions
One monthly compilation for revision — not five

notes.p:
Write **topic-wise**, not date-wise. Keep separate pages (or digital notes) for: defence, awards, sports, summits and organisations, schemes, science and space, appointments, and important days. Under each item write only the testable core: **who, what, where, when** — for example, the name of a joint exercise, the partner country, the location and the edition.

**Link static with current.** If you note a joint military exercise with a country, also note that country's capital and currency, and where the exercise was held. If a new scheme is launched, note the ministry. One news item then prepares you for two or three possible questions.

**Monday to Saturday:** 30–40 minutes of newspaper reading plus 10 minutes adding items to topic pages. **Sunday:** revise all topic pages for the week and attempt one 25-question quiz. **Month-end:** go through a monthly compilation to fill gaps.

**Last month before the exam:** stop collecting new sources. Revise the previous **8–10 months** of your notes two or three times and practise previous years' GK papers to understand the level.

Many aspirants collect huge amounts of material and revise none of it. Others memorise numbers (budget figures, rankings) that are rarely asked in NDA or change quickly. Avoid both. Focus on **names, places, firsts and defence-related news**, which repeat most often. If a question asks about a recent figure you haven't verified, remember the negative marking — skip a pure guess.

notes.h: Worked example: one news item, many questions
notes.p:
Suppose you read that India held a joint army exercise with a neighbouring country. Don't just note the exercise name. Write a compact entry:

**Exercise:** name, edition, partner country, location, dates.
**Static links:** partner's capital and currency; the Indian Army command or regiment involved, if mentioned; earlier editions' venues.
**Possible questions:** "Exercise X is held between India and which country?", "Where was the latest edition held?", "What is the capital of the partner country?"

Do the same for awards (who, which field, which year), sports (event, venue, Indian medal winners) and appointments (post, person, predecessor if known). Ten such entries a week add up to hundreds of revision-ready facts by exam time — always verified from official sources.
Check yourself against this list each week.
points: About 40 marks of current events in GAT (per syllabus)
Focus on the last 6–12 months
PIB and one newspaper are enough
Topic-wise notes: who, what, where, when
Link every news item to static facts
Weekly revision + monthly compilation
Always confirm changing facts from official sources

cards.title: Defence structure
cards.body: The **President** is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. The post of **Chief of Defence Staff (CDS)** was created with the first CDS, General Bipin Rawat, taking office on 1 January 2020; the CDS heads the Department of Military Affairs. Check official sources for current service chiefs.

cards.title: Tracking personalities and events
cards.body: For each news item record: **who**, **what**, **where**, **why it matters**, and the **static link** (an article, a place on the map, an institution). Confirm names and figures from official sources such as PIB, ministry websites and the official sites of sporting bodies before revising them.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: NDA questions on current events usually test well-established facts behind the news: which country a joint exercise is with, which award is the highest, which trophy belongs to which sport. Build these static tables first; then add the year's news on top.

cards.q: The Air Force rank equivalent to an Army Major is:
cards.explain: Major = Lieutenant Commander (Navy) = Squadron Leader (Air Force).

cards.q: Navy Day in India is observed on:
cards.explain: 4 December commemorates the Navy's attack on Karachi (Operation Trident) in 1971.

notes.p:
Current events in the GAT cover India and the world over roughly the past year, including prominent personalities in culture and sport. Because the news changes every year, many candidates find this section unpredictable. The way to reduce that uncertainty is to build **static anchors** — stable facts that keep reappearing — and attach fresh news to them.

For example, if a joint exercise is held, the stable facts are the partner country and the service involved; if an award is announced, the stable facts are the award's rank and field.

notes.p:
Gallantry awards are announced mainly on Independence Day and Republic Day. **Param Vir Chakra** is the highest wartime gallantry award and **Ashoka Chakra** the highest peacetime one. The **Bharat Ratna** is India's highest civilian honour; Padma awards are announced on the eve of Republic Day.

Other well-known awards include the **Jnanpith** (literature), the **Dadasaheb Phalke Award** (cinema), and international prizes such as the Nobel Prizes and the Ramon Magsaysay Award. When a new winner is announced, note the name, field and any "first" — for example, the first woman or the first from a particular state.

Learn the stable facts first: trophies and their sports, terms used in each game, the number of players, and the venues and frequency of major events (the Olympics and Commonwealth Games every four years, the Asian Games every four years).

For the current year, track India's medal tallies, notable records, first-time achievements and major hosts of upcoming events. Use official sources such as the Sports Authority of India, the IOC and federation websites to confirm names and results.

Step 1: Each day, read one national newspaper and note five items under fixed headings — Defence, Polity, Economy, International, Science, Sports, Awards, Personalities.
Step 2: For each item, write the static link in one line.
Step 3: At the weekend, revise the week's notes and attempt 20 questions.
Step 4: Every month, make a one-page summary per heading and discard trivial items.
Step 5: In the last month before the exam, revise only the monthly summaries and static tables.
Revise before each mock.

cards.title: Sectors of the economy
points: Primary — agriculture, fishing, mining (uses natural resources directly)
Secondary — manufacturing, construction, electricity
Tertiary — services: trade, transport, banking, IT
The services sector contributes the largest share of India's GDP

cards.title: National income terms
points: GDP — value of final goods and services produced within the country in a year
GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad
NNP = GNP − depreciation
Per capita income = national income ÷ population
Real GDP removes the effect of price changes

cards.title: Inflation
cards.body: **Inflation** is a sustained rise in the general price level. In India it is measured mainly by the **Consumer Price Index (CPI)** and the **Wholesale Price Index (WPI)**. The RBI's monetary policy targets CPI inflation. Deflation is a fall in the general price level.

cards.title: RBI and monetary policy
cards.body: The **Reserve Bank of India** (established 1935, nationalised 1949) issues currency, regulates banks and controls money supply. Its **Monetary Policy Committee** sets the **repo rate** — the rate at which the RBI lends to banks. Raising it makes loans costlier and helps control inflation.

cards.title: Budget and taxes
cards.body: The Union Budget is the **Annual Financial Statement** (Article 112). **Direct taxes** (income tax, corporate tax) are paid by those on whom they fall; **indirect taxes** (GST, customs) are passed on to consumers. **GST** came into force on **1 July 2017**, replacing many indirect taxes.

cards.title: Economic reforms of 1991
cards.body: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis, India began **LPG reforms** in 1991 — **Liberalisation** (fewer licences and controls), **Privatisation** (greater private role) and **Globalisation** (opening to trade and foreign investment). The industrial licensing ("licence raj") system was largely dismantled.

cards.title: Banking milestones
points: 14 major banks nationalised in 1969; six more in 1980
NABARD (1982) — rural credit
SEBI — regulates securities markets (statutory status 1992)
Jan Dhan Yojana (2014) — basic bank accounts for all

cards.title: Poverty and unemployment
cards.body: **Poverty** is measured against a poverty line or with multidimensional indicators of health, education and living standards. **Disguised unemployment**, common in agriculture, means more people work than are needed. **Seasonal** and **structural** unemployment are other forms. Check the latest NITI Aayog and NSO reports for current estimates.

cards.q: GST was introduced in India on:
cards.explain: GST came into force on 1 July 2017.

cards.q: An increase in the repo rate by the RBI generally:
options: makes borrowing costlier and helps control inflation
cards.explain: A higher repo rate raises banks' cost of funds, so lending rates rise and demand cools.

notes.p:
An economy is often divided into three sectors. Over time, as countries develop, the share of the **primary sector** in output falls and the shares of **industry** and **services** rise. In India, services now contribute the largest share of GDP, while agriculture still employs a large share of the workforce — which is why raising farm productivity and creating non-farm jobs are central policy aims.

India has a **mixed economy**: both public and private sectors operate, with the government regulating markets and providing public goods.

**GDP** counts the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year; intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting. **GNP** adds income earned by citizens abroad and subtracts income earned by foreigners in the country. **NNP** subtracts depreciation (wear and tear of capital).

**Example.** If GDP is ₹200 lakh crore, net factor income from abroad is −₹2 lakh crore and depreciation is ₹20 lakh crore, then GNP = 198 and NNP = 178 lakh crore. (These are illustrative numbers only.)

The **National Statistical Office (NSO)** publishes official estimates.

Moderate inflation is normal in a growing economy, but high inflation hurts people on fixed incomes and the poor. Causes include excess demand (**demand-pull**) and rising costs such as fuel (**cost-push**).

The RBI uses tools such as the repo rate, reverse repo, cash reserve ratio (CRR) and statutory liquidity ratio (SLR). Under the flexible inflation-targeting framework, the government sets a CPI inflation target for the RBI (check the current target and band). Commercial banks accept deposits and give loans; **financial inclusion** schemes aim to bring every household into the banking system.
The government earns **revenue** from taxes and non-tax sources (dividends, fees) and spends on defence, subsidies, interest, salaries and development.

notes.p:
The **1991 reforms** cut import duties, removed most industrial licensing, allowed more foreign investment and began disinvestment of public sector units. Growth accelerated in the following decades, though challenges of jobs, inequality and rural distress remain.

Development is measured not only by income but by health, education and living standards — for example, the UNDP's **Human Development Index (HDI)** combines life expectancy, education and per capita income. Check the latest Economic Survey for current data.
Revise before each mock.
